CHAPTER-IV
POLICE FORCES
Central Police Forces
4.1 There are seven CPFs under the Ministry of Home Affairs, namely Assam Rifles (AR),
Border Security Force (BSF), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), Central Reserve Police
Force (CRPF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), National Security Guard (NSG) and Sashastra
Seema Bal (SSB). AR, BSF, ITBP and SSB are the border guarding forces while CRPF assists the
States in matters related to law and order and is trained and equipped for internal security
management. The Rapid Action Force (RAF) and Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (CoBRA)
are specialized wings of the CRPF to deal with riots and left wing militancy respectively. CISF
provides security and protection to vital installations, Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), Important
Private Sector Industries and Establishments, airports, industrial buildings, museums and
Government buildings. NSG is a specialized force for counter-terrorism and anti-hijacking
operations. It is also entrusted with the task of securing high risk VIPs.
4.1.1 The Committee took note of a newspaper report stating about 45,000 officers, staff
deserting Central Forces. The Chairman of the Committee raised the issue before the Home
Secretary in the meeting of the Committee held on 28
th March and 4 th April, 2012. The Home
Secretary submitted as under:-
...This news is entirely incorrectly headlined. There has been no general desertion. What has
happened and what happens every year is that there are certain number of voluntary
retirements which one can apply for and get after 20 years of service and some resignations.
The total number of voluntary retirements and resignations over a period of five years,
comes to about 50,000 for all the forces taken together. The total strength of the Forces
which we have is about 9 lakh. About 50,000 in five years means about 10,000 per year.
V oluntary retirement is a preference. It is not something about somebody wanting to go away
in between. Resignations are purely because people have got better jobs and they are better
educated and manage to get better jobs. Some of them also resign for family and personal
reasons. But the voluntary retirements are 43 to 45 thousand odd and resignations are about
five thousand odd. Now, this is over a five year period. So, the number of resignations over
the entire period in one year in all the forces is about 1000 only and voluntary retirement
is for, say, nine thousand per year. So, the percentage comes to just 1.13 per cent. It is,
in fact, lesser than the separations which one finds today in public sector undertaking,
private sector undertakings. So, this is something which has been incorrectly presented in
the news report. The percentages are not only normal but even they are less than normal.
We have total retirement of about 3.3 per cent per year.
4.1.2 Explaining about the reasons, the Home Secretary submitted as under:–
…The reasons for these are two, mainly one. We have been expanding at a rapid pace.
Every year we have been sanctioning new raising in the forces to provide for the increased
number of the BOPs etc. and to provide for our increased requirements for internal security
duties. Every year, in every force, we raise about five to six new battalions. Over the past
three years, we have raised 51 battalions.

lakh, 30 thousand vacancies would be on account of that. So, that is a normal vacancy

thousand posts for constables (GD) and we may manage to get about 70 thousand people.

4.1.18 The Ministry in response thereto made the following submissions:–

transfer policy has been laid out which ensures the movement of Force personnel
between the hard and static/soft postings. The policy has been drawn keeping in mind
the family obligations of the jawans in addition to the Force requirements. Since CRPF
is not a border guarding force, there is no fixed location/point of duty, but the same
changes as per the internal security situation in various parts of the country as well
as the request made by various State Governments/UT administrations as per
developing security scenarios.

7 Company in a Battalion as a training Company was to give proper rest and

to vacancy and administrative convenience as per the following guidelines:–
a. CRPF formations/institutions/units have been categorized as “Peace” and “Field”
stations for regulating the transfer of the Force personnel.
b. After completion of 8 years field service in case of male; and 4 years field service
in case of female, after basic training, the force personnel are eligible for first
peace station/static posting. Subsequent peace station/static posting can be/is done
after completion of a total of 8 years field service from the completion of last
static posting.
c. For posting to a peace station/static location, preference is given to those having
longest service in the field Battalions.
d. Normal stay of posting in a Group Centre/static institution/peace station is 4
years. This may be extended upto 5 years only in case of training staff posted
in training institution as a special case.
e. After deployment of the Force personnel in the hard areas, like Left Wing
Extremism affected areas, they are generally posted to static postings. Such
jawans are also asked to give their preference of posting on leaving the LWE
areas out of the five options, namely Rapid Action Force/ Duty Battalions/ Group
Centre/Training Institution/Deputation.
f. Personnel having good record of service and free from disciplinary and vigilance
angle, may be posted to near their home towns, 2 years before attaining the age
of superannuation, subject to availability of vacancies.
g. In order to maintain continuity at a place, a maximum of 25% of the strength is
moved every year from one operational theatre to another within a sector.
• In order to keep the Force personnel in their cultural milieu as also for effective and
better utilization, a maximum of 50% of the total personnel posted in a place are from
the local area. In case of other Forces like BSF, as far as possible, recruit Constables
on completion of their basic training are posted to their Frontiers located near their
home states, depending upon the vacancy position.
• Therefore, all efforts are made to help the Force personnel live with their families
intermittently during the static postings /peace stations. The tenure of such peace
postings has been earmarked as 4 years after due consultation with the Force
personnel as also keeping in mind the general good of the maximum number of Force
personnel in CRPF.

4.2.19 The Committee is concerned over the fact that there are large number of complaints
for not registering FIRs by the Police Personnel at the Police Stations in Delhi. The
Committee apprehends that actual figures may be bigger than the number of complaints
came to light since most of the people especially poor and illiterate ones might have
returned without lodging their complaints which have not been reflected in the figures
during the year 2010, 2011 and 2012. The Committee recommends that there should be a
separate cell of Delhi Police for registering such complaints where representatives of NGOs,
local bodies etc. may be involved so that people trying to lodge such complaints would do
it. The Committee is of the opinion that non-registering of FIR complaint by police
personnel should be viewed as dereliction of duty as well as unbecoming of the police

against Delhi Police. The Committee is exasperated over the fact that although 877 and 941
such complaints were registered against non-registering of complaints in 2010 and 2011
respectively, however, only 33 and 46 cases were found to be genuine. The Committee is of
the considered view that stringent action is required to be taken against the concerned
officers for non registering of FIRs.

stations are functioning without regular buildings. It is very unfortunate that in the Capital
city of the country, the police stations are functioning without regular buildings. The
Committee recommends that the Government should take immediate steps to provide
regular buildings to these 72 police stations at the earliest.

view that prevention of crime against women should be a priority issue of the Delhi Police.

non-cooperating attitude of police personnel in Delhi. In view of this, the Committee
recommends that more and more women officers should be employed at lower as well as
higher level in Delhi Police so that female victims would approach them without hesitation.
4.2.22 The Committee takes note of the fact that the figures given by Delhi Police do not
match the cases reported in media about rape and molestation. Stringent action should be
taken against the culprits involved in harassing girls. The Committee understands that
merely counting the number of incidents does not justify the general perception. The
Committee believes that a mass campaign should be organised by Delhi Police against such
incidents.

MODERNIZATION OF ST ATE POLICE FORCES (MPF)
4.3 The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for Modernization
of State police forces since 1969-70 to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in
modernizing their police forces. The Scheme provides assistance to the State Governments, as 50%
grant-in-aid and 50% loans for purchase of vehicles, equipment for forensic science labs, finger
print bureau, police training, weaponry, construction of housing for police personnel, police
stations, training buildings etc. An equal matching contribution was expected from the State
Governments.
4.3.1 The main objective of the scheme is to meet the identified deficiencies in various aspects
of police administration, worked out in 2000 by the Bureau of Police Research and Development
(BPR&D) in a study, according to which a requirement of about Rs.25,000 crore, was needed for
the purpose. Another objective of the scheme is to reduce the dependence of the State
Governments on the Army and Central Para Military Forces to control internal security and the law
and order situation. The above non-Plan Scheme has been under implementation in States since
1969-70 on a cost sharing (50:50) basis.
4.3.2 The Ministry has submitted that the Annual Action Plans under the MPF Scheme are
formulated by States based on the available Central allocations and also depending on the assessed
requirements of State police forces. The naxal affected States have, inter-alia, made provisions for
items such as troop carriers, motor cycles, modern weaponry, BP vehicles, mine-protected
vehicles, BP jackets and helmets, BP patkas, BP morchas, night vision equipment etc. in their MPF
Annual Action Plans for 2011-12, based on their requirements.
4.3.3 The Ministry was asked about State/UT-wise budget allocation so as to help them
modernizing their police forces and whether these allocations were according to the demands of

the Committee in its sitting held on 4
th April, 2012, the Home Secretary submitted as under:–
“After the last five-year plan of modernisation of State police force expired, we had
proposed an extension for another five years. This extension is still under consideration in
consultation with the Ministry of Finance. We have had discussions with the Ministry of
Finance. All those discussions have reached a certain stage. In the meantime, till that
scheme was finalised, they extended it for one year, that is, for the last year and now again,
they have extended it for this year. They have made an interim provision of Rs.900 crore.
I agree that it is not sufficient for the requirements which are there and we have been
saying that we need much more funds. We have conveyed this to the Ministry of Finance
as well as to the Planning Commission. I am quite sure that when the scheme is sanctioned,
we will get more funds. So, the provision of Rs.900 crore is an interim provision. This is
not the final provision. I am quite sanguine; I am quite confident that when the scheme
is sanctioned, the provision will be much more because much more is required. I do believe
that. In fact, when we started off in the year 2000, the provision was Rs.1,000 crores. So,
Rs.900 crore for this year is absolutely inadequate, as far as the modernisation of State
police force is concerned. It is under funded, and, I think, the Committee can make a
recommendation.”

4.3.13 Du ring the oral evidence of the Home Secretary before the Committee, one Member raised
the issue of Policemen not doing shooting/firing practices in the States. The Ministry in its written
reply has submitted that Police being a State subject as per the Seventh Schedule to the
Constitution of India, the question relating to lesser or no firing practice by State police personnel
is not within the purview of Central Government. The Home Ministry has further submitted that
the Central Government, however, provides funds to the States under the Scheme for
Modernization of State Police Forces (MPF Scheme) to help them upgrade the equipment,
weaponry, mobility, security gadgets, etc. The Ministry apprised that as far as Central Armed Police
Forces are concerned, the police personnel regularly undergo fire practice except BSF which is
having some problem in terms of availability of long firing ranges.
4.3.14  During the oral evidence of the Home Secretary before the Committee on 4 th April, 2012,
a Member of the Committee raised the issue of obsolete weapons being produced by the ordinace
factories and used by the police forces. The Home Secretary while replying made following
observations:–
“As far as weapons are concerned, there are two categories. The first one is SLR (Self
Loading Rifles), INSAS Rifle, etc., which are the basic weapon for the infantry in the
Army as well as for our CPMFs. Apart from this, there is special equipment. The
special equipment is something which we buy on a global tender basis. So, we are
buying MP3, MP5 Sub-Machine Guns through the process of global tender. We buy
pistols and we also buy Glock Pistols through open tender. The MP3, MP5 and Glock
Pistols are not only for NSG but are also meant for all our forces. We are buying semi-
automatic weapons from Beretta through global tender. So, it is not that we are
depending only on the Ordinance Factories for our specialized weapons. As far as
INSAS Rifle is concerned, today, there may be better rifles. I cannot say INSAS is the
most modern; it is not. There will be more modern weapons. When we find that our
objectives are not served by INSAS Rifle, we will then think about switching over and
go in for global tender. But, basically, when something is being manufactured in our
country, in a facility which is owned by the Government and if it is something which
meets our requirements, we would rather buy it from within the country than importing
the same. Giving ammunition to the State Police Force is something which we can
propose. But, I can virtually guarantee that the Ministry of Finance will not agree. I
can guarantee. But, nonetheless, I will try to include it as one of the items under the
MPF Scheme. In fact, Sir, when we want to include, along with the procurement of
weapons under MPF , we said that you also allow procurement of some ammunition to
go with the equipment. So, after a lot of discussion, it was allowed. But, for revenue
expenditure, the Ministry of Finance is very, very reluctant to sanction any funds for
revenue expenditure under the MPF Scheme. But, we shall try to do it.”
4.3.15 The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the BE provision for the financial
year 2011-12 under the Scheme for Modernization of State Police Forces (MPF) of Rs.1111
crore was reduced to Rs.800 crore at RE 2011-12 stage and again in the BE 2012-13 pr ovision
for the scheme is Rs. 900 crore. The Committee feels that this lesser budgetary provision
is bound to affect modernization of State police forces. The Ministry apprised the Committee
that the funds are inadequate and they would move for additional funds at RE stage. The
Committee strongly recommends that additional funds sought by the Ministry should be
allocated at RE 2010-11 stage for modernization of State police forces, which is sin quo non
for internal security.

74
4.3.16 The Committee understands that this police modernization scheme plays an
important role in modernizing the police forces of States/UTs. In view of this, the
earmarked provision for the scheme must be utilized fully and optimally by the concerned
States/UTs. The Committee suggests that the State/UT Governments should submit
utilization Certificates in time so that they could avail of the funds from the Centre under
the scheme. The Committee is unhappy to note that States/UTs have unspent balances of
Rs.47.83 crore for 2008-09 and Rs.194.76 crore for 2009-10 lying with them. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up this matter at Chief
Ministers’ level to impress upon the State Governments to fully utilize the fund under the
scheme in a time bound manner.
4.3.17 The Committee notes the details of State-wise sanctioned and actual strength of total
police force and the police population ratio and expresses its displeasure over the fact that
some States are having vacancies of even more than 50%. The Committee recommends that
the Ministry of Home Affairs should impress upon the State Governments for filling up
vacancies at the earliest. The Committee desires that the Ministry of Home Affairs should
link this issue with provision under scheme of Modernization Police Forces (MPF) and the
fund for States lagging in filling vacancies may be deducted.
4.3.18 The Committee agrees that Police being a State subject as per the Seventh Schedule
to the Constitution of India, the question relating to lesser or no firing practice by State
police personnel is not within the purview of Central Government. However, the Committee
desires that the Ministry of Home Affairs may issue an advisory suggesting all the State/
UT Governments to make their police force personnel undergo fire practices at regular
intervals as in the case of CPFs personnel.
4.3.19 The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should impress upon the States
to procure high-end weapons which could be from Indian Ordinance Factories or from other
resources. The Committee desires that the Home Ministry should place its requirements of
modern weaponry before Defence Ministry which could help improve products of Indian
ordinance factories. The Committee understands that in addition to modern training
facilities to State police forces, they should also be provided with modern arms,
ammunitions, equipment, surveillance devices, better communications facilities, etc.

4.5.5 The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India vide its judgement dated 22.09.2006 in Writ Petition
(Civil) No.310 of 1996 – Prakash Singh and others vs UOI had issued several directions to the
States, UTs and the Central Government on Police Reforms. One of these directions pertains to
separation of investigating police from law and order police. The Ministry was asked whether it has
plan to separate the investigating and law and order function. The Ministry has replied that a copy
of Supreme Court judgment was sent to all State Governments for consideration and appropriate
action. According to the Ministry, vide its subsequent order dated 16.5.2008, the Hon’ble Supreme
Court constituted a Committee under the chairmanship of Shri Justice K.T. Thomas, retired Judge
of Supreme Court, inter alia , to examine the affidavits filed by different States in compliance to
the Court’s directions. The Ministry has further informed that the Terms of Reference for the
Committee, inter-alia, included to examine the affidavits filed by the different States and the Union
Territories in compliance to the Court’s directions with reference to the ground realities; advise the
Respondents wherever the implementation is falling short of the Court’s orders, after considering
the Respondents’ stated difficulties in implementation; bring to the notice of the Court any genuine
problems the Respondents may be having in view of the specific conditions prevailing in a State
or Union Territory etc. The Ministry has further informed that the Committee has submitted its
report to the Hon’ble Supreme Court and a copy of the report has been circulated to all States/
UTs by the Registry of Supreme Court on 4.10.2010. The Hon’ble Court is now examining the
status of implementation of its directions. As per this report a number of States have taken steps

84
to implement this direction of the Supreme Court either through executive orders or through their
respective Police Acts.
4.5.6 According to the Ministry, various Committees/Commissions on Police Reforms, i.e., the
National Police Commission (1977), the Padmanabhaiah Committee on Police Reforms (2000) and
Malimath Committee on Criminal Justice System (2002) in their respective reports recommended
for separation of investigation from law and order. The Ministry has apprised that the
recommendations of the Commission/Committees were sent to State Governments and Union
Territory Administrations from time to time for consideration and appropriate action. The Ministry
has further apprised that as a follow-up of the Prime Minister’s announcement at the Annual
Conference of DsGP in November, 2004, the Ministry of Home Affair constituted a Review
Committee vide  order dated 21.12.2004 to short list those recommendations of all the
Commissions/Committees on Police Reform which had not been implemented or implemented only
partially and to recommend the course of action needed. The Minstry has submitted that this
Committee short-listed 49 recommendations as being crucial to the process of transforming the
police into a professionally competent and service oriented organization and one of these 49
recommendations pertains to separation of investigation from law and order. The Ministry has
submitted that a copy of the recommendations was sent to all State Governments to initiate action
on these recommendations on 5
th May, 2005. According to the Ministry, as per Seventh Schedule
of the Constitution of India ‘Police’ and ‘Law and Order’ are the State subjects and it is the State
Governments which have to implement the police reforms measures. The Ministry feels that the
Centre can at best persuade the States from time to time to bring the requisite reforms in the Police
administration to meet the expectations of the people.
4.5.7 The Committee notes with deep anguish that out of 27 projects of CFSLs which were
approved for Eleventh Five year plan, 10 projects had to be dropped on account of non-
viability. The Committee, denounces this casual approach on the part of the Government
that these projects were found to be deserved for approval upto the level of a Five Year Plan
of the country and suddenly at the end of the Five Year Plan they were found to be
unviable. The Committee feels that the Government should have assessed the viability of
the Plans before taking up. This lackadaisical attitude is not acceptable to the Committee.
4.5.8 The Committee is disappointed to note the plain justification of the Ministry that the
budgetary allocations in 2011-12 at RE stage was reduced due to delay in acquisition of land
at Pune, Bhopal and Guwahati for establishment of new CFSLs and expansion at Chandigarh
CFSLs, delay in recruitment of contractual manpower for ongoing projects. The Committee
understands that land acquisition is the base stage for any project envisaged and the
Government should keep this in mind while planning any project. The Committee,
recommends that proper planning of the projects on CFSLs should be made and concerted
efforts be made to complete projects within a time frame.
4.5.9 The Committee notes that the allocation of Rs. 78.61 crore in BE 2012-13 should be
properly utilized in a time bound manner for creation of facilities of DNA data base,
Regional Forensic Science Laboratories (RFSLs), District Mobile Forensic Units, Network
among CFSLs and FSLs etc. The Committee understands that upgradation of existing
CFSLs, FSLs and creations of new ones would go a long way in revamping our Criminal

Science Development regulatory Authority (FRDA) at the earliest. Consideration of the

that the candidates opting for police service have to have/should have a different attitude
which this examination system is not able to guarantee. It has been seen that people who

5.1 In our country, 58.6% area is earthquake prone, 12% area is floods prone and 68%
cultivable area is drought prone. The Ministry has stated that when a comparison is made for
similar disaster happened in USA and Japan with that of India, it is found that loss of lives in USA
and Japan are much less as compared to that of India. The factor influencing losses is attributed
to the better preparedness in USA and Japan. The Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2005 .
The Ministry has further stated that prevention and mitigation contribute to lasting improvement in
safety and, should therefore be integrated in the disaster management.

submitted before the Committee in its sitting held on 4
th April, 2012 as under:–
“...I think, we are still some distance away from full preparedness. We have now started the
National Cyclone Mitigation Project, and approximately an amount of Rs. 70 crores has
been spent on it, but, it is still at the initial stage. Once that project is on the ground, then
we will be better prepared for handling cyclones. The Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project
has still not got off the ground. We need to get it off the ground, and that is something
which we need to do. However, we are better prepared than we were earlier because now
we have the National Disaster Response Force. So, our response capability is there, and that
Force is quite effective. But we have still some distance to go in this. We will send you
a detailed  reply.”
5.1.2  The Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2005. This act provides for the effective
management of disasters and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.  The Ministry
in its subsequent written reply has furnished a detailed note on the preparedness of the country
to meet disasters, since the enactment of the Act on the subject.
• Institutional Mechanism – Disaster Management Authorities at National, State and
District level, National Disaster Response Force, National Institute of Disaster
Management etc. have been put in place. The State Governments have the basic
responsibility for undertaking rescue, relief and rehabilitation measures in disaster, by
providing logistic and financial support in case of severe natural calamities. The Central
Government supplements the efforts of the States as and when needed. Other
institutional mechanisms like Civil Defence, Fire Services, Home Guards, National Fire
Service College and National Civil Defence College are also in existence to support the
disaster management activity in the country.
• Financial Arrangements – As provided under the DM Act, National Disaster Response
Fund and State Disaster Response Fund have been established.
• Capacity Development – National Institute of Disaster Management has been set up at
national level. It conducts training, research and development for implementation of
comprehensive human resource development. At State level, Administrative Training
Institutes run their disaster management centers. These are Institutes assisted with

91
financial and technical help from NIDM. The States are provided Capacity
Development grant to strengthen and upgrade the capacity of machinery responsible
for Disaster Management.
• National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) – NDRF has been constituted as specialist
response force for a threatening disaster situation or disaster. It has 10 battalions
across the country, located on the basis of vulnerability to natural disasters. The
States/UTs have also been advised to set up their own Specialist Response Force for
responding to disasters on the lines of NDRF. Many States have started the process
to set up such force and train them for response purposes.
• National Policy – National Policy on DM has been issued. It aims to build a safe and
disaster resilient India by developing a holistic, proactive and multi disaster oriented
technology driven strategy through culture of prevention, mitigation, preparedness and
response.
• Guidelines/Reports – NDMA have released about 15 disaster specific and thematic
guidelines and 10 reports, which have been circulated to all the stakeholders.
• Preparedness and Response: National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) in Ministry
of Home Affairs functions 24x7 to monitor disasters or disaster like situation. For
forecast purposes, agencies like the Indian Meteorological Department for Cyclone,
Central Water Commission for flood, Defence Research and Development Organisation
(DRDO) for Avalanche, Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services
(INCOIS) for Tsunamis etc. have been strengthened and upgraded.
• Advisories are issued to the States/UTs concerned, based on the forecast for keeping
watch on the developing situation and take necessary measures such as evacuation of
vulnerable persons, operation of relief camps, prepositioning of essential commodities
etc. State and district level emergency operation centres are also functional during
disaster situations.
• Prevention and Mitigation – Government of India is implementing several plans for
mitigating disasters such as Flood Management Program by Ministry of Water
Resources, Drought Prone Area Program by Ministry of Agriculture, Integrated Coastal
Zone Management Project by Ministry of Environment and Forests etc. NDMA is
working on the National Flood Risk Mitigation Project, National Landslide Risk
Mitigation Project, National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project etc. The National
Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project is under implementation with an initial outlay of
Rs. 1496.71 crore.
• Government of India is also implementing externally aided schemes in collaboration
with UNDP and USAID for disaster risk reduction. These aim at reducing vulnerability
to disaster and build capacity of key Indian institutions and to strengthen the institutional
structure to undertake disaster risk reduction activities at various levels including risk
being enhanced due to climate change and develop preparedness for recovery.
• International Cooperation – India is closely working with various bodies of United
Nations (UN) on DRR, and other international and regional organisations such as
ASEAN Regional Forum, Asian Disaster Reduction Centre, GFDRR etc. International
Cooperation are aimed at sharing the best practices, expertise and also for technical
assistance on DRR.
• Way Forward – In the area of prevention, mitigation, response and capacity
development several initiatives, as mentioned above have been taken. However, the

92
man-made disasters are yet to be given similar due attention. Various efforts given
below have been contemplated to strengthen the process of Disaster Risk Reduction
(DRR).
a. Developing a centralized database on different kind of disasters.
b. Strengthening the early warning system and developing communication and
connectivity to the last mile.
c. Modernising the emergency operation centres and to make them work on real time
basis.
d. Mainstreaming DRR into the development and planning process.
e. Strengthening the regulatory mechanism in the Urban Planning.
f. Mainstreaming Corporate Social Responsibility in DRR.
g. Integrating the Climate Change with the process of Disaster Risk Reduction.

and the National Platform be merged together and a single event be organized which

5.1.10 In view of the vulnerable geo climatic condition of the country, the Committee
understands the need for disaster preparedness at the grass root level. The Committee
takes note of the fact that most of the new porjects such as National Cyclone Mitigation
Project, Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project etc. are at the rudimentary stages and it seems
it would take considerable time for these new projects to take off.
5.1.11 The Committee is constrained to note that a specialized force like National Disaster
Response Force (NDRF) has 10 battalions only for entire country. In a vast country like
India which is vulnerable to natural and man-made disasters, it is needed to raise more
battalions of this force. The Committee feels that merely advising the States/UTs to have
their own Specialist Response Force for responding to disasters will not serve the purpose.
The Committee impresses upon the States/UTs to set up their own specialised force and
train them for disaster preparedness and NDMA should play a pivotal role in helping the
State/UT Governments in this regard.
5.1.12 The Committee, recommends that the offices and residential infrastructures of NDRF
should be put in place at the earliest by enhancing allocation in 2012-13 at RE stage.

96
Regarding provision for deputation allowance to the personnel of NDRF, the Committee is
of the view that the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance may consider this
proposal and approve for this allowance as it would work as a motivating factor for them.
5.1.13 The Committee notes that to strengthen the process Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR),
one of the various efforts contemplated is to mainstreaming corporate social responsibility
in DRR. A mock drill was conducted by Delhi Disaster Management Authority in
collaboration with NDMA and preceding this, a major earth quake preparedness exercise was
also under taken. The Committee welcomes this move and recommends that necessary steps
may be taken to rectify the shortcomings noticed during the mock drills. The Committee
also notes that NDMA is in the process of preparing a template for conducting such mock
drills across the country on the basis of the experience gained. The Committee recommends
that the template may be prepared at the earliest for the benefit of all the State
Governments.
5.1.14 The Committee appreciates that the NIDM has been helping the State/UT
Governments in organising Mock Drill across the country which will go a long way in
disaster mitigation. The Committee commends the initiative taken by the Centre to evolve
the National Platform on Disaster Risk Reduction (NPDRR) which aims at bringing together
organizations and individuals in diverse disciplines and sectors and assemble, synthesize,
manage and further disseminate academic as well as practical knowledge on disaster
management in all sectors including policy making and development plans of the Government.
5.1.15 The Committee notes with displeasure that NIDM is still functioning from a rented
premises of Indian Institute of Public Administration. The Committee is unable to
understand the inordinate delay in the matter of providing land to the Institute. Now that
the land has been identified by Delhi Development Authority, the Government should take
possession of the land at the earliest and start construction of the building without further
delay. The Committee further recommends that all the 124 posts in NDMA be filled up at
the earliest. The Committee also recommends that review of the Disaster Management Act
may be completed at the earliest so as to have a more efficient and implementable
legislation in the country.

SERVICEABILITY OF HELICOPTERS
5.5 During the oral evidence of the Home Secretary on Demands-for-Grants (2012-13) by the

106
Committee in its sitting held on 4 th April, 2012, the Chairman and the Members of the Committee
stated that 50 per cent availability of helicopters is extremely poor and this must be above 90 per
cent. The Home Secretary on this issue replied as under:–
“...to begin with the last point, one is about the serviceability of the helicopters. It depends
on two things, one is the availability of the spares and the other is about the workshops,
etc. For availability of spares and workshops, for both these we are dependent on the Air
Force. We have three MOUs with the Air Force. The spares etc. are procured from the Air
Force and most of the major repairs are done by the Air Force. But as far as availability
of spares is concerned, it is not that Air Force is not deliberately giving us spares, they
also do not have the spares. This is a problem the Air Force is grappling with. Helicopters
were purchased in 2003. As I said, there has been a disruption in the manufacturing
facilities of this type of helicopters and availability of spares for the Air Force itself is very
low. When I compared it with the Air Force, I had only pointed out that this is something
which is not limited only to the Ministry of Home Affairs, this is something which is being
faced by us as a country because we are dependent on a country which broke up and where
manufacturing facilities were dispersed. Some helicopters are actually 2002-2003 vintage. In
some cases they have been closed down and in other places they are near closing down.
The Ministry of Defence is procuring some of the additional helicopters and we have asked
them to add our requirements to their procurement.”
5.5.1 The Ministry further explaining the position made following written submissions:–
• 6 MI-17 1V helicopters were procured by Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) through
the Ministry of Defence (MoD) in 2003. These helicopters are operated under the
Military Registration, i.e. as per the approved norms of Indian Air Force. At the time
of procurement of these helicopters, an assurance was taken from MoD that Indian Air
Force (IAF)/ MoD will provide the required support for operation and maintenance of
this fleet in terms of pilots, technical manpower, spares backup and repair facilities.
Accordingly, as per the agreed terms and conditions, three Memorandum of
Understandings (MoUs) were signed between MHA and MoD, after induction of this
fleet, for providing the required support.
• Though, IAF/MoD are making their best efforts to provide the service as per the terms
and conditions of the MoUs, however, some time they are not able to extend the
required support in terms of pilots, technical manpower, spares backup and repair
facilities due to their own operational constraints. The pilots as well as technical
manpower to handle this fleet is not available in the open market and has to be
necessarily sourced from IAF/MoD. As per the MoUs, the spares of this fleet are
sourced by MHA through the IAF/MoD. IAF/MoD have a much larger fleet, and as a
result they are able to negotiate better terms and conditions as well as price with the
OEMs. However, after the breakup of the erstwhile USSR, IAF/MoD are also finding
it difficult to source spares from different CIS countries manufacturing different parts.
•  Also due to their own increased volume of repair works because of the ageing fleet,
the Indian Air Force sometimes is not able to accord the required priority deserved by
the fleet of BSF. Though, the repair facilities have been established by IAF, they are
yet to establish the repair facilities of certain major components at their “3 Base Repair
Depot, IAF Chandigarh”. As a result, such components are still required to be sent to
the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) overseas which takes lot of time.
•  Now, with the introduction of the Service Bulletin issued on 24
th December 2009 by
‘Military Moscow Helicopter’ plant for Mi-17 series helicopters, the Service life and

107
Service time between the two overhaul of Mi-17 series helicopters have been extended
in respect of certain components. Therefore, though the serviceability has been
improved to some extent, however the same is affected to an extent due to the non-
availability of the spares/components whose life has not been extended by the said
service bulletin. Also the procurement of these spares from Original Equipment
Manufacturer/Authorised agent have a long lead time.
•  As a result, presently 2 MI-17 1V helicopters (Z-4102 & Z-4104), out of a fleet of
6 with MHA, are in unserviceable condition i.e. Aircraft on Ground (AOG) due to non-
availability of the critical components/spares, including Aero Engines and Main Rotor
Blades. The list of deficient major critical spares/components for the two helicopters
are given below :–
Z-4102 has been grounded for want of following major components :–
(i) Aero Engines Quantity – 2
(ii) APU Quantity – 1
(iii) M ain Rotor Blade Quantity – 1 set
(iv) GPS Trimble Quantity – 1
(v) Control panel of FDR Quantity – 1
(vi) Radio Altimeter Quantity – 1
(vii) Main Rotor Hub Quantity – 1
(viii) Hydraulic boosters Quantity – 1 set
(ix) MGB needs to be extended from 1500 hrs to 2000 hours by Russian
Specialists under the contract of IAF.
• Out of the remaining 4 MI-17 1V helicopters, generally at least 3 remain serviceable,
while one at times remain under the scheduled maintenance. All four helicopters are
likely to become serviceable within 2 weeks. Concerted efforts are on to further
improve the serviceability status of this fleet. It may be mentioned that the overall Rate
of Effort of BSF fleet is comparable to/better than their IAF/MoD counter parts.
• The efforts made so far to improve the serviceability of this fleet are as under:–

/head2rightThe recruitment process to fill up all posts on priority is in progress so as

/head2rightWherever, IAF/MoD is not able to provide the required critical components

/head2rightThe matter is being vigorously pursued with MoD by MHA for providing

5.5.2 During the said sitting, some Members raised the issue of growing number of fatal
accidents of helicopters which is much larger when compared to other countries. The Home
Secretary made following reply:–
“...unfortunately, the accidents that happened, involving prominent personalities, were
generally with Western-origin helicopters. I am not aware of accidents involving Mi-17IV
Helicopters. We have six such Mi-17IV helicopters. At this point, what we need to rethink
is this. First is, these helicopters are old. We have bought them in 2003. Modern technology
has progressed much thereafter. The second one which we have been thinking about and
which is occupying our minds is the fact that after sales the spares support from Russia has
been a problem. So, this is something which we have to consider when we procure the next
lot of helicopters. I am quite sure that the Ministry of Defence will also consider this. What
we have done this time is, we have asked the Ministry of Defence to club our requirements
with theirs. This time, I believe, the procurement which they are in the process of finalizing
is a Russian-origin helicopter. That is something on which I do not have authoritative
statement from the Ministry of Home Affairs. But, they have an open system of procurement
where they float tenders, different manufacturers submit their tenders from different parts of
the world, including the Western manufactures and they might have or might not have
competed. But, that is something which I still do not have any authoritative information
on this. But, with regard to helicopter accidents, for example, the accident involving the
Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh, the helicopter Acureuil AS-350 B-3 from the
Eurocopter (France) is involved.
5.5.3 The Committee is constrained to note that Helicopters are not functional due to
scarcity of spares. Such a situation should not have been allowed. Ideally India should
diversify its supplies in terms of purchase of helicopters. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Home Ministry should impress upon the Ministry of Defence to supply
adequate number of helicopters to it so that it never faces problem of non-availability of
helicopters alongwith a guarantee of spares.
5.5.4 The Committee takes serious view of the fact that despite MoU signed between MHA
and MoD, the Airforce is not able to extend the required support in terms of pilots,
technical manpower, spares backup and repair facilities to the Ministry of Home Affairs due
to their own operational constraints. When MoU was signed, the Ministry of Defence should
honour this without fail. The Ministry of Defence should plug these operational constraints.

balance amount required to complete the scheme has only been provided in the Demand for Grant
for the year 2012-13.
5.6.2 The Ministry has furnished details of steps taken under the centrally sponsored scheme of
Revamping the Civil Defence set up by the Ministry for revitalization of Civil Defence during the
previous year which is as follows:–
• As against strengthening of physical infrastructure of existing State Training Institutes
in 17 States, renovation/ upgradation of physical infrastructure has since been
completed in 4 States and the process for procurement of equipments commenced in
11 States.
• As regards creation of New Training Institutes in 10 States, land already allotted in all
States except Chandigarh where new Training Institute is not feasible.
• For creation of 100 multi hazard districts, all States have already identified their
location for physical infrastructure and process for procurement of equipments also
commenced in most of the States.
• As regards pilot project for involving civil defence in internal security matters in 40
towns, training of 214 master trainers completed and 4280 CD volunteers also trained
as envisaged in the project.
• As regards training camps/exercise and demonstrations, firm commitments has already
been received from 14 States for contribution of matching funds on the basis of 50:50
between the Central Government and State Govt and funds also released to some of
the States.
5.6.3 Home Guards are basically a voluntary organization whose members are drawn from the
public. There is no Central Government legislation. Home Guards are raised/trained and deployed
under the Home Guards Acts/Rules of the respective States/Union Territories. Home Guards serve
as an auxiliary to the Police and generally help in maintenance of law & order except crime
investigation. It is for the State Government to utilize the service of Home Guards.
5.6.4  According to the Ministry, the Central Government reimburses 50% of the cost of raising,
training and equipping of Home Guards for North Eastern States excluding Assam and 25% of such
costs for all other States. The Ministry has informed that the duty allowance is reimbursed by
specified rates when Home Guards are called upon for duty. The Ministry has further informed that
as the rates for reimbursement are fixed, the demand for grants is made on the basis of number
of claims for reimbursement and the claims as received from the State Governments after being
duly audited at the State level. The Ministry has submitted that the allocation by Central
Government for this purpose in the last 7 years have been found adequate and met the requirement
of reimbursement to the States.

the attention of the Members to the serious difficulties being faced by States in implementing the
community policing initiatives. The Home Minister further stated that the foundation of
community policing is the beat constable and there are large numbers of vacancies in the
constabulary across the country. The Home Minister further stated that the idea of a separate
‘Community Police Force’ is attractive and BPR&D was asked to prepare a concept paper in
consultation with Delhi Police.

st October, 2006, for appropriate consideration as Police is

5.6.9 The Ministry has submitted that the project ‘Soft Skill Training for Police Personnel’ was

Police Academy, Phillaur in December, 2010. The Ministry has further submitted that so far 3 ToTs

have been trained. Besides, training Programmes have been conducted for Delhi Police also. The

of impact study. The Ministry has further apprised that another project on Police Community
Partnership and Overarching Model of Community Policing is under consideration for approval of

Police Mission has demanded a Plan Budget for NPM related projects. The Ministry also stated that
in order to incentivize the implementation of Police Reforms by States, a Reserve Fund of 5% of
Modernization of Police Force Scheme’s annual allocation is proposed to be set aside for
disbursement to States who achieve benchmarked standards.
5.6.10 The Committee takes a serious note of the fact that allocation for civil defence
(3601) has now been drastically decreased to Rs.74.39 crore in BE 2012-13 from Rs. 137.52
crore at RE stage in 2011-12, which needs to be seriously looked into. Though the Ministry
has tried to explain the reasons, the Committee is not convinced with those explanations.
The Committee desires that the two schemes namely, revamping of Civil Defence set up in
the country and Strengthening of Fire and Emergency Services in the country may be
completed in the next financial year as claimed by the Ministry. The Committee also
recommends that the Government may expedite projects such as strengthening of physical
infrastructure in remaining States, creation of New Training Institutes in 10 States, pilot
project for involving civil defence in internal security matters in 40 towns.
5.6.11 The Committee appreciates Community Policing Models being implemented in
various States of the country. The Committee is of the view that the other State/UT
Governments should also emulate this model. The Committee, however, desires that the
BPR&D should prepare a concept paper on Community Policing.
MODERNISATION OF PRISONS ADMINISTRATION
5.7 ‘Prisons’ is a State subject under List-II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of
India. The management and administration of Prisons falls exclusively in the domain of the State
Governments, and is governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 and the Prison Manuals of the respective
State Governments. Thus, States have the primary role, responsibility and authority to change the
current prison laws, rules and regulations.
5.7.1 Considering the “appalling condition” of prisons in the States, the Union Home Ministry has
initiated the process of formulating the second phase of the scheme for modernisation of prison
Administration. During the oral evidence of the Home Secretary on Demands-for-Grants (2012-13),
one Member of the Committee raised the issue of prison modernization. The Home Secretary in
response made following observations.

112
“The second phase of prison modernization, again, is something which we had proposed.
We proposed it last time. I would like the Committee’s support on this. We have again
moved it. We believe that it is necessary. We need to help the States to modernize prisons.
In many States, there is still a lot of overcrowding. In many States, the condition is very
bad and the States just do not have enough funds to modernize.”
5.7.2 The Committee understands that the State/UT Government cannot go beyond a limit
in modernizing their prisons due to financial constraints. Keeping in view the appalling
condition of various jails in the country, the Committee is of the view that the Second
Phase of the scheme of modernisation of prison administration should be given approval at
the earliest because a lot of work is yet to be done through the scheme.  The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the Planning Commission and the Department of
Expenditure should give attention to this and approve the proposal of the Ministry of Home
Affairs for Second Phase of scheme of modernization of prisons at the earliest.
