CHAPTER-II
TRAINING COMPONENTS AND METHODOLOGY
TRAINING PROGRAMMES
2.1 The Academy management informed the Committee that essentially the training programmes
being conducted at the Academy fall under two broad heads, viz., Basic Training for freshly
recruited IPS Officers (Officer Trainees) and In-service Training for serving IPS officers, gazetted
police officers from various police forces and senior officers from other All India, Central and
State Services.
Basic Training for IPS Probationers
2.2 The Committee was informed that the main objective of the training to IPS probationers is
to develop strength, endurance, flexibility and body coordination, to develop leadership qualities,
high levels of confidence, to inculcate a strong sense of internal and external discipline required
of an officer of the Indian Police Service, to build attitude to take in stress and work for long
hours without physical and mental fatigue, to develop skills of teamwork, to learn command and
control, to improve turnout, posture and personal drill of an officer of the uniformed service, so
as to act as a role model and earn respect of People, to develop pride in uniform. Further,
probationers are trained to learn skills of firing, weapon handling, tactical operations, combat, riot
control and others, which are critical and essential for any professional police officer.
2.2.1 During the course of presentation, NPA Director informed the Committee that the Basic
Course Training covers all the major modules and programmes conducted for the IPS Probations.
It covers modules on investigation, adventure sports, confidence building etc., and innovations such
as Interrogation Module by the CBI. The training is also conducted outside the Academy under
Jungle Survival Module at Satya Mangalam Forest, Tamil Nadu as well as Major Bandobust
attachments programmes in Elections, Common Wealth Games, Kumbh Mela, Ganesha Utsav. The
training encompasses innovative teaching methods such as brain storming sessions, public speaking
modules for development of professional standards. Measures are taken for instilling integrity and
strength in character of the IPS Probationers.
2.2.2 The Committee was apprised that the National Police Academy imparts training to the new
entrants to the IPS and so far 62 batches comprising 4486 officers of the Indian Police Service
and other officers of CPOs/State Police organizations have passed out of this Institution. 151
Probationers of 2010 batch including 4 Royal Bhutan Police Officers, 4 Maldivian Police Officers
and 3 Nepal Police Officers were being imparted training at the time of visit of the Committee.
2.2.3 The Academy management apprised the Committee that a number of subjects are covered
during the training programme which inter-alia include Physical Training, Drill (Lathi Drill, Tear
Gas Drill and Riot Control Drill and Sword Drill and Ceremonial Drill) and Weapon Training and Firing,
Yoga, Un-Armed Combat (UAC), Swimming, Field Craft and Tactics and Map Reading, Equitation,
First Aid and Ambulance Drill and Motor Mechanism. Other activities and Adventure Sports activities
include Rock Climbing – ITBP Team, Mysore, Powered Hang Gliding – by NAF, Para Sailing –
Army Adventure Sports Wing, Secunderabad, ITBP Module on River Rafting- ITBP, District
Practical Training (in 2 Phases), Life Saving and Scuba Diving- Dive Goa, Modules on Tactics
(Special Tactics Wing, NPA), Exposure to General Assembly Elections in 2 Southern States: Kerala

16
and Tamil Nadu, Attachment with Central School for Weapons and Tactics, BSF Indore, Attachment
with Spl. Task Force, Tamil Nadu at Satyamangalam for Reflex firing, Jungle Survival modules and
Attachment with Greyhounds. Moreover, annual athletic meet, annual aquatic meet and tonk cup are
also organized.
2.2.4 The Committee was given to understand that the duration of Basic Course Training was of
104 weeks, which included foundation course of 15 weeks, Basic Course Training Phase-l of 46
weeks. After passing out from the Academy, the probationers undergo attachments at various
CPOs/CPMFs for 5 weeks. The probationers have to undergo District Practical Training for 27
weeks and again they have to report to the Academy for Phase-II training of 4 weeks.
2.2.5 During Phase-I and II of Basic Training Course, the Probationers are evaluated through
Indoor and Outdoor Examination for 1200 and 600 marks, respectively, besides the Director’s
assessment for 400 marks. The Committee was further apprised that the final evaluation consists
of 600 marks which is done through Physical Training, Drill (including Sword and Ceremonial
drill), Weapon Training and Firing, Yoga, Unarmed Combat/Krav Maga, Swimming, Field Craft and
Tactics/ Map Reading, Equitation and First Aid and Ambulance Drill.
2.2.6 When the Committee sought to know the rationale for earmarking 400 marks to
probationers under Director’s assessment, the Academy submitted that the training, as defined by
the Gore Committee (1971) on Police Training, is a conscious effort to impart, improve or increase
knowledge and skills and to develop attitudes and values of an individual in a desired direction. The
SVP National Police Academy, in addition to imparting knowledge and skills, endeavours to
inculcate right attitude in the probationers whereas the transfer of knowledge to the probationers
and acquisition of skills by them is assessed through examinations in indoor and outdoor subjects,
the conduct and attitude are given due weightage through an objective process called “Director’s
Assessment’.
2.2.7 The Director’s Assessment Marks are meant to gauge these aspects that training seeks to
inculcate. While awarding marks for Director’s Assessment, the overall conduct and performance
of the probationer under training is taken into consideration. The probationer is expected to imbibe
the values and attitudes, which the Service demands. The focus is on discipline, integrity, ability
to work in a team, leadership aspects, attitude towards gender and weaker sections of the society,
fairness and objectivity, positivity, etc.
2.2.8 The Committee was further informed that the Director’s Assessment Marks were raised
from 100 to 400 in 1993 as a follow up to the introduction of sandwich pattern of training
wherein the probationers after institutional Phase-I training at the Academy, go for District Practical
Training in the allotted State and then come back to the Academy for Phase-II training. It was
deemed necessary to assess the overall conduct of the probationers not only during Phase-I training
at NPA but also during the District Practical Training and Phase-II training. Therefore, now the
Director’s Assessment takes into account the conduct as well as the core values, as mentioned
above, exhibited by the probationer during Phase-I Basic Training and during Phase-II Field
Training.
INDOOR VS. OUTDOOR TRAINING
2.3 The Probationers are taught fifteen subjects during the training at the Academy which
includes Police in Modern India, Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Indian Penal Code, 1860, Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973, Special Laws, Crime Prevention and Criminology, Investigation I and II,
Forensic Medicine, Forensic Science (Theory and Practical), Maintenance of Public Peace and
Order, Internal Security, Police Leadership and Management, Rule of Law, Ethics and Human
Rights and Information and Communication Technology.

17
2.3.1 The Committee was apprised that the probationers are educated through modules and
simulation exercises like Public Speaking, Police Station, Traffic Management, Interrogation, Hurt,
Property Offences, Homicide, Investigation Module, Moot Court, Anti-Corruption, Economic
Offences, Disaster Management, Riot Module, Or ganised Crime, VVIP Security, Media
Management, SP and Supervision, Terrorism, IT, SIB, Tactics etc. to make them understand the
subject better. Moreover, various methods of teaching are adopted to make the subject easier and
interesting by using Case Study Method, Lectures, Recap, Forecast, SNAP Test, Squat
Presentations, Quizzes, Ex-tempore Public Speaking, Simulation exercise, Brain Storming,
Debriefing Presentations by Probationers and Discussion on current events of relevance to Police.
2.3.2 Commenting on the proportion of indoor as well as the outdoor training an expert suggested
as under:–
“.....I think, the indoor as well as the outdoor training is very important for the police
officers. It is difficult to qualify it in terms of percentage but even then, I would say that
if it is 60 per cent indoor, at least, 40 per cent outdoor has to be there, if not fifty-fifty.
An officer who is physically not fit, who is not trained in jungle warfare, who cannot
operate against insurgents, who cannot operate against Maoists, who cannot deal with the
North-Eastern rebels, who cannot operate in J&K, he would be a misfit in the police force.
He has to be good in outdoor training.”
2.3.3 Responding to the views of the expert, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the
emphasis as well as co-relation in regard to indoor and outdoor training is always maintained.
2.3.4 Though the quantum of the indoor and outdoor training cannot be fixed in terms of
percentage, however, sufficient outdoor training must be imparted to have the physical fitness
of the police personnel while indoor training should be so adequately imparted to ensure that
the police personnel possess requisite understanding of law and jurisprudential knowledge.
The NPA may have a relook at the present curriculum and reviewed with experts.
Field Visit
2.4 The Committee was further apprised that for the practical training, probationers are sent to
Infosys Training Centre, Village Visit, Burns and Post-Mortem Wards, Moharrum Bandobust, Ganesh
Chaturthi Bandobust, Police Station, Jail Visit, Study-Cum-Cultural Tour to give them first hand
information and to make them observe/learn the security arrangement/bandobust and management. In
recent past, they were sent to witness State Assembly Election held in Kerala and Tamil Nadu,
Kumbh Mela, Commonwealth Games, Rath Yatra. As a part of training they were also attached to
the various CPOs/CPMFs like CRPF , Army, BPST, NAI, E-Court, IB, CBI, SPG, RAW, etc.
2.4.1 The Committee is of the view that the basic training modules of the Academy must
consist of the courses keeping in view stark reality of society and the aim of the training
programme should be to impart knowledge and skill to face the ground challenges of the
country. The Committee also feels that training on management and administration should
also be provided. When the officers grow higher up the ladder, they are also required to
handle administration and finance. Training needs to be given on these aspects as well and
some modules may be prepared for these aspects.

SPECIAL TACTICS WING
2.6 The Committee was informed that on reviewing the police response to 9/11 attack on
Mumbai, it was felt that there was a big gap between training and present requirement of tactical
skills among Indian police. To meet the requirement of tactical training to Police officers, the NPA
took the initiative and established the Special Tactics Wing (STW) to impart tactical training to
Police Officers from State Police and CAPFs to enable them to conduct tactical operations against
anti national elements in Jungle and Urban environment.
2.6.1 The STW is manned by an Assistant Director, four Inspectors and 9 Constables from
various CAPFs which are on deputation against existing vacancies of NPA. In addition to this, MHA
has approved attachment of one Inspector/SI, one Head Constable and 5 Constables each from
BSF, CRPF, CISF and ITBP till dedicated manpower for STW is sanctioned. Recently 274 posts
of various ranks have been sanctioned to NPA which includes posts for STW also.
2.6.2 The tactical training inputs are imparted through training modules at three levels, namely,
foundation, functional and directional levels.
2.6.3 The tactical training inputs to officer trainees has been increased manifold. Apart from
modules conducted with Grey hounds, BSF and Tamil Nadu STF, trainees are imparted tactical
training in three phases, with progressive stages of incomplexity and difficulty and in the last
phase, the trainees are required to plan and execute operations on their own. Moreover, they are
also exposed to self sustained operations without administrative support.
2.6.4 The Officers of the ranks of SPs, ASPs and Dy. SPs and equivalent ranks from CPAF are
imparted tactical training through “Course on Tactics” which includes:
(i) Inputs on drills to combat terrorists and insurgents in Jungle and Urban environment
which includes simulation of incidents requiring police action and self-sustained-two-
day operations in Jungle adhering to the principle of “Fight the Guerilla like a
Guerilla”. The participants are also exposed to latest weaponry and equipment and
emergency drills like combat first aid rescue operations, etc. So far, the STW has
trained a total of 1074 officers in 28 “Course on Tactics” which comprise of 168
IPS, 595 State Police Officers and 311 from CPOs.
(ii) In addition to the courses conducted in NPA, the STW has taken the initiative of
providing tactical training assistance to State police by conducting requirement
specific courses at respective State police academies. So far NPA has conducted
eight such courses at Gujarat Police Academy, Ghandhi Nagar; NEPA, Shillong;
Karnataka Police Academy, Mysore (two courses); Kerala Police Academy, Thrissur;
EFR training centre, Midnapur, West Bengal; Bhilai, Chhattisgarh and Force One,
Pune.

21
2.6.5 The STW plans to start tactics course for senior officers of the rank of DIGs and above
exposing them to tactical knowledge to plan and execute counter terrorist operations in a more
efficient manner.
2.6.6 The Committee was informed that 400 Acres of land, separate STW Building, firing ranges
and latest tactical equipment and weapons has been sanctioned and the STW has the following
plans to be implemented shortly:
(i) Commencing Course on Tactics for Senior officers;
(ii) Providing training module on explosives and IEDs;
(iii) Developing the allotted piece of land to tactical training area;
(iv) Run simultane ous courses on Jungle and Urban warfare; and
(v) Planning and conducting need specific training modules at State police academies.
2.6.7 The Committee notes the initiatives and activities taken by NPA in imparting special
tactical training to police officers. The Committee, however, also takes note of the fact that
STW is having its man power on ad-hoc basis. This will not help in better functioning of
the work. Efforts may be made to put in place dedicated manpower at the earliest.
Directional level tactics course for senior officers of the rank of DIG and above be started
at the earliest. Fund requirements of NPA for developing allotted land for tactical training,
separate STW Building, procurement of equipments and weapons may be looked into
promptly so as to make the Special Tactics Wing par excellence. This level of excellence
may further be used for revenue generation by imparting such training to the police officers
of other countries.
FOREIGN TRAINING
2.7 The Committee received a proposal from the Academy that the IPS Probationers should be
sent to countries like Japan, Singapore and Australia for foreign exposure visits on community
policing, forensic criminology, etc. The proposal was forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs
for furnishing its comments.
2.7.1 In  this regard, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Home Affairs that the
Academy has sent a proposal to the MHA vide letter No. 11011/19/2010-Trg. IPS.(P) 62 RR (SV)
dated May
 19, 2012 for a 10-days foreign study tour during the Phase-II training of IPS
Probationers to Japan and Singapore which would help the probationers to improve their
perspectives through vivid demonstration of best practices being followed in other countries. This
is under consideration of MHA.
2.7.2 The Committee recommends that the proposal to send IPS probationers to Japan and
Singapore for training during phase – II  may be positively considered by Ministry of Home
Affairs. The Committee feels that community policing can play a major role in  curbing
crimes in India keeping in mind the low police population ratio and a big democratic set-
up in the country.
2.7.3 The Committee sought to know whether the quality of the training imparted in the Academy
is comparable with the training given in countries viz., USA, UK and other European countries. The
Committee also desired to know whether the trainees were sent there so as to give them exposure
to the latest modules of trainings. In  response to that, the Committee was informed that Indian
Police Service, as a service has no parallel in USA, UK or other European countries. The level of
induction in Police Service in USA, UK and other European countries is not at comparable level

22
to IPS who are trained to assume leadership position. Therefore, it would not be possible to
benchmark the training imparted at NPA with that of the Police Training Academies of USA, UK
and other European countries.
2.7.4 The Committee was further informed that the IPS Probationers are not sent to USA, UK
and other European countries or any other country abroad to give them exposure to latest modules
of training. In  the three compulsory Mid-Career Training Programmes (MCTP), junior, middle level
and senior IPS Officers are being sent respectively to Australia in MCPT Phase-III and to England
in MCTP Phase-IV and V .
2.7.5 Commenting further on the foreign trainers and foreign visits an expert viewed as under:–
“.....I find that the National Police Academy, not for probationers but for certain other
courses, has started getting trainers from Australian universities. I found Australian trainer
during one of my visits there. Trainers from the United Kingdom are coming. I think, it is
complete waste of money. A police officer from Australia has no clue of the ground conditions
in India. In fact, he would need one year to understand the ground conditions of India or
the kind of problems which the Indian officers have to deal with. It may be fashionable but
it should be dispensed with. It would mean a saving of foreign exchange also. In fact, the
probationer may, if the finances permit, go to the neighbouring countries or countries where
the conditions of work would be somewhat similar to those in India. I said about the United
Kingdom because a lot of police culture has flown in from there. They could go to China,
Sri Lanka, Indonesia or neighbouring countries, where conditions of work would be somewhat
similar, where you find Asian culture. For their education, they could go abroad.”
2.7.6 The Ministry of Home Affairs responded that the objective of MCTP is to explore IPS
officers to advanced system of policing. MCTP has been introduced for in-service officers after
careful consideration by MHA. For Indian police officers, it is more beneficial to be exposed to
such developed countries where democratic policing is the norm and not where the polity is
autocratic or theocratic etc.
2.7.7 Expressing the view on the foreign visit another expert felt that during the programme, for
the last phase they should be sent abroad for one or two weeks. He further emphasized that what
is taught to IPS officers must be based on experience, sound logic and principle.
2.7.8 The Ministry of Home Affairs is in agreement with the suggestion of the expert over the
foreign visit of probationers and the Committee was informed that IPS officer trainees may be sent
for foreign study tour in Phase-II. A proposal in this regard is under consideration with MHA.
Phase-II will serve this purpose very well wherein the training is evaluated on the basis of
experiences that the OTs gain during their field training phase.
2.7.9 Foreign visit of the probationers in phase-II of the training schedule is the
appropriate time when the probationers, after having an understanding of the system within
the country, can have a comparative study of the system of obtaining abroad. The
Committee recommends that the proposal under consideration of MHA may be examined
soon and an early decision may be taken.

COORDINATION WITH OTHER POLICE ACADEMIES
2.13 One of the experts emphasized the need for integrated police training in the National Police
Academy and the States. He observed that what has been covered in the National Police Academy,

2.13.1 Deliberating on the issue another expert stated as under:–
“National Police Academy has a mission statement which says that it would give guidance/
consultancy to the State police training institutions. Unfortunately, we are not able to live

Most of them have become dumping grounds of inefficient, demotivated elements. No

2.13.2 The Committee feels that internal security is a major concern across the Country
and supervision and surveillance by the Police Personnel around the country is of utmost
significance.  With the sophistication and changing nature of crimes, a well equipped and
professional police personnel are required all over the country. Integrated police training is,
therefore the natural corollary. The Committee recommends that NPA should act like what
the NCERT does for other training schools of States and the experience gained at the NPA
must percolate to the State and the district training schools for the benefit of the police

ISSUES AND EMERGING AREAS OF TRAINING
LAW AND JURISPRUDENCE IN TRAINING MODULES
3.1 An expert emphasing on the need to give impetus to incorporate modules on knowledge of
law and jurisprudence in the training curriculum stated as under:–
“In the initial years of IPS training in the 50s and 60s, a training was more or less divided
into two parts. One was law and the other was order. There was little else taught apart from
law. Even subjects like forensic science and all were very much related to investigation
aspect of law. But over the years, the training curriculum was broadened, the horizons were
broadened and various other subjects were brought in. As a result, the emphasis on law,
particularly the jurisprudential aspects ‘of law has come down considerably, and this is very
often evident even in the manner in which senior IPS officers react with the media on the
TV channels and elsewhere. They do not emphasize on the legal points of their case and
go into sort of side issues. That is the first thing that we need to do, particularly on the
jurisprudential aspects. If you need to appreciate evidence particularly, you should also
understand jurisprudential principles behind such evidence.”
3.1.1 Responding to the above views, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the emphasis on
law has since been enhanced with the introduction of a ‘composite code approach’ which in
nutshell means that the major laws are to be contextualized in the backdrop of constitutional and
human rights provisions. Further, re-visiting sessions have been planned in respect of important
legal aspects to re-enforce the learning.
3.1.2 The Committee agrees that an in-depth understanding of jurisprudential principles would
inject legal insight to the IPS officer which would certainly help them solve the legal issues
involved in the case. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is further scope for enhancing
the module on law and jurisprudence in the training curriculum of IPS officers. Therefore, the
entire module on law and jurisprudence may be revisited involving some legal experts.
Case Study

ETHICAL AND MORAL V ALUES AND INTEGRATION
3.3 Some Members of the Committee sought to know about any special inputs given to the IPS
Probationers on ethical and moral values as there is a perceptible decrease in quality and standard
of public life particularly the police department. One expert felt that although there is emphasis on
ethical dimensions of policing in NPA but a greater emphasis should be given to it. Training of
probationers should not be confined to acquisition of skills only, rather equal emphasis on
inculcation of ethical values, sound judgment and discretion should be given.
3.3.1 The Director, in response thereto, apprised the Committee that integrity related issues are
getting maximum emphasis in the Academy. The topic of corruption is dealt head on by means of
brain-storming sessions, group discussions, case studies, address and interaction with the Police
and other leaders of impeccable integrity. The ill-effects of corruption in police are brought out
clearly to the Probationers. The malaise of corruption in lower ranks and also in senior level is
also taken up during these sessions. It was further stated that IPS officers with impeccable
reputation are invited to address and interact with the probationers and are presented as role models
to them. A special module on anti-corruption by officers from CBI is being conducted. The
importance of transparency and accountability in governance is further highlighted by giving inputs

30
on RTI Act. These topics are also made a part of debate/Elocution Competitions that are held at
the Academy every year. In the written reply it was further stated that ‘Ethics and Human Rights’
forms a full-fledged subject in IPS training curriculum. ‘Purity of Means’ is emphasized in all
aspects of practical policing. In addition, Sensitization modules, which include field visits also, have
been introduced on the themes which inter-alia  include Gender Sensitization, Juvenile Justice,
Marginal Communities, Communal Harmony and National Integration and Integrity.
3.3.2 The Committee is of the view that since policing does have a bearing on the lives
of individuals and, therefore, Police Personnel, particularly officers should possess high
moral and ethical values so as to arrest the declining trend in quality and standard of public
life. The Committee believes that when the pursuit of social commitment and integrity is
effectively imbibed into police personnel irrespective of rank and file, the malaise and
qualms of corruption could be eradicated from public life to a large extent. Transparency
and public accountability is a pre-requisite for good governance. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the training modules prepared for probationers and also for in-service
officers must cover the lessons on ethical traits and moral behaviour.
3.3.3 The Committee observes that Officer is generally vested with the power which
extends at times to taking life and liberty of the people but what matters is how he
exercises his power. Therefor e, emphasis should also be given as to how to use the power.
The Committee is also given to understand that in other countries like Japan training
curriculum contain the constant emphasis on ethical aspects in policing so that while doing
a particular job, a set of principles has to be adhered to. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that adequate emphasis should be laid in the training programme of Officers
Trainee and NPA should teach probationers good policing practice which is practicised
globally. Modules on ethical values and morality should also be included in the MCTP
programmes as it is equally required at that stage as well.
3.3.4 In regard to the training given by the Academy on ethical reorientation, sense of justice to
the weaker sections of the society and the role of IPS Officers during communal incidents, the

violence and have been praised by public and judicial commissions. The loss of credibility which
police may face, if it displays any bias, and the resulting damage to the moral authority of the

with the probationers the successful experiments carried out in different places like Bhiwandi,
Mumbai, Coimbatore, etc. He also apprised the Committee that the Academy removes regional
biases and promotes camaraderie by forming Squads of Probationers in which persons from
different regions are put together.
3.3.5 The Committee desires that the message of the Preamble to the Constitution of India,
being “Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic” should not only be read and
understood by the police personnel but should also be imprinted into their ‘hearts and minds’
to be reflected into their actions while dealing with actual incidents. Keeping in view the fact
that India is a vast country with complex social structure i.e. multi-lingual, multi-ethnic,
multi-religious, training modules must give emphasis to these aspects. A sense of justice and
sensitivity towards the people particularly of weaker sections should be initiated by them.

with the help of intelligence bureau and AP State intelligence Branch, NPA is carrying out exclusive
training for probationers in this direction.
3.12.2 The Committee was further informed that inputs on collection of crime related intelligence
are imparted to the Probationers through conduct of simulation exercises as part of investigation
module—how to get clues, identifications, develop and engage a source in property offences,
murder, etc.
3.12.3 The Committee is surprised to find that although probationers are given elaborate
training on the intelligence collection and analysis but there is no dearth of intelligence
failures which led to massive incidents killing several innocent persons. Though, intelligence
success is rarely reported in the media its failure attracts immediate attention of the media
besides immensely affecting the lives of the people. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the training modules on intelligence collection and analysis must be comprehensive and
the same may be replicated at the State and District Police Training Centre.
LAW & ORDER
3.13 One of the experts while emphasizing the need on imparting training on order part of the
policing suggested as under:–
“.....the training is more theoretical in terms of investigation, criminal law, etc., etc. But
today Police are increasingly facing order issues. It is not the law part, but order part of
the policing, like crowd control, religious congregations, etc. Almost every year, we have
huge religious congregations in India whether it is Kumbh Mela or Ardh Kumbh Mela, some
other Pushkaram or something like l that. We do not have enough exposure to these order
issues given to the IPS trainees now because, 1 think, the theoretical training pre-empts
most of the time and they do not get enough time. Probably, we will have to give some
attention to this.”
3.13.1 It was also felt that probationers must be exposed to crowd control where it is at its best
or at its worst.
3.13.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Committee that there is an integrated module
now on the aspect of ‘Non-lethal management of crowds’. The OTs are also given practical
exposure of large scale crowd management e.g. Ganesh Visarjan, Moharrum, etc. The Bandobast
arrangements of Kumbh Mela are discussed with OTs by the guest faculty who themselves have
actual experience of handling it.

37
3.13.3 In regard to dealing with peaceful and volatile demonstrations, the Committee was informed
that the Academy trains the probationers exclusively and extensively on dealing with non-violent
agitations and on use of minimum force in any situation. The Academy trains them practically, and
the RAF Unit comes to the Academy and gives the demo on how to control a demonstration and
how to use minimum force. In simulation exercises, the probationers are to act as Police Officers.
While protecting themselves they are required to disperse the mob. The force they can use is tear
gas, water canons, lathi charge, etc. The doctrine of use of minimum force is emphasized at every
stage. This simulation is very useful for the trainees.
3.13.4 The Committee notes the doctrine of use of minimum force by the police personnel
to deal with the volatile and peaceful demonstration. However, the people in general have
police-phobia as the impression of colonial attitude of the police personnel persists in the
minds of the public. Some of the police outrage our incidents linger in the hearts of the
people. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that probationers and in-service
officers should emphasize on handling the peaceful and volatue demonstration with acute
care and sympathy towards the people because India is a democratic country and people of
the nation have every right to express their genuine demands through peaceful
demonstration within the parameters of the Constitution. The officers, when on duty are
required to take on the spot decision as there may not be time to consult seniors.
Therefore, emphasjs should be laid in the training on dealing with such situations.
TRAINING ON DISASTER MANAGEMENT
3.14 One expert underlined the need for IPS probationers to be put through principles of disaster
management.
3.14.1 Explaining about training modules on Disaster Management, the Director, NPA, replied that
police is the first responder in any major disaster. Police is the most visible and best organized
arm of the Government in such cases. Expert speakers from National Disaster Management
Authority and Police and Administrative Officers, who have handled major disasters like Tsunami,
Earthquake, major accidents, etc. are called to share their experiences and the lessons learnt. The
Director stated that the preparation of disaster management plan at district level is covered in the
training including aspects of preparedness and peace time rehearsals are emphasized.
Contingencies like break down of mobile/wireless communication, road approach and
establishment and working of Incident Command Centre near the place of disaster are
emphasized. Important role of dissemination of information to general public through media,
important role of NGOs in mitigation of the effects of disaster and establishment of Trauma and
Counselling Centres for victims is also emphasized. The use of Media for educating and
counselling the public is also stressed upon.
3.14.2 Within a period of twenty months, in Kolkata itself, forty-three people died when
fire gutted the fifth and sixth floors of the Stephen Court building and more than ninety
people lost their lives in Advanced Medicare and Research Institute (AMRI) Hospital. When
five major fire accidents occurred in large hospitals in London between January, 2008 and
February, 2009, nobody died; in fact, not a single case of “significant adverse health affect”
was reported. In Northwick Park Hospital, a large district-level health care facility, 123
patients, including the brain injured, were safely evacuated in 23 minutes, while it took
fifteen minutes to the rescuer to reach AMRI Hospital costing several lives. The Committee
feels that there needs more practical training including simulation. Whenever any disaster
takes place, they should be sent for real time experience and training. The Committee
recommends that NPA should keep in these things in mind and prepare the requisite
training modules on disaster management in the country.

38
NATIONAL SECURITY/INTERNAL SECURITY
3.15 One of the experts indicating that National security issues now-a-days are very important
and take a lot of attention at the national and the State levels, therefore, NPA should introduce a
course preferably, a few lectures on national security issues should be devoted.
3.15.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Committee that NPA organizes lectures on the
issues of National Security and also runs a full training seminar on National Security which is
attended by officers from IAS, IPS, IFoS, Defence Services and Central Police Organizations.
3.15.2 India is a dominant player of the global economy and global politics and there are
a lot of geo-political and the national security issues which are of utmost concern, therefore
training modules covering National Security issues are indispensable. Therefore, training
modules should not only cover the course in terms of terrorism or left wing extremism but
also in terms of security of vital installations like Dams, Atomic Energy installations,
Refineries and various other security considerations with in the territory of the country.
3.15.3 An expert suggested that IPS probationers should have to be put through a training of
unarmed combat, close quarter combat. A greater proficiency in handling weapons is required.
Emphasising on the same issue another expert added that an IPS officer need to get exposure to
real problems like insurgency that prevail in India and training to conduct operations against
insurgents.
3.15.4 A member of the Committee was of the view that officers training should also include
exposure to modern and sophisticated arms and weapons and after the completion of their
curriculum they can be sent to the areas where criminal activities are going on where the jungle
warfare is going on. The Ministry of Home Affairs replied that Applied UAC is an integral part of
training. A separate Tactics Wing is there to impart training in operational combat, reflex shooting.
3.15.5 The Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Committee that all IPS trainees undergo a one
week attachment with Greyhounds, AP to familiarize them with anti-naxal operations. Inputs on
tactical operations by the police are given by the Tactics Wing of NPA through demos, practical
exercises, case studies, jungle camp, urban intervention modules etc.
3.15.6 They are also addressed on various aspects of urban intervention by the experienced
practitioners drawn from all over the country. The States affected with Naxalism etc. have their
own protocols to address the needs of IPS officers allotted to those States in this regard. The
Ministry further added that NPA is soon going to acquire 400 acres of land to create its own jungle
training platforms and combat shooting ranges. An Urban Intervention training infrastructure is fast
coming up at the NPA campus and is likely to be completed by early 2013.
3.15.7 The Committee is of the view that Officers Trainee should be imparted training to
handle the latest and sophisticated weapons to ensure that the police are always ahead of
the criminals in terms of handling guns and weapons. Early action may be taken to have
the infrastructure for urban intervention training.
EMERGING AREAS OF CRIMES
3.16 One expert pointing out the emerging areas of crimes and the need for imparting requisite
and adequate training to police personnel, felt that times have changed and we have modernized
and crimes are becoming more and more sophisticated, more and more diabolical. Things like cyber
crimes, economic offences, white collar crimes of various kinds are taking place. We need to
device training modules to tackle these aspects of criminal law enforcement. Today, most of the
offences that we deal with are of this kind.

39
3.16.1 In response to above suggestions, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that at present in
NPA probationers are being exposed to various modules which inter-alia includes Tactics, Cyber-
crime, Simulated crime, Police Station, Documentation, Case file scrutiny, Interrogation, Core
Intelligence, Forensic, Visible crime, Visible intelligence, Empowered Society, Turn-around
strategy, Sensitization (Sectarian conflict, Marginalized section, Gender, Human Trafficking,
Visibly Lost Children, Integrity, Third degree), Non-lethal crowd management, Composite code,
Drug, Traffic, Media, Soft Skills, Budget-Financial Management, Disaster Management, Strategic
Leadership.
3.16.2 As regards the training imparted to officers on cyber crimes and cyber laws, the
Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the IPS officers are given adequate training in Cyber
Laws, detection and investigation of cyber crimes including e-mails and other messages, etc.
In addition to giving these inputs, during basic training, to IPS probationers, the Academy runs
courses on “Cyber Crimes” (Basic and Advanced levels) to train in-service officers in the
Cyber domain.
3.16.3 The Ministry further stated that the IPS probationers are given extensive inputs on Cyber
Crimes. This include provisions of IT Act, Cyber Forensic Tools for detection and collection of
evidence. This is reinforced with practical hands-on exercises in Cyber Forensic Lab at the
Academy. Cyber Crime Experts are called from outside for specialised inputs. It was also stated
that the Academy has developed a Module on Sensitization of the IPS Probationers towards
Communal Biases and Problems. This has helped in removing personal biases among the trainers
and in upholding the spirit of the Constitution.
3.16.4 In the modern world, police officers need training not only on cyber laws, but also
the nuances of hacking to decode encrypted e-mails and other messages. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that NPA should give thorough training to the police
officers to deal with computer hacking and related cyber crimes.
3.16.5 The Committee understands that a lot of sophistication is being brought into the
crime, and therefore, corresponding modification in training modules to cover changing
aspects of crime are but natural. The Committee desires that there is an urgent need to
reverse the general perception “that the police are always behind the criminals in terms of
training and knowledge as well as the use of arms and weapons”. NPA may take a lead in
this regard.

DEVELOPMENT INTERVENTIONS (ODIS)

(iii) The Academy is not able to attract required instructional/support staff by way of

(v) There is no pool of quality field trainers during District Practical Training which

CHAPTER-IV
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATONS
OF THE COMMTTEE — AT A GLANCE
MISSION STATEMENT
The Committee notes with appreciation the purpose of the Academy and its vision.
The Committee hopes that the Academy would continue to endeavour to implement the
vision of Sardar Vallabbhai Patel and make it a world class police training institute.
(Para 1.2.4)
MANAGEMENT BY ACTIVITIES AND MANAGEMENT BY OBJECTIVES
The Committee, while taking note of the fact that the academy is guided by
Management by Activities (MBA) as well as the Management by Objectives (MBO), is of the
view that the academy should always be open for continuous improvement and change in
achieving the set objectives. (Para 1.5.4)
DIRECTOR : POWER AND FUNCTIONS
The Committee understands that Director of NPA is of a significant position in the
Academy so far its functioning is concerned. The personality of the Director leaves a lasting
impression on the functioning of the Academy. His job profile requires him to be a good
leader, motivator and communicator. Therefore, there should be a well laid procedure for
selection of the Director, NPA. The Committee also feels that the fixed tenure of the
Director would give a certain period for him for planning and executing the set objectives.
Since, the Directors of IB, CBI and RAW are given a fixed tenure, the Director of NPA
should also be given a fixed tenure on the same analogy. Since the Ministry has agreed for
careful selection with a fixed tenure, the Committee recommends that Government may lay
down an appropriate selection procedure. The Committee agrees with the Ministry view
point that the Director should be a serving officer. (Para 1.6.5)
The Committee takes note of the comparative position of delegated powers to
Director, NPA and LBS NAA. The Committee is constrained to note that Director, NPA, is
comparatively at a disadvantageous position so far the exercise of delegated financial powers
are concerned even after the revision. The Ministry should have given similar powers to
Director, NPA at par with Director, LBS NAA. Now that the proposal is already under
consideration, the Committee recommends that an early decision may be taken in the
matter. (Para 1.6.9)
SELECTION OF FACULTY
The Committee feels that since the nature and style of crimes are changing due to
technological development, modernization and sophistication, faculty needs to be chosen with
great care. Stringent yardsticks have to be laid down for the selection of faculty not only
at the teaching staff level but also at the level of Assistant Directors and Deputy Directors.
The teaching staff from all fields viz . law, business management, human resource
43

44
management, police science, forensic sciences, criminology, sociology, Psychology, etc. must
be selected with due care keeping in view the requirement of the academy and also taking
into account its role and the responsibility. The Committee also understands that the post
of the Assistant Directors, is very important and their selection should be done through a
stringent selection procedure. High caliber, integrity and efficiency should be the criteria for
selection. (Para 1.7.6)
PAY-SCALES OF OFFICERS AND STAFF
Since the Ministry of Home Affairs has agreed for pay parity of Director, NPA with
the Chiefs of IB, CBI, BSF and CRPF, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may
finalize the proposal and send it to appropriate Ministry for approval at the earliest.
(Para 1.8.3)
The Committee agrees with the proposal of Ministry of Home Affairs that the pay
structure of the Academy should be brought at par with the CPMFs. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Finance may reconsider the case. The Ministry of Home
Affairs may, accordingly, pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning
Commission. (Para 1.8.5)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may explore other
incentives in addition to the above so that efficient staff is  attracted to the Academy.
(Para 1.8.7)
V ACANCIES IN NPA
The Committee feels that serious efforts are required to fill up the vacant posts. The
Ministry may make serious efforts for posting of IPS officers in NPA. In regard to filing
up of group B posts, advance action may be initiated and regularly pursued with UPSc. The
recruitment rules for the newly created posts may be got approved at the earliest so that
the new staff are in place soon. (Para 1.9.1)
INFRASTRUCTURE
The Committee, while taking note of the basic infrastructure of the academy and
future expansion, recommends that all projects pertaining to expanding the existing
infrastructure should be completed without time and cost over-run and to achieve that end,
Government should extend requisite fund in time. The process of acquiring additional land
for special tactics wing and other purposes may be completed soon so that other works
thereon may be taken up. (Para 1.10.3)
RESEARCH WING OF NPA
The Committee is given to understand that the National Institute of Administrative
Research (NIAR) was established by LBSNAA, Massorie established in 1995 as a Training
and Research Wing of the Academy. The Committee recommends that the NPA may set up
an ‘Institute for Applied Police Research’ instead of a Centre for Applied Research on the
line of NIAR. An early decision may be taken and sufficient infrastructure may be created
near the campus of the Academy for the purpose. (Para 1.11.6)
PUBLICATIONS DIVISION
The Committee understands that the Academy, being the nodal centre of Police

45
Training in India, has to playa leading role in capacity building of State Police Training
Institutions in the country by way of developing and publishing training literature. To this
end, it is necessary to strengthen the Publication Wing in the Academy to publish Research
Papers, books, journals, monographs and other training material from time to time. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Publication Division of the Academy
may be appropriately strengthened. The Committee takes a serious note of the fact that the
sanctioned staff are not in place. Director, NPA may take immediate necessary action in this
regard. (Para 1.12.2)
COMPUTER AND IT
Since, in the contemporary electronic cyber age, success of crime investigation
and intelligence analysis is increasingly dependent upon well equipped computer lab, it
is very much pertinent that the academy management must ensure that NPA’s computer
section is equipped with latest technology and updated programming system. The
Committee is of the view that skilled, and well trained staff should be deployed to
discharge the duties and responsibilities of the computer cell. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that NPA management should take up the issue of constraints of the
manpower with MHA for early filling up of requisite staff. The Committee hopes that
the project in pipeline must be completed within the set time frame. The Committee
also recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may take up the issue of setting up
Training Unit of NIC in NPA with NIC and Ministry of Communication and Information
Technology (CIT). (Para 1.13.6)
RECRUITMENT TO IPS
The Committee in its 161st Report on Demands for Grants (2012-13) made a
recommendation for exploring the possibility of conducting a separate examination for IPS
where the attitude and aptitude of the candidate must be thoroughly tested besides their
mental makeup and inclination for policing. The Committee further recommended that the
Government may impress upon UPSC to conduct a separate examination for recruiting of
IPS officer and SVPNPA may also be consulted in this regard. The Committee, reiterating
the recommendation made in its 161
st Report, desires that the Ministry may hold
consultation with the DoPT and UPSC and take an early decision for holding separate
examination. (Para 1.14.2)
The Committee is of the view that age relaxation under different Government
services is a policy decision keeping in view various considerations. However, the
suggestions of the expert may be looked into. (Para 1.14.5)
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
The Committee, while taking note of budgetary provision to meet the plan and non-
plan expenditure and also of the trends of actual expenditure during last five years,
observes that budgetary provisions have been optimally spent. The Committee further
desires that earmarked allocation for on-going infrastructural projects would be released in
time for completion of projects without time and cost overruns. The Committee also
recommends that sufficient allocations may be made available to NPA to complete the
ongoing infrastructure projects, CNE works and other new projects and also for
strengthening publication division. Grants may also be provided for setting up the Research
Institute in case it is decided to set up the same. (Para 1.15.4)

46
AUDIT OBJECTION
The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that out of 20 audit paras
on non-plan expenditure, only one para was dropped and response to the 19 paras were
further objected to. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that due care may be
taken in incurring expenditure, both plan and non-plan. (Para 1.16.2)
TRAINING PROGRAMMES: INDOOR VS. OUTDOOR TRAINING
Though the quantum of the indoor and outdoor training cannot be fixed in terms of
percentage, however, sufficient outdoor training must be imparted to have the physical
fitness of the police personnel while indoor training should be so adequately imparted to
ensure that the police personnel possess requisite understanding of law and jurisprudential
knowledge. The NPA may have a relook at the present curriculum and reviewed with
experts. (Para 2.3.4)
Field Visit
The Committee is of the view that the basic training modules of the Academy must
consist of the courses keeping in view stark reality of society and the aim of the training
programme should be to impart knowledge and skill to face the ground challenges of the
country. The Committee also feels that training on management and administration should
also be provided. When the officers grow higher up the ladder, they are also required to
handle administration and finance. Training needs to be given on these aspects as well and
some modules may be prepared for these aspects. (Para 2.4.1)
MID CAREER TRAINING PROGRAMME (MCTP)
The Committee notes that the Academy is collaborating with some of the foreign
universities of reputation viz Cambridge, Charles Sturt, London School of Business for
conducting its pioneer Mid-Career Training Programme for senior police-personnel.
However, the Committee feels that the Academy should also explore collaboration with
institution in other countries having expertise in Police Training and Development (T&D for
Police) with the purpose of not only improving capabilities and skill among serving police
officers to combat effectively the ever changing wide ranging challenges of terrorism,
naxalism, caste and communal conflict, drug trafficking, accidents, natural calamities and
other disasters, but also to evolve different training modules concerning standard policing
practices to make the Academy a centre of excellence. The Committee, in this regard,
recommends that NPA management should prepare a comprehensive strategy in this
direction for further foreign collaboration and seek the requisite approval from the
Government for implementation. Besides different phases of MCTP programmes, need based
refresher courses may also be organized for a week at regular intervals. (Para 2.5.8)
The Committee is of the opinion that exposure to best policing practices should also
be imparted at training stage, if feasible, preferably in countries with similar democratic
political set up. The Committee believes that training modules consisting of foreign
collaborations having police agencies of the country having similar political and economic
condition as that of India would have immense impact so far as their policing skill is
concerned. The Academy may consider this aspect. (Para 2.5.10)
SPECIAL TACTICS WING
The Committee notes the initiatives and activities taken by NPA in imparting special

47
tactical training to police officers. The Committee, however, also takes note of the fact that
STW is having its man power on ad-hoc basis. This will not help in better functioning of
the work. Efforts may be made to put in place dedicated manpower at the earliest.
Directional level tactics course for senior officers of the rank of DIG and above be started
at the earliest. Fund requirements of NPA for developing allotted land for tactical training,
separate STW Building, procurement of equipments and weapons may be looked into
promptly so as to make the Special Tactics Wing par excellence. This level of excellence
may further be used for revenue generation by imparting such training to the police officers
of other countries. (Para 2.6.7)
FOREIGN TRAINING
The Committee recommends that the proposal to send IPS probationers to Japan and
Singapore for training during phase-II may be positively considered by Ministry of Home
Affairs. The Committee feels that community policing can play a major role in curbing
crimes in India keeping in mind the low police population ratio and a big democratic set-
up in the country. (Para 2.7.2)
Foreign visit of the probationers in phase II of the training schedule is the
appropriate time when the probationers, after having an understanding of the system within
the country, can have a comparative study of the system of obtaining abroad. The
Committee recommends that the proposal under consideration of MHA may be examined
soon and an early decision may be taken. (Para 2.7.9)
Faculty and Linkages
The Committee is of the view that if the Academy feels that linkages with training
institutions of developed countries such as USA, UK, etc. would be useful the Academy may
prepare a blueprint of the proposal and take up the matter with the Ministry of Home
Affairs. But the linkages should be productive, and result oriented instead of just
ornamental. (Para 2.8.1)
The Committee notes that the Academy does not invite faculty or resource persons
from abroad and the main reason is lack of incentives and remunerations. However under
institutional tie up for MCTP, for eign resource persons are also involved. The Committee
is of the view that whenever any foreign experts comes to India, such visits may be made
use of by organizing their sessions for both basic training and MCTP. (Para 2.8.5)
Tie up with foreign police agencies would definitely give an opportunity to the trainee
officers to understand the nuances of working of police agencies in other countries. The
Committee is of the considered view that the faculty exchange programmes with other
foreign police agencies and training institutes would give an opportunity for exchange of
views among the faculty and to refresh their knowledge. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that tie-ups with foreign institutes for both trainees and faculty may be
organized for better exposure. (Para 2.8.7)
The Committee feels that the training module introduced in 2012 may be assessed
and complete literature and manuals may be prepared. (Para 2.8.11)
LACK OF QUALITY TRAINING PROGRAMME
The Committee, however, feels that there is a lack of quality training programmes
for the faculty. For better training of the police officers, the faculty should have better

48
exposure to latest methodologies, technologies available within the country and abroad. NPA
may have a relook into this. (Para 2.9.1)
COMPARATIVE STUDY OF POLICE STRUCTURES AND POLICE SYSTEMS
The Committee feels that teaching of a comparative study of police structures and
police systems over the world at NPA at the induction stage also would enable the
probationer to have a much wider horizon and a much larger perspective, and would further
enable them to introduce small improvements in police working on the basis of their
knowledge of the overall police systems and police structures. There should be a course on
comparative police systems. NPA may look into this. (Para 2.10.1)
Training on Administrative, Financial and Social issues
The Committee desires that NPA may have a relook at the present modules and
incorporate specific aspects on administrative and financial management if they are not
sufficiently covered. (Para 2.11.2)
TRAINING SCHEDULE
The Committee is not satisfied with the cryptic reply of the Ministry. The Committee is,
therefore, of the view that there needs to be some institutional safeguards to the syllabi and
curriculum. Attempt to derail the training schedule should not be allowed. (Para 2.12.1)
COORDINATION WITH OTHER POLICE ACADEMIES
The Committee feels that internal security is a major concern across the Country and
supervision and surveillance by the Police Personnel around the country is of utmost
significance. With the sophistication and changing nature of crimes, a well equipped and
professional police personnel are required all over the country. Integrated police training is,
therefore the natural corollary. The Committee recommends that NPA should act like what
the NCERT does for other training schools of states and the experience gained at the NPA
must percolate to the state and the district training schools for the benefit of the police
training at the grass root level. The Committee agrees with the suggestion of the Ministry
for setting up of a common forum for all State Police Training academies with the NPA at
Apex and under its Aegis. A serious thought may be given to this suggestion. (Para 2.13.2)
LAW AND JURISPRUDENCE IN TRAINING MODULES
The Committee agrees that an in-depth understanding of jurisprudential principles
would inject legal insight to the IPS officer which would certainly help them solve the legal
issues involved in the case. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is further scope for
enhancing the module on law and jurisprudence in the training curriculum of IPS officers.
Therefore, the entire module on law and jurisprudence may be revisited involving some
legal experts. (Para 3.1.2)
Case Study
The Committee agrees that case based study would enrich the knowledge of trainees.
An early decision may be taken to set up Case S tudy Wing in the Academy. All the training
modules may contain the case study so that it leaves a lasting impact in the minds of
trainees. (Para 3.2.2)

49
The Committee hopes that the introduction of Integrated Training format would
enable the IPS officers to have in depth understanding of rejoinder of crimes. The format
may be thoroughly assessed after one year. (Para 3.2.7)
ETHICAL AND MORAL V ALUES AND INTEGRATION
The Committee is of the view that since policing does have a bearing on the lives
of individuals and, therefore, Police Personnel, particularly officers should possess high
moral and ethical values so as to arrest the declining trend in quality and standard of
public life. The Committee believes that when the pursuit of social commitment and
integrity is effectively imbibed into police personnel irrespective of rank and file, the
malaise and qualms of corruption could be eradicated from public life to a large extent.
Transparency and public accountability is a pre-requisite for good governance. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the training modules prepared for probationers
and also for in-service officers must cover the lessons on ethical traits and moral
behaviour. (Para 3.3.2)
The Committee observes that Officer is generally vested with the power which
extends at times to taking life and liberty of the people but what matters is how he
exercises his power. Therefor e, emphasis should also be given as to how to use the power.
The Committee is also given to understand that in other countries like Japan training
curriculum contain the constant emphasis on ethical aspects in policing so that while doing
a particular job, a set of principles has to be adhered to. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that adequate emphasis should be laid in the training programme of Officers
Trainee and NPA should teach probationers good policing practice which is practicised
globally. Modules on ethical values and morality should also be included in the MCTP
programmes as it is equally required at that stage as well. (Para 3.3.3)
The Committee desires that the message of the Preamble to the constitution of
India, being “Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic” should not only be read
and understood by the police personnel but should also be imprinted into their ‘hearts and
minds’ to be reflected into their actions while dealing with actual incidents. Keeping in view
the fact that India is a vast country with complex social structure i.e. multi-lingual, multi-
ethnic, multi-religious, training modules must give emphasis to these aspects. A sense of
justice and sensitivity towards the people particularly of weaker sections should be initiated
by them. (Para 3.3.5)
TRAINING MODULES ON LEFT-WING EXTREMISM AND TERRORISM
The left wing extremism is spreading its tentacles across the country and a well
prepared module needs to be prepared for training on dealing with this. Greyhounds of
Andhra Pradesh Police has been successful in dealing with this and they can be a role model
in regard to this training. If possible, the probationers may be attached with greyhounds for
some period. NPA should become centre of excellence in giving training on dealing with left
wing extremism. (Para 3.4.2)
PSYCHOLOGICAL PROFILING
The Committee desires that psychological profiling may be made use of for better
counselling and de-stressing. Yoga is a good tool for de-stressing and to rein in the mind
and this may be used to the maximum extent. (Para 3.5.2)

50
PEOPLE-FRIENDLY POLICING
The image of Government depends more on the reaction of the rank and file of the
law enforcing agencies particularly police officers towards the common man, when the
common man approaches them in the hour of need. The Committee, therefore, feels that
police being at the cutting edge level needs to adopt courteous behavior and friendly
temperament so that people may approach them without fear and with faith to have redressal
of their grievances. The Committee, therefore, recommends that training modules and
practical training courses as imparted by NPA must include all behavioral and attitudinal
aspects and the Academy should work on this. The Ministry should oversee the
implementation of the Mission. An early decision may be taken in this regard. (Para 3.6.5)
ACCESS OF SUB-ORDINATES TO SENIOR POLICE OFFICER
The Committee firmly believes that open access of constabulary to higher police
personnel and hassle-free communication among them would ensure higher degree of trust
and faith amongst each other which would not only lead to redressal of grievances of
constabulary but would also help in taking strategic decisions, formulation of pragmatic
plans based on the situation and experience at grass root level and execution thereof to
achieve set objectives. This will also improve the efficiency of the forces. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the training modules should invariably exphasise this. This
needs to be done both in the NPA as well as the training courses of States and District
Training Centres. (Para 3.7.2)
PREPARATION OF CHARGE SHEETS ETC.
Despite the training being imparted to IPS probationers by NPA on the supervision
of preparation of the criminal charge sheets, the shortcomings continue to persist in
making the charge sheets at the initial stage which have been in many cases found faulty
by the various courts, resulting in acquittal of the accused and putting on sorry figure for
the police, as a whole. It is a known fact that in several cases, justice is either denied or
yet to see the light of the day due to lacunae in FIR and incomplete framing of the charge
sheet. In this background, the Committee recommends that IPS probationers as well as the
in-service officers must be imparted adequate training to enhance their supervising skill so
that FIRs and charge sheets must be prepared in a comprehensive manner. The
probationers should be made fully conversant with the procedure of preparation of charge
sheet and framing charges. (Para 3.8.1)
TRAINING ON COURT PROCEDURES
Though moot court Proceedings at the Academy are good and give theoretical aspect
but does not give the true picture of the courts. Dealing with court cases is an important
aspect of the policing. The actual procedure of the courts is not only complex but
cumbersome also, and the attachment of the probationers for a period of seven days does
not appear sufficient. The Committee therefore, recommends that probationers should be
given sufficient actual court exposure so that inadequacies on the part of the agencies of
the Government do not become a stumbling bloc in the disposal of the case. NPA should,
therefore, consider to give sufficient emphasize on this. (Para 3.9.1)
COMMUNITY POLICING
The Committee notes that one of the Police Mission set out by the Prime Minister is

51
on Community Policing and the Ministry is considering the report of the Committee thereon.
After it is decided to implement it, NPA may take a cue from this and include it in the
course. On the basis of experience of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, NPA may prepare a manual on
community policing which can be useful for probationers of NPA and all other States Police
Organisation. The Committee views that community policing implies people’s participation in
local security arrangement and, therefore, leads to much interaction between the police and
people. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the mission on Community Policing
should be included in the State and District Police Training Centres of various States and
literature procured at the centre must also be disseminated. (Para 3.10.1)
DEALING WITH THE CHALLENGES OF TERRORISM
Though after reviewing the police response to Mumbai attack and finding that there
was a big gap between the training imparted and the actual requirement of tactical skill to
combat the potential menace of terrorism, a separate wing called ‘Special Tactics Wing
(STW)’ has been set up in NPA with the objective of imparting training to State Police and
Central Armed Police Forces to enable them to conduct tactical operation against the
terrorists in jungle and urban environment, the efforts are not complete as yet. The urban
intervention training infrastructure is likely to be completed in 2013. This may be
completed as per schedule. (Para 3.11.3)
NPA should think and act ahead of the terrorists on the possible techniques and
technologies likely to be used by terrorists and start training in advance. Government may
provide necessary infrastructure to NPA. Training on ‘preventive steps to prevent the
possible terrorist attack is required. Lesson from USA are required to be learnt where
9/11 incident has not been repeated. The Committee recommends that NPA has to take
initiative to make headway in training in this regard. (Para 3.11.4)
The Committee is of the view that since the country is facing terrorist threats
counter Intelligence techniques and anti-terrorism operations need to be included in the
curriculum so that the officers who come out are well-versed in the counter-terrorism
intelligence techniques. (Para 3.11.5)
INTELLIGENCE COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS
The Committee is surprised to find that although probationers are given elaborate
training on the intelligence collection and analysis but there is no dearth of intelligence
failures which led to massive incidents killing several innocent persons. Though, intelligence
success is rarely reported in the media its failure attracts immediate attention of the media
besides immensely affecting the lives of the people. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the training modules on intelligence collection and analysis must be comprehensive and
the same may be replicated at the State and District Police Training Centre. (Para 3.12.3)
LAW AND ORDER
The Committee notes the doctrine of use of minimum force by the police personnel
to deal with the volatile and peaceful demonstration. However, the people in general have
police-phobia as the impression of colonial attitude of the police personnel persists in the
minds of the public. Some of the police outrage our incidents linger in the hearts of the
people. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that probationers and in-service
officers should emphasize on handling the peaceful and volatile demonstration with acute
care and sympathy towards the people because India is a democratic country and people of

52
the nation have every right to express their genuine demands through peaceful
demonstration within the parameters of the Constitution. The officers, when on duty are
required to take on the spot decision as there may not be time to consult seniors.
Therefore, emphasis should be laid in the training on dealing with such situations.
(Para 3.13.4)
TRAINING ON DISASTER MANAGEMENT
Within a period of twenty months, in Kolkata itself, forty-three people died when
fire gutted the fifth and sixth floors of the Stephen Court building and more than ninety
people lost their lives in Advanced Medicare and Research Institute (AMRI) Hospital.
When five major fire accidents occurred in large hospitals in London between January,
2008 and February, 2009, nobody died; in fact, not a single case of “significant adverse
health affect” was reported. In Northwick Park Hospital, a large district-level health
care facility, 123 patients, including the brain injured, were safely evacuated in 23
minutes, while it took fifteen minutes to the rescuer to reach AMRI Hospital costing
several lives. The Committee feels that there needs more practical training including
simulation. Whenever any disaster takes place, they should be sent for real time
experience and training. The Committee recommends that NPA should keep in these
things in mind and prepare the requisite training modules on disaster management in
the country. (Para 3.14.2)
NATIONAL SECURITY/INTERNAL SECURITY
India is a dominant player of the global economy and global politics and there are
a lot of geo-political and the national security issues which are of utmost concern, therefore
training modules covering National Security issues are indispensable. Therefore, training
modules should not only cover the course in terms of terrorism or left wing extremism but
also in terms of security of vital installations like Dams, Atomic Energy installations,
Refineries and various other security considerations with in the territory of the country.
(Para 3.15.2)
The Committee is of the view that Officers Trainee should be imparted training to
handle the latest and sophisticated weapons to ensure that the police are always ahead of
the criminals in terms of handling guns and weapons. Early action may be taken to have
the infrastructure for urban intervention training. (Para 3.15.7)
EMERGING AREAS OF CRIMES
In the modern world, police officers need training not only on cyber laws, but also
the nuances of hacking to decode encrypted e-mails and other messages. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that NPA should give thorough training to the police
officers to deal with computer hacking and related cyber crimes. (Para 3.16.4)
The Committee understands that a lot of sophistication is being brought into the
crime, and therefore, corresponding modification in training modules to cover changing
aspects of crime are but natural. The Committee desires that there is an urgent need to
reverse the general perception “that the police are always behind the criminals in terms of
training and knowledge as well as the use of arms and weapons”. NPA may take a lead in
this regard. (Para 3.16.5)

53
KEY CONCERN AREAS OF WORKING OF THE ACADEMY AND ORGANIZATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT INTERVENTIONS (ODIS)
The Committee notes the key concern areas affecting the working of the academy
and is of the considered view that in order to overcome key concern areas of the working
of the academy, specific Organizational Development Interventions (ODI) are required to
enable the Academy to achieve its objectives and mission. Some of the issues such as staff/
faculty, research wing and foreign training have already been dealt, in detail, in the
preceding paragraphs. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry may
consider all the issues and find solution to them so as to strengthen the Academy. The
Ministry may help NPA management undertake concerted efforts to implement
organizational development interventions to strengthen organizational structure and to
enhance the functional proficiency of the Academy. (Para 3.17.1)
PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF NPA
The Committee hopes that the outcome of performance evaluation of NPA done by
Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI), Hyderabad would be of immense use for
strengthening NPA and its programmes. The Committee also desires that BPR&D may
conduct an independent evaluation of the basic and MCTP Training imparted at NPA.
(Para 3.18.3)
SWOT - ANALYSIS OF THE WORKING OF THE ACADEMY
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should take note of the SWOT
(Strength, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats) analysis of the Academy and make
strategies to overcome its weaknesses and threats. The Government should also take
advantages of NPA’s strength and opportunities in making it the world class training centre.
In this regard, the Committee recommends that the management should also evolve new
training platforms and training methodologies and make continuous revaluation, self-
introspection and self-review, 3rd Party Audit, Seminars, Workshops, adaptations to change.
The management may further formalize institutional tie ups with the police training
academies of other countries with the purpose of learning the best practices in training of
other countries and catch up the standards achieved by the western countries.
(Para 3.19.1)
The Committee has dealt most of the issues in preceding paras and gave its
recommendations. One area of concern for the Committee is lack of priority for training
for police in the States. This is a big challenge and needs to be addressed. The Ministry of
Home Affairs may start a new scheme for strengthening police training in the States. On
making Academy training more relevant and reducing gap between rule of law and field
reality, existing modules may be revisited with more field orientation. (Para 3.20)

Mohan Rao, Former DGP & Former Governor of Tamil Nadu; (ii) Shri Shanker Sen, Ex-Director,
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy and Senior Fellow, Institute of Social Sciences;
