STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The Legislative Assembly of Karnataka passed a resolution on
17.3-2010 and the Legislative Council of the State also passed a
similar resolution on 18.3.2010, to make special provisions for the
Hyderabad-Karnataka areas of the State of Karnataka. The
Government of Karnataka has also endorsed the need for special
provisions for the region. The resolutions seek to accelerate
development of the most backward region of the State and promote
inclusive growth with a view to reducing inter-district and inter-
regional disparities in the State.
2. The special provisions aim to establish an institutional
mechanism for equitable allocation of funds to meet the development
needs over the said region, as well as to enhance human resources
and promote employment from the region by providing for local
cadres in service and reservation in educational and vocational
training institutions by an amendment to the Constitution of India.
3. It is accordingly proposed to insert a new Article 371J in
the Constitution to provide for special provisions for the erstwhile
Hyderabad-Karnataka areas of the State of Karnataka which consist
of the districts of Gulbarga, Bidar, Raichur, Koppal and Yadgir and
additionally include the Bellary District. The article in the form of a
special provision seeks to provide for:—
(a) establishment of a separate Development Board for
the aforesaid region mentioned above;
(b) provide for equitable allocation of funds for
development over the said region subject to the requirements
of the State as a whole;
(c) provide reservation in public employment through
the constitution of local cadres for domiciles of the region;
and
(d) provide for reservation in education and vocational
training institutions for domiciles of the region.
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

CHIEF MINISTER BANGALORE- 560 001

Respected Sir,
Sub: Furnishing opinion to the Government of India on the Constitution of
India (118 th Amendment) Bill, 2012 proposing to insert Article 371-J
conferring special status to the Hyderabad-Karnataka area.
As you are kindly aware, Government of India has placed the Constitution of India (118th
Amendment) Bill, 2012 before the Rajyasabha to insert the Article 371-J in the Constitution of India
as approved by the Union Cabinet. In pursuance to this, Rajya Sabha has constituted a
Parliamentary Committee to deliberate on the contents of the above bill and have circulated certain
questionnaire. The Government of India have also solicited the opinion of the Government of
Karnataka.
It is seen from the records available in the State Government that no consultation was held
with the State Government on the contents of the Article 371-J prior to either bringing it before
the Union Cabinet or before introduction in the Rajya Sabha. The State Government have examined
the contents of the above Bill and has come to know that it is a combination of contents of Article
371(2) aplicable to the State of Maharashtra and the Article 371-D applicable to the State of Andhra
Pradesh. As you are aware, the Government of Karnataka and the people of Karnataka have always
been requesting only for regional reservation in technical education and employment as provided in
the Article 371-D. The intent of the resolution passed by both the Houses of the State Legislature
is also limited to the same.
Government of India had been suggesting for ceation of Development Boards in Karnataka
on the lines of Maharashtra under Article 371(2) of the Constitution. The State Government has
examined the Maharashtra Model in 2005 itself and felt that special Developmental Plan as visaged
by the High Power Committee headed by Dr D.M. Nanjundappa on regional balance is much suited
to the Karnataka situation rather than establishing Regional Development Boards on the pattern of
Maharashtra. It is for this reason, the State Government took a decision to implement the
recommendations for Special Development Plan for a period of eight years commencing from
2007-08 and during the preceding four years (2007-08 to 2010-11) Rs.9161 crores has been
earmarked for SDP. Since the efforts made during Annual Plan Discussion during 2007-08 with
Planning Commission to pursuade the GoI to con-finance the SDP failed, the same is being
implemented as a subset of the normal plan programme.
The implementation of SDP has shown diverse progress across the districts. While
utilisation of resource is satisfactory and higher in Non-Hyderabad Karnataka districts, it is much
lesser in Hyderabad Karnataka region districts, the key reason being lack of trained man power.
Hence a major impediment in achieving its objective of balanced regional development in the
46

47
delivery of key services in the social sector is lack of adequate personnel at the cutting edge. This
is due to the lack of provision for regional reservation which would have enabled local people to
gain employment for the posts at the district and sub-district level.
It is for this reason the State Government had urged that a constitutional amendment under
Article 371-D is necessitated for providing regional reservation. Since the Government of India and
the Planning Commission are not coming forward to finance the Special Development Plans
implemented by the State Government, there is no justification to opt for provisions similar to
Article 371(2) on the pattern of the State of Maharashtra for constitution of Regional Boards etc.
This State Government is confident that, with regional reservations in employment and technical
education, its own multipronged regional balance programme and the regional boards would be
effective in redressing the imbalance. Hence State Government feels that there is no justification
and need for the provision for the constitutional status to the regional boards.
The State Cabinet in its meeting held on 6-11-2012 has deliberated the matter at length and
has decided to furnish its considered opinion on the proposed Constitution of India (118
th –
Amendment) Bill 2012 proposing to insert Article 371-J regarding special status to Hyderabad
Karnataka region and to request the Government of India and the Hon’ble Parliamentary Sub-
Committee on the amendment as follows :–
(i) The Constitution (118
th Amendment) Bill, 2012 for inserting the Article 371-J
may be modified in conformity with the Article 371-D conferring similar special
status to the Hyderabad-Karnataka Areas as per the resolution passed by both
the Houses of the State Legislature and to drop all other provisions similar to
the Article 371(2) applicable to the State of Maharashtra.
(ii) The Government of India and the Planning Commission are requested to allocate
special funds for the development of the Hyderabad - Karnataka Area.
The State Cabinet noted that this decision is in consonance with the unanimous resolution
of both the houses of the State Legislature.
In view of the above, the State Government of Karnataka earnestly request you Sir, to
unably modify the proposed Constitution of India (118
th Amendment), Bill 2012 proposing to insert
Article 371-J regarding special status to Hyderabad-Karnataka region on the lines of the opinion
furnished above.
With warm regards,

1.3 INTRODUCTION OF EXPENDITURE MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
1.3.1 The Committee appreciates introduction of expenditure management and feedback
mechanism in the Ministry to monitor the projects undertaken. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry should further enhance this mechanism to check leakages. The Committee feels that the
officials of the Ministry should be provided training on internal audit, information system audit
and fraud examination in acclaimed institutions. While giving enhanced financial delegation to
field organizations, efforts should also be made to ensure that there are no leakages in the
expenditure and delays in implementation. (Para 2.21.8 ibid)

1.3.2 The recommendation of the Committee is to have a functional and efficient internal audit

6
regime in the Ministry and to build upon the initiatives already taken in this area. There has been

internal audit and fraud investigations. Even the expenditure incurred in taking these courses is
being reimbursed. Training programs are being organized to up-grade skills in the area of risk based
auditing, report writing and Computer Assisted Auditing Techniques (CAATs). As a step towards
decentralization, enhanced powers are being delegated to field offices. Internal audit universe has
been planned to ensure coverage to a large number of these field offices to ensure that financial
procedures are being followed and there are no leakages in the system.
1.3.3 Also, to further strengthen and modernize the internal auditing systems in the Ministry
training programs would be organized and attended both at the national as well as international
levels. The skill upgradation of officers/officials at the cutting edge level would be the primary
focus of the organization.

Recommendation

to the internal security of our country. Though, the casualities have come down in 2011 the figure
was showing upward trend till 2010. The Committee notes that the Government has approved
extension of Security Related Expenditure (SRE) Scheme for LWE-affected States for another 5
years beyond 31
st March, 2011. The Government should regularly watch implementation of the
scheme. (Para 3.2.15 ibid)
Action Taken
1.4.2 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State subjects, action with respect to maintenance of law
and order lies primarily in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with the
various issues related to Left Wing Extremist (LWE) activities in the States. The Central
Government monitors the situation closely and supplements and coordinates their efforts in several
ways, inter-alia, including reimbursement of expenditure incurred by the State Governments on
Anti-naxal Operations under the SRE Scheme.
1.4.3 Considering the usefulness of the SRE Scheme, the Central Government has approved
extension of the Scheme for a further period of five years beyond 31.3.2011. Also, the Scheme
has now been extended to 20 more LWE affected districts, taking the total coverage to 103
districts.
1.4.4 The SRE Scheme, being a reimbursement scheme, the expenditure is first incurred by the
State Governments and thereafter reimbursed by the Central Government after conducting audit in
the respective States. However, 25% advance of the approved Annual Work Plan outlay is provided
to the State Governments concerned in the beginning of the financial year for smooth
implementation of the Scheme.
1.5 SOCIAL SCHEMES OF NAXAL AFFECTED AREAS
Recommendation
1.5.1 The Committee is aware of the fact that the naxal affected regions are underdeveloped areas
with less infrastructure facilities. The Committee is of considered view that schemes such as
Integrated Action Plan (IAP) for Selected Tribal and Backward Districts for accelerated

7
development and Security Related Expenditure (SRE) Scheme should be implemented at a fast pace
in the naxal affected areas. The Committees desires that the Government should make efforts for
implementing the flagship programmes in a proper manner to ensure that the targeted groups are
benefited. The Committee believes that providing employment opportunities to disgruntled youths,
good governance and proper implementation of major development schemes in the areas dominated
by the Maoists, can check the growth of Left Wing Extremism (LWE). Development is the panacea
for the ills of LWE areas. All actions should be directed towards development. The Government,
therefore, should work in tandem with NGOs, local bodies, peoples representatives to spread
awareness among the masses against the outdated ideology of Maoists which is undemocratic and
which believes that power comes through barrel of the gun. (Para 3.2.16 ibid)
Action Taken
1.5.2 The Government’s approach is to deal with Left Wing Extremism (LWE) in a holistic
manner, in the areas of security, development, enforcing rights of local communities, good
governance and public perception management. However, ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State
subjects, action with regard to maintenance of law and order lies primarily in the domain of the
State Governments concerned. The Central Government monitors the situation closely and
supplements the efforts of the State Governments over a wide range of schemes on both, security
and development fronts. The underlying philosophy is to enhance the capacity of the State
Governments to tackle the LWE menace in a concerted manner.
1.5.3 The Planning Commission is implementing the Integrated Action Plan (IAP) in 82 Selected
Tribal and Backward Districts, inter alia , including 71 LWE affected districts, for accelerated
development of the affected areas. The nature of works taken up under the IAP includes public
infrastructure and services which create a perceptible impact on the ground and among the local
communities. An amount of Rs.3840 crore has been released for financial years 2010-11 and 2011-
12 against which expenditure of Rs.2522.06 crore (65.68%) has been reported (up to 15.6.2012).
1.5.4 The Planning Commission, through a Management Information System (MIS), has been
monitoring the implementation of important development programmes/flagship schemes in the IAP
districts and also reviewing the progress through Video Conferences.
1.5.5 The Central Government has approved extension of the Security Related Expenditure (SRE)
Scheme for a further period of five years beyond 31.3.2011, to continue the support provided to
the LWE affected States by way of reimbursing Anti-Naxal Operations related expenditure incurred
in the covered 103 districts.
1.5.6 In order to wean away the potential youth from the path of militancy or Left Wing
Extremism, recruitment guidelines have been revised to permit 40% recruitment in Central Armed
Police Forces from the border areas and areas affected by militancy or Left Wing Extremism.
1.5.7 It is the belief of Government of India that through a combination of development, security
and Forest Rights related interventions, the LWE problem can be successfully tackled. However,
it is clear that the Maoists do not want root causes like underdevelopment addressed in a
meaningful manner since they resort to targeting school buildings, roads, railways, bridges, health
infrastructure, communication facilities etc in a major way. They wish to keep the population in
their areas of influence marginalized to perpetuate their outdated ideology.
1.6 STRENGTHENING SECURITY FORCES
Recommendation
1.6.1 The Government should also explore the channels/agencies such as NGOs/Social Activists

8
who can build pressure on the Maoists to eschew violence and come to the talking table and join
the mainstream. The Committee feels that the schemes implemented by the Government are not
yet yielding the desired results. Government may consider strengthening security forces of States
on the lines of greyhounds in Andhra Pradesh. Joint elite forces can also be an alternative.
(Para 3.2.17 ibid)
Action Taken
1.6.2 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ are State subjects and action with respect to maintenance of law
and order primarily lies in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with specific
issues related to Left Wing Extremism (LWE) activities in the States. The Central Government
closely monitors the situation and supplements and coordinates the efforts of the State
Governments over a wide range of schemes/issues .
1.6.3 The State Governments have from time to time appealed to the Left Wing Extremists,
especially the CPI (Maoist), the most violent group, to abjure violence and hold talks on any issue
of concern to them. But, no concrete results have emerged so far. The CPI (Maoist) Party believes
in overthrowing the present system of Parliamentary democracy through “Protracted People’s War.”
The Central Government would welcome talks between the concerned State Governments and the
Left Wing Extremists, provided the latter abjure violence and give up their so called armed struggle
against the Indian State.
1.6.4 The Government of India has urged the State Governments time and again to raise Special
Forces on the pattern of Greyhounds in Andhra Pradesh, to deal with the LWE menace. Most of
the LWE affected States have taken action and raised such forces to effectively deal with the LWE
problem.
1.7 MODERNISATION OF CENTRAL AND STATE FORCES
Recommendation
1.7.1 The Committee views that although the multi-pronged development strategy is required to
check spread of Left Wing Extremism, the Government should also provide required training to the
Central Police Forces as well as state police forces and modernize them. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the police personnel should be trained properly before sending them to the naxal
affected areas. The Committee also recommends that these personnel should be equipped with all
necessary modern weapons and gadgets. (Para 3.2.18 ibid)
Action Taken
1.7.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing the Scheme for Modernisation of State
Police Forces (MPF Scheme) which is aimed at modernizing the State Police Forces to meet the
challenges to internal security in the form of terrorism and naxalism, law and order problems etc.
1.7.3 ‘Police’ being a State subject as per the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, it
is the responsibility of the concerned State Governments to provide adequate training to the State
Police personnel in keeping with the changing needs. However, the Ministry of Home Affairs has
extended financial assistance to the State Governments under the MPF Scheme, inter-alia , to
upgrade their training infrastructure facilities such as for setting up of police training schools,
police training academies, district training centres etc., setting up of firing ranges, for acquisition
of police training aids/equipment such as grenade simulator, firing simulators, basic infrastructure
required for training schools such as lecture halls, classrooms, projectors etc.

9
1.7.4 Under the Scheme, funds have also been provided to States for acquiring modern arms/
weaponry such as Glock pistols, AK 47 rifles, Insas Rifles, 9 mm pistols, Under Barrel Grenade
Launchers etc.
1.7.5 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State subjects, action with respect to maintenance of law
and order lies primarily in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with the
various issues related to Left Wing Extremist (LWE) activities in the States. The Central
Government monitors the situation closely and supplements and coordinates their efforts in several
ways, inter-alia, including providing Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) to assist the State
Police Forces to deal with the LWE problem. The Central Government also provides assistance in
training of State Police Forces through the Ministry of Defence, Central Police Organisations and
Bureau of Police Research and Development.
1.7.6 The CAPF battalions, prior to their induction in the LWE affected States, undergo Counter
Insurgency/pre-induction training at two stages. At the first stage, they undergo pre-induction
training of four weeks with the Army Infantry units and thereafter familiarization/ orientation
training of 15 days under the respective State Police arrangements.
1.7.7 Besides, in order to strengthen the training inputs of the State Police Forces, Government
has approved setting up of 21 Counter Insurgency and Anti-Terrorist (CIAT) Schools in the States
affected by insurgency and terrorism including Left Wing Extremism. Fifteen such CIAT Schools
have been established in the LWE affected States of Bihar (3), Chhattisgarh (4), Jharkhand (4),
Odisha (3) and West Bengal (1).
Further Observation
1.7.8 The Committee observes that the frequent casualties of the Central Police Forces
while combating the menace of Naxalism in the LWE affected areas reveal the need for
extensive training of forces and equipping them with latest weapons and gadgets before
sending them for actual field operation. The remaining six CIAT Schools may be set up on
priority basis. Adherence to Standard Operating Procedures must be impressed invariably
and non-observance of the same should be viewed seriously.
1.8 COUNTERING NORTH EAST INSURGENCY AND MILITANCY
Recommendation
1.8.1 The Committee notes that the Government of India has initiated talks with some erstwhile
underground insurgent groups which could help establish peace in the region. The Committee also
takes note of the fact that the Government of India has initiated talks with some friendly
neighbouring countries to check these insurgent groups which had earlier become safe haven for
them. But the steps taken have not yet yielded the desired results. Though, there is a separate
Ministry for development of North East region, the insurgent activities are unabated. The
Committee feels that there needs to be a change in the strategy adopted to deal with North East
insurgency and militancy. Steps are required to be taken to bring the people into the mainstream
of the society. (Para 3.3.8 ibid)
Action Taken
1.8.2 The strategy adopted by the Government for bringing peace in the North East through
negotiations with the militant outfits to bring them to the mainstream is bearing fruit over the years.
The violent incidents have come down to 627 in 2011 from 1489 in 2007.

10
1.8.3 The strategy of the Government is to hold talks with any militant group/outfit which is
willing to abjure violence, lay down arms and seek a solution to their demands within the
framework of Constitution. Such talks have been initiated with several outfits and is yielding results
as detailed below:–
(i)  Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) has been signed with United People’s Democratic
Solidarity (UPDS) on 25.11.2011 of Karbi Anglong in Assam and the organization has
dissolved itself. 1695 cadres belonging to following 9 different outfits active in Assam
including their commanders/important cadres, surrendered on 24.01.2102 along with
203 weapons before the State Government in the presence of the Union Home
Minster:–
• Kuki Revolutionary Army (KRA)
• Hmar People Convention (HPC)(D)
• Adivasi People’s Army (APA)
• Santal Tiger Force (STF)
• Adivasi Cobra Military of Assam (ACMA)
• Birsa Commando Force (BCF)
• All Adivasi National Liberation Army (AANLA)
• United Kukigam Defence Army (UKDA)
• Kuki Liberation Army (KLA)/Kuki Liberation Organization (KLO)
(ii) On 24
th March, 2012, an agreement has been signed by the Government of India and
the Government of Manipur with United Tribal Liberation Army (UTLA) and Pakan
Reunification Army (PRA) under the umbrella of Kuki National Organisation (KNO) to
formalize Suspension of Operations (SoO)and cease hostilities with immediate effect.
The ground rules giving effect to the SoO have also been framed.
(iii) Peace talks are going on with NDFB/P, KNLF/ULFA in Assam and with ANVC in
Meghalaya.
(iv) Memorandum of Settlement with DHD/J and DHD/N finalized.
(v) Talks are going on with NSCN (IM).
1.8.4 However, as suggested by the Committee, possibility of adopting alternative strategies will
also be explored.
Further Recommendation
1.8.5 The Committee observes that despite various strategies adopted for bringing peace in
the North-Eastern Region, the Region has not yet got conducive and peaceful environment
for investors for ensuring accelerated economic growth. Need of the hour is to undertake
Confidence Building Measure and employment generation besides ensuring security and
safety of human being and their belongings.
1.9 NEED FOR MULTI-PRONGED STRETEGY TO COUNTER INSURGENCY
Recommendation
1.9.1 The Committee is of the view that counter-insurgency strategies in the North-East should be

11
multi-pronged. Developmental ministries of the Government of India in tandem with concerned
State Governments of North-East can play effective role in countering these insurgent groups. The
Committee believes that fast pace of economic development in the region can be an effective tool
to bring misguided people into the mainstream. Besides, the Committee believes that the police
establishment, the army and paramilitary forces engaged in counter-insurgency operations in the
region should be given special training. In all trade discussions with the countries bordering North
East States, a clause should be included on closure of training camps for the insurgent groups
being run on their land. (Para 3.3.9 ibid)
Action Taken
1.9.2 The Government is following a multi-pronged policy to deal with insurgent and militant
activities in the North East Region. The policy includes a willingness to talk to any group provided
they lay down arms, surrender, abjure violence, and seek a resolution of their demands within the
frame work of the Indian Constitution and come into the mainstream of national life. The strategy
adopted by the Government to improve the situation in the North East includes accelerated
infrastructure development, stress on employment and good governance and de-centralization,
building friendly relations with neighbouring countries, willingness to meet and discuss legitimate
grievances of the people as also a resolve not to tolerate violence.
1.9.3 Due to persistent persuasion and meetings at different levels with the neighbouring
countries, there has been significant improvement in the check on cross border terrorism. Myanmar
is showing openness and willingness to act against NE insurgent groups. Some camps have been
destroyed in 2011 and 2012. The recent visit of the Prime Minister in May, 2012 to Myanmar has
added momentum to the Indo-Myanmar bilateral relations in security issues. There has been
indication to the effect that Myanmar has taken steps to clip the presence of IIGs in their land.
Our strategy and energy is in right direction and the results will be visible on the ground soon.
1.9.4 As regards training the Police, funds are provided under the scheme of Modernisation of
Police Forces (MPF) as also under the scheme of re-imbursement of Security related Expenditure
(SRE). Further steps are also taken up to set up or upgrade the police training institutions in the
North East.
Further Recommendation
1.9.5 The Committee notes the steps taken as part of the ongoing multi-pronged policy
and strategy of the Government to deal with insurgency and militancy in North-East region.
However, the Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome of all efforts so
undertaken.
1.10 T ACKLING TERRORIST INFRASTRUCTURE
Recommendation
1.10.1 The Committee feels that the Government should not be complacent with the situation in
Jammu and Kashmir which has improved in recent period in terms of the number of accidents and
the number of casualties. The Committee cautions that the Government should keep vigil on the
terrorist infrastructure functioning in “troubled neighbourhood”. (Para 3.4.5 ibid)
Action Taken
1.10.2 Though there has been a perceptible decline in the levels of terrorist violence, the
Government is taking all efforts to counter terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir. The Central

12
Government in tandem with the State Government has adopted a multi-pronged approach to contain
cross border infiltration and pro-active action against terrorists within the State, including various
counter terrorist methods to neutralize the efforts and capabilities of militants. The Government has
also encouraged policies to mainstream the youth and discourage the local youth from joining
militancy.
Further Recommendation
1.10.3 The Committee however feels that there is need for keeping continued vigil on the situation
and prevent any terrorist threats.
1.11 PROMOTION OF TOURISM IN JAMMU AND KASHMIR
Recommendation
1.11.1 The Committee is of the view that the people of Jammu and Kashmir should be made to
understand about negative consequences of terrorism and the Government of India should initiate
more developmental measures in the State to bring back the people who are misled into the
mainstream. The Committee further believes that tourism is the backbone of the economy of the
State which has the potential for huge employment to the population. The Committee, therefore,
feels that efforts be made to boost tourism in the state. More development projects and industries
should be taken up in the state giving it a development orientation. (Para 3.4.6 ibid)
Action Taken
1.11.2 The Central Government has been continuously supporting and assisting the State
Government in their efforts to bring about all-round economic development, and to provide
avenues for gainful employment to the people, with focus on planned and balanced regional
development. Priority has been accorded to building physical, economic and social infrastructure,
thereby improving the productive potential of the State besides improving the quality of life of
the people.
1.11.3 As a special initiative in the above direction, the Prime Minister during his visit to Jammu
and Kashmir on November 17-18, 2004, had announced a Reconstruction Plan for Jammu and
Kashmir involving an outlay of approximately Rs.24,000 crore, which broadly includes Projects/
Schemes aimed at expanding economic infrastructure and provision of basic services, imparting a
thrust to employment and income generation activities, and providing relief and rehabilitation for
different groups affected by militancy in Jammu and Kashmir. The current estimated cost of all
the schemes included in the Prime Minister’s Reconstruction Plan is Rs.32,489 crore. During the
current financial year, allocation for Prime Minister’s Reconstruction Plan is Rs.1,200 crore.
1.11.4 As regards tourism, Projects for setting up of 50 tourist villages across the state and
establishing new circuits have been sanctioned under PMRP at a estimated cost of Rs. 31.50 crore
and Rs. 21.79 crore respectively. Eight villages have been completed and the remaining tourist
villages are likely to be completed by 2013-14. Work on establishment of circuits is going on, 12
Tourism Authorities have been set up. These projects will give a boost to the tourism in the State.
1.11.5 As per the information furnished by Ministry of Tourism, apart from above mentioned
PMRP tourism projects, many training programmes are being conducted by Institute of Hotel
Management, Srinagar for building the capacities of Tourism industry personnel and development
of skills of youth for employment/self employment in tourism industry. From 2009-10 to 2011-12,
3380 persons have been trained in various sectors of tourism as follows:

1.11.6 As a part of the eight point plan outlined by the All Party Parliamentary delegation in
September, 2010, two Special Task Forces (STFs) were constituted for the Jammu and Ladakh
regions. The STF for Ladakh region recommended (January 2011) short term projects costing
Rs.415.70 crore for implementation (in two years). The STF for Jammu region recommended
(February 2011) short term projects costing Rs.496.63 crore. In the Union Budget 2011-12, Special
Plan Assistance (SPA) of Rs.150 crore and Rs.100 crore for Jammu and Ladakh regions
respectively have been allocated for implementation of the STF projects. Government of Jammu
and Kashmir  have furnished the list of priority projects identified for implementation (28 for Jammu
region, 43 for Kargil region and 34 Leh region).
1.11.7 In the second Round Table Conference on Jammu and Kashmir convened by the Prime
Minister in May 2006, five Working Groups were constituted to look into all issues affecting
J and K and work towards finding a common ground. Based on the recommendations of the
Working Groups, Prime Minister announced a package for Jammu and Kashmir in April 2008 which
broadly covers assistance to widows and orphans and victims of militancy, measures for cross LoC
travel and rehabilitation of Kashmiri migrants.
1.11.8 The State of Jammu and Kashmir has a large talent pool of youth who are well educated
but are unable to find employment due to lack of soft skills or lack of practical/hands on training.
The basic challenge is the sense of alienation and disconnect with the rest of India. The paradigm
needs to change by enhancing the connect through soft power of India and giving the new
generation a stake in the country. This would require a strategy to engage the youth by increasing
their employability, enhance educational opportunities and sustain the process of integration by
building a favourable environment.
1.11.9 To meet the above objective, on the recommendation of the Expert Group constituted by
PMO under the Chairmanship of Dr. C. Rangarajan (February 2011), the Scheme ‘Special Industry
Initiative for J&K’ was approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on 7
th July, 2011.
The SII J&K Scheme is to provide skills and enhance employability to 8000 youth from J and K
per annum over a 5 year period in key high growth sectors. The programme is targeted at
providing well-paying jobs to the trained manpower. The Scheme is being implemented by National
Skill Development Council NSDC) and the corporate sector in PPP mode. The Scheme will cover
graduates, post graduates and professional degree holders. So far Project Approval Committee
(PAC) has approved proposals for training of 13440 youth of Jammu & Kashmir by 10 corporates.
1.11.10 Another scheme recommended by the Expert Group is ‘Skill Empowerment and
Employment Scheme for Jammu and Kashmir’ called Himayat. “Himayat” has been launched in the
State for skill development training and placement of youth between the age group of 18-35 years.

14
Projects are sanctioned to the Implementing Agencies by the Ministry of Rural Development for
imparting training in different trades. Training in Hospitality and Tourism is one of the trades being
taken up under such projects. Ministry of Rural Development has so far sanctioned 8 projects
under Himayat benefitting a total of 54380 youth in the State over a period of 5 years. As per the
latest available information, 1727 youth have been trained out of which 958 have been placed for
employment within or outside the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
Further Recommendation
1.11.11 The Committee desires that the projects recommended by STFs for Jammu and
Ladakh Regions be taken up on priority. The Committee feels that Special Industry
Initiative for J and K and skill Empowerment and Employment Scheme needs to be given
widen publicity.
1.12 DRUG-TRAFICKING AND TERROR FUNDING
Recommendation
1.12.1 The Committee is of the view that trafficking of Narcotics, as an organized cross border
crime has now become a threat to internal security of India because of its diabolic alliance with
terrorist groups. Because these drugs are the major source for funding terrorism and insurgency in
the country, the Committee understands that smuggling of narcotics is a matter of serious concern.
The Committee is aware of the fact that the economy of Pak-Afghan frontier is dependent on the
production of poppy and cannabis. The issue of drug trafficking needs to be taken up in bilateral
and multilateral fora and discussions. The Government should take more serious steps in this
regard. (Para 3.6.4 ibid)
Action Taken
1.12.2 The Government has received reports regarding trafficking of South West Asian heroin into
India through the international border with Pakistan. The details of South West Asian heroin
intercepted by the Drug Law Enforcement agencies during the last three years and the current year
are given below:–
2009 2010 2011 2012
(till May, 2012)
Heroin Seizures 218.08 277.472 236.792 150.68
(in Kg.)
1.12.3 The issue of South West Asian heroin interception by Indian drug law enforcement agencies
is being raised in various international and regional fora during the co-ordination meetings.
1.12.4 DG level talks between the DG , NCB, India and DG, ANF, Pakistan was held in Islamabad
with effect from 12
th September, 2011 to 14 th September, 2011. A Memorandum of Understanding
(MoU) on drug demand reduction and prevention of illicit trafficking in narcotics drugs, psychotropic
substances and precursor chemicals and related matters has been signed during the talks.
1.12.5 Besides, inputs received from various agencies regarding Pakistan/Afghanistan links are
being shared with the concerned agencies in Pakistan and Afghanistan as the case may be.
1.12.6 The issue of cross-border trafficking of drugs between Pakistan and India was addressed
during the recently concluded Home Secretary level talks between the two nations.

15
1.12.7 The recommendations and the concern of the Parliamentary Committee have been noted and
the issue of drug trafficking would be taken up in future bilateral and multilateral fora and
discussions.
1.13 NA TIONAL INTELLIGENCE GRID (NATGRID)
Recommendation
1.13.1 National Intelligence Grid (NATGRID), is the first of its kind project, which will link
various databases between user (intelligence and investigative agencies) and provider organizations
(such as telecom companies) to enhance our counter terrorism capabilities. The Committee desires
that all physical and financial targets fixed in the current year may be achieved. The project should
take off as envisaged without any time and cost overruns. (Para 3.8.3 ibid)
Action Taken
1.13.2 Based on the ‘in principle’ approval of Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS), given on
06.06.2012, a proposal was submitted to EFC and the EFC appraised the project for an amount
of Rs.1,002.97 crore on 23.01.2012 which includes Foundation, Horizon-I and some elements of
Horizon-II. The same was approved by the CCS on 14.06.2012. Rs.435 crore have been provided
for implementation of the project in 2012-2013 Budget. All efforts necessary to avoid time and cost
overruns are being taken, as also to ensure achievement of all physical and financial targets fixed
as per the implementation plan.
Further Recommendation
1.13.3 The Committee, while appreciating the steps taken by the Government desires that
the Ministry of Home Affairs may apprise the Committee of actual physical and financial
targets with regard to setting up of organizational structure of National Intelligence Grid
(NATGRID).
1.14 COASTAL SECURITY
Recommendation
1.14.1 In view of the 26/11 terror attack on Mumbai where attackers entered the city through the
sea route, the Committee understands the necessity of coastal security mechanism. Keeping in view
that India has a vast coastline of more than seven thousand kms, the Coast Guard, the State police
and the Navy have major responsibility for coastal security in the country. The Committee therefore,
recommends that foolproof arrangements may be made for coordination and synergy among
different agencies. (Para 3.10.8 ibid)
Action Taken
1.14.2 The Indian Navy has been designated as the authority responsible for overall maritime
security which includes coastal security and offshore security. The Indian Navy is assisted by
Coast Guard, State Marine Police and other Central and State Agencies for coastal defence of the
nation. The Indian Coast Guard has been additionally designated as the authority responsible for
coastal security in territorial waters including areas to be patrolled by Coastal Police. The
Director General, Coast Guard is designated as Commander, Coastal Command and is responsible
for overall coordination between Central and State Agencies in all matters relating to coastal
security.

16
1.14.3 A National Committee for strengthening maritime and coastal security against threats from
the sea has been constituted by the Cabinet Secretariat in the month of August, 2009, under the
chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary. The Committee consists of representatives of all the concerned
Ministries/ Departments/Organisations in the Government of India as well as Chief Secretaries/
Administrators of the coastal States/UTs.
1.14.4 Six meetings of the National Committee were held on 4
th September 2009, 22 nd January
2010, 14 th May 2010, 23 rd November 2010, 29 th July 2011 and 22 nd June 2012 wherein the progress
of implementation of all the major decisions in respect of the coastal security have been reviewed.
The various decisions taken in these meetings are being followed up by the concerned agencies.
1.15 SUR VEILLANCE OF COASTAL AREAS
Recommendation
1.15.1 The Committee recommends that the Government should step up coastal areas vigilance
by strengthening infrastructure for patrolling and surveillance of the coastal areas. Executive and
technical posts should be filled in at the earliest. The Committee desires that Coastal Security
Scheme, Phase-II should achieve its targets in given time period. Necessary legal frame work
such as amendment to the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 may be completed at the earliest.
(Para 3.10.9 ibid)
Action Taken
1.15.2 The Government is continuously taking steps for strengthening infrastructure for patrolling
and surveillance of the coastal areas, including filling up of executive and technical posts. All
efforts are being made to achieve targets of Coastal Security the Scheme Phase-II in given time
period. Necessary steps are being taken by Ministry of Shipping for amendment to the Merchant
Shipping Act, 1958.
1.16 BIO-METRIC ID CARDS FOR FISHERMEN
Recommendation
1.16.1 The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to complete issuance of Bio-metric ID cards to
fishermen as per the target. There should not be any delay in this regard. Appropriate technology
for Automatic Identification system may be selected immediately after the study of the pilot project.
Fast Interceptor Crafts (FICs) may also be procured at the earliest in a transparent manner.
(Para 3.10.10 ibid)
Action Taken
1.16.2 Matters relating to issuance of bio-metric ID cards to fishermen, selection of Automatic
Identification System (AIS) and procurement of Fast Interceptor Crafts (FICs) are also being
suitably handled by the concerned Ministries/Departments.
1.17 EFFECTIVE BORDER MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
1.17.1 In view of the fact that India has 15,106.7 km. of land border, the Committee believes that
securing it against hostile interests and taking measures to counter threats such as illegal migration,

17
smuggling, infiltration by terrorists, smuggling of arms, narcotics and FICNs while facilitating
legitimate trade and commerce across the border should be the main objective of effective border
management which is vital for internal security. The Committee also recommends that construction
of 1377 km road on Indo-Nepal Border should be undertaken in a time bound manner.
(Para 3.11.24 ibid)
Action Taken
1.17.2 The Cabinet Committee on Security has approved the development of 1377 Km roads of
operational strategic significance in areas along the Into-Nepal border, (173 Km in Uttarakhand, 640
Km in Uttar Pradesh and 564 Km in Bihar.)
1.17.3 The proposed roads will primarily run parallel to the border, thereby adding to the mobility
of the Border Guard Forces (BGFs) and enabling them to dominate the sensitive borders more
effectively.

1.22 PROPER TRANSFER/POSTING POLICY FOR PARA-MILITARY FORCES
Recommendation
1.22.1 The Committee observes that the Government has established the Counter Insurgency and
Anti-Terrorism School for CRPF personnel. The Committee also notes that Risk Allowance for
CRPF personnel deployed in 35 specified districts in Left Wing Extremist areas has been increased.
The Committee is however given to understand that the frequent transfer/posting and posting of the
CRPF personnel to such areas where they are not able to communicate due to language problem
add to their woes and adversely affect their working proficiency. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that a proper policy should be formulated on transfer/posting of the CRPF . The
Committee further recommends that in order to give adequate relief to the personnel of all Central
Police Forces a posting/transfer policy should be reflected on ground. The Committee is of the view

20
that personnel working in CRP should be stationed in a particular place for, at least, three years
without disturbance unless they are hard-pressed to go to some other area because moving from one
place to other in a short span of time causes difficulties not only to them but also to their families.
The Committee is also of the view that these personnel should be posted to the extent possible in
the areas where they know the local language and culture so that there is no communication gap
between the locals and the CRPF personnel. (Para 4.1.20 ibid)
Action Taken
1.22.2 In order to give adequate rest and relief to the CRPF personnel, a proper posting/ transfer
policy has been laid out which ensures the movement of Force personnel between the hard and
static/soft postings. The policy has been drawn keeping in mind the family obligations of the
jawans in addition to the Force requirements. Since CRPF is not a border guarding force, there
is no fixed location/point of duty, but the same changes as per the internal security situation in the
various parts of the country as well as the request made by various State Governments/UT
administrations as per developing security scenarios.
1.22.3 In order to provide adequate rest and recuperation to the CRPF personnel it has recently
been decided that, as far as possible, the training companies shall not be deployed for active duties
as the main motive of keeping one Coy out of every 7 Coys in a Battalion as a training Coy was
to give proper rest and recuperation to the jawans on rotation basis in addition to honing their skills
in various fields.
1.22.4 Besides, the jawans in CRPF and other CAPFs are eligible for static posting subject to
vacancy and administrative convenience as per the following guidelines:–
(i) CRPF formations/institutions/units have been categorized as “Peace” and “Field”
stations for regulating the transfer of the Force personnel.
(ii) After completion of 8 years field service in case of male; and 4 years field service in
case of female, after basic training, the force personnel are eligible for first peace
station/static posting. Subsequent peace station/static posting can be/is done after
completion of a total of 8 years field service from the completion of last static posting.
(iii) For posting to a peace station/static location, preference is given to those having
longest service in the field Battalions.
(iv) Normal stay of posting in a Group Centre/static institution/peace station is 4 years.
This may be extended upto 5 years only in case of training staff posted in training
institution as a special case.
(v) After deployment of the Force personnel in the hard areas, like Left Wing Extremism
affected areas, they are generally posted to static postings. Such jawans are also asked
to give their preference of posting on leaving the LWE areas out of the five options,
namely Rapid Action Force/ Duty Battalions/ Group Centre/ Training Institution/
Deputation.
(vi) Personnel having good record of service and free from disciplinary and vigilance angle,
may be posted to near their home towns, 2 years before attaining the age of
superannuation, subject to availability of vacancies.
(vii) In order to maintain continuity at a place, a maximum of 25% of the strength is
moved every year from one operational theatre to another within a sector.
1.22.5 In order to keep the Force personnel in their cultural milieu as also for effective and better
utilization, a maximum of 50% of the total personnel posted in a place are from the local area. In

21
case of other Forces like BSF, as far as possible, recruit Constables on completion of their basic
training are posted to their Frontiers located near their home states, depending upon the vacancy
position.
1.22.6 Therefore, all efforts are made to help the Force personnel live with their families
intermittently during the static postings /peace stations. The tenure of such peace postings has been
earmarked as 4 years after due consultation with the Force personnel as also keeping in mind the
general good of the maximum number of Force personnel in CRPF.

1.30 SECURITY IN DIPLOMATIC AREAS
Recommendation
1.30.1 The Committee takes serious view of the bomb blast in an Israeli Embassy car in a high-
security area which occurred in Delhi using sticky bomb. The Committee recommends that proper
security arrangements should be made by Delhi Police in Diplomatic areas so that this kind of
incident does not happen in future. (Para 4.2.23 ibid)
Action Taken
1.30.2 Security arrangements for diplomatic missions and diplomats of foreign countries located in
India are reviewed periodically on the basis of inputs given by the Central Security Agencies and
appropriate advisories issued to Delhi Police/State Police. Based on the inputs given by the Central
Security Agencies, Delhi Police/State Police take suitable measure to strengthen security. Further,
for the security arrangement of Diplomatic Mission located in Delhi, Government has constituted
Diplomatic Security Force (DSF). A sizable number of Police personnel/Central Armed Police
Forces personnel have been deployed under the operational control of DSF on static guard duties
at various Embassies and diplomatic premises.
1.30.3 Delhi Police has taken a large number of anti-terrorist measures in the city to combat
terrorism. These measures can be grouped under the following heads:
1. Armed Response Teams
2. Terrorist related intelligence collection
3. Security audit of Vital Installations
4. Eyes and Ears scheme and Tenant verification

25
5. Checking of Public Places
6. Installation of CCTV System in Markets and Border Check Posts
Their details are as follows:–
Armed Response Teams:
1.30.4 Delhi Police has deployed more than 200 Armed Response Teams across the city. A large
number of them are mobile, whereas some of the teams are on foot to cover a smaller area or
a specific location. Besides we have also (630+139) PCR vans/motorcycles across Delhi. These
Armed Response Teams and PCR Vans/Motor Cycles, have been deployed to deter any terrorist
attack as well as respond suitably. The details of the armed response teams are as follows:–
(i) Quick Reaction Teams  include Cobra and Vajra teams. They are all in vehicles, round
the clock, armed with semi-automatic weapons, wireless sets and protective gears.
Each QRT is headed by an officer or a head Constable, ready to respond to any armed
attack.
(ii) Mobile Striking Parties : Mobile striking parties deployed at strategic locations is
headed by an officer/Head Constable with 1-2 Constables. Officer/HC is equipped with
small weapon and Constable with INSAS/AK-47 rifle and suitable wireless
communication. Each mobile party patrols their assigned area in two shifts from early
morning to late evening depending upon the operational requirement of the area.
(iii) Foot/Static Armed Parties: Foot/Static armed parties, each consisting of 2-4 HC/Cts
armed with SAF/INSAS rifles/pistols/revolvers have been deployed at sensitive
locations like entry/exit of Metro Stations, Five Stars Hotels, Schools etc. They are
on foot and cover the specific areas given to them to counter any terrorist attack. The
timings of deployment are as per the operational requirement of the location.
(iv) CP’s Reserves: CP’s Reserves, with armed component, have been positioned round
the clock at several locations in Delhi. They will be rushed to the spot for assisting
the local police in forming cordons and also respond to the situation, as required by
circumstances.
(v) Mobile Patrol Vans (MPVs): Keeping in view the vulnerability of certain targets
within their beat areas, the bases of some of the MPVs in all the PCR zones have
been re-located so that these vans are located nearest to the vulnerable target area
such as a market place, metro station, hospital, etc. They are also in a position of
operational readiness to respond to exigencies. The checking/patrolling by MPVs is
also being coordinated regularly by the CPCR (Central Police Control Room) with
specific instructions to vulnerable target areas, such as schools, colleges, metro
stations, temples, mosques etc.
(vi) PCR Vans and PCR Motor Cycles: There are 630 bases of PCR Vans and 139
Motor Cycle PCR bases in Delhi. Besides responding to any incident in their respective
beats, they will also rush to any place of terrorist attack and respond according to
the requirement of the situation. The response time of PCR van to reach any place
of occurrence in urban areas is about 10 minutes and rural areas about 20 minutes.
(vii) Emergency Response Vehicles (ERVs): ERVs have been provided one each in 155
police stations of Delhi. They are manned by one upper subordinate and 3 other ranks
and equipped with at least two long range weapons and small arms and wireless sets.
They act as the first responder to all crime and major law and order calls. They are

26
deployed in two shifts from 0800 hrs to 2400 hrs. midnight. Inspector Anti Terrorist
Officer (ATO) also spend at least two to three hours in a day in ERVs to supervise
the anti terrorist tasks allotted to him in his jurisdiction.
(viii) Special Weapon and Tactics Teams (SWAT): The Delhi Police has set up a SWAT
team consisting of 3 officers and 70 commandos well equipped to respond to any
armed attack with a capacity to neutralize armed terrorists attack. SWAT teams has
been stationed at Special Cell Lodhi Colony, New Delhi. The team is well armed with
semi-automatic weapons and protective gears. The SWAT teams have been subjected
to specialized training in counter terrorism at NSG , Manesar. SWAT teams have also
been provided with three Light Armoured T roop Carriers (LATC) for operational
requirements. The strength of the SWAT team is being increased to 100.
Terrorist related Intelligence collection :
1.30.5 Entire system of terrorist related intelligence collection system has been reviewed. The
details are as follows:–
(i) Human Intelligence Collection: The entire system for collection of terrorist related
intelligence has been revamped. The Special Cell is a dedicated unit for anti-terrorist
operations. The officers/staff of this Cell functions primarily on the basis of
intelligence gathered either by them or other agencies. Within the Special Cell
additional ten teams of officers have been constituted and deployed in various sensitive
areas of Delhi to collect terrorist related information. They are not assigned any other
job except collection of intelligence. Analysis teams of special cell, analyse the
intelligence, pursues it and mount operation at appropriate time.
(ii) T echnical Intelligence:  System for technical intelligence collection is also under
upgradation.
(iii) Revamping of Beat Patrolling system : Beat patrolling system has been revamped
and oriented towards collection of criminal/terrorist related intelligence, implementation
of anti-terrorist measures etc. A revised Standing Order No.331/2007 has been issued
to redefine the duties of Beat Officers.
(iv) Inspector (Anti terrorist operations) and Intelligence Collection by Police
Station Staff : One of the Inspectors posted in every police station in Delhi has been
designated as Inspector (Anti terrorist operations) and assigned the task of
implementation of anti terrorist measures including intelligence collection, in police
station area. Besides, special responsibility has been imposed upon the local police
towards collection of intelligence relating to terrorists by closely studying their modus
operandi in past cases, and interaction with Community Leaders, Residential Welfare
Associations, Market Associations, Hotel/Guest House workers/employees etc. A
separate S.O. No.78/08 has been issued in this regard.
Security Audit of Vital Installations
1.30.6 475 important and sensitive establishments including Iconic Monuments, Government
buildings, Pvt. Buildings, Malls, Cinema Halls, Hotels/Guest Houses, Markets and other public
places have been identified as Vital Installations in Delhi. Most of the owner/Estate Managers have
been issued the security guidelines/advisories suggesting them to take specific security measures to
prevent any terrorist attack in their establishments. Meetings are also held with them individually
or with associations to convince them to implement security measures. Their security status is

27
being monitored and efforts are being continually made to convince them to comply with the
guidelines and make their establishments more secure. The Vital Installations have been classified
in five colour codes i.e. green, purple, yellow, orange and red to define the satisfaction level of
various security parameters with respect to perimeter security, access control, Anti-Sabotage check
and parking control etc. The security status of all the 464 vital installations is reviewed on regular
basis by Delhi Police. Market/Traders Associations are also being persuaded to install CCTVs in
front of their shops.
Eyes and ears scheme and Tenant verification:
(i) Eyes and ears scheme : Delhi Police has launched a scheme captioned ‘Public As
Eyes and Ears of the Police’ with special emphasis to sensitize all the stake-holders
such as Rehri Patriwalas, Chowkidars, guards, vendors, parking attendants TSR
drivers, residents/traders welfare associations etc. to keep a watch and look for
suspicious persons and share the information with local police immediately. Regular
meetings are held by all the officers to sensitize and motivate them. The scheme is
catching up with the public and they are coming forward to help the police. 87
criminal cases in the year 2011 were worked out with the help of stake holders of
the scheme and 21 public persons were rewarded in the year 2011 by Delhi Police
to recognize their help in solving crime in Delhi.
(ii) T enant Verification:  In order to detect any terrorist or any person with a dubious
character taking shelter in Delhi as a tenant, Delhi Police carries out regular tenant
verification. The owners of the house are required to inform local police whenever
they keep a tenant. Special drives are also conducted for verification of tenants. In
the year 2011, 199972 forms were filled for tenant verification.
Checking of public places
1.30.7 All kinds of public places in Delhi are being checked regularly. The details are as follows:–
(i) Checking of Cyber Café:  Division Officers and beat officers of local police and
selected teams of Special Cell regularly check the Cyber Cafes all over Delhi to ensure
that Cyber Café owners maintain a record of proof of identity carrying the
photographs and addresses of Cyber Café users. This record will be useful in tracing
the persons who send threat through e-mail from Cyber Café.
(ii) Checking of Guest Houses and hotels:  Officers of Local Police and Special Cell
regularly check the hotels and Guest Houses all over Delhi to ensure that they maintain
proper record of guests and ascertain the identity of persons staying there, conduct
random checks and interrogate suspicious looking persons to ascertain their bonafides
and purpose of visit.
(iii) C hecking hideouts, Cinema Halls, Airport, Railway Stations, ISBTs, Taxi stands,
Chemical shops, Public offices, Gurudwaras, Masjids, Mandirs and STD booths:
Local police as well as officers of Special Cell regularly conduct checking to keep
watch on such places as mentioned above to detect any suspicious person. Suspicious
looking persons are also questioned to ascertain their identity and bonafides. The
Railway Station and ISBTs authorities have been requested to make regular
announcements over the public address system advising public to be on the look out
for any unattended object and inform the police.
(iv) Checking of vehicles and buses: Local Police checks buses and other vehicles
regularly by placing barricades on the road at selected places. DTC Depot Managers

28
and private bus operators are also briefed about precautions to be taken by them and
their drivers/conductors. DTC has also been requested to install CCTVs inside the
buses as well as outside the entry door to keep a watch over public.
(v) Checking of trucks/public carriers: Local Police and Special Cell teams conduct
regular checking of trucks/public carriers carrying goods, vegetables/fruits etc.
entering Delhi, to detect any smuggling of arms/ammunition/explosives etc. Their
drivers/cleaners are also verified.
(vi) Second hand Car/Scooter/Motorcycles dealers: Local Police keeps a liaison with
dealers of second hand cars/scooters/motorcycles to know about the identity of
persons buying them. They have also been instructed to inform local police, in case
of any suspicious person or transaction.
(vii) Wir eless Integrated Public Address System: Delhi Police has installed a centrally
operated Wireless Integrated Public Address System at 31 markets and 11 Metro

Observations/Recommendations in respect of which

3.1 FAKE INDIAN CURRENCY NOTES
Recommendation
3.1.1 The Committee takes serious view of the fact that the country is flooded with fake currency
notes and large amount of Fake Indian Currency Notes (FICN) are being seized. The Committee
is concerned to note that despite the fact that the Ministry is working in tandem with various other
government agencies to thwart the circulation of FICNs, the circulation of FICN continues
unabated. The Committee recommends that all porous borders should be plugged to prevent
smuggling of FICNs. (Para 3.5.3 of 161
st Report )
3.1.2 The Committee understands that all border checkposts and major international airports
should be modernized to check the smugglers of FICNs. The Committee in this connection,
recommends that the Reserve Bank of India should constantly upgrade security features of Indian
currency and the people should be made aware on these security features to enable them to easily
distinguish fake from real notes. The Committee recommends that note sorting machines should be
installed at all bank branches to detect fake currency notes as soon as they enter the banking
channel. Since, Nepal and Bangladesh are main transit points for smuggling of FICNs into India,
the Committee feels that India should help train Nepalese and Bangladeshi customs officials in
identifying and keeping watch over FICNs. The Committee also recommends that India should
pursue these countries for the installation of hi-tech luggage scanners at their major airports and
land check posts so that the baggages of passengers are thoroughly checked for counterfeit
currency. (Para 3.5.4 ibid)
Action Taken
3.1.3 To address the multi-dimensional aspects of the FICN menace, several agencies such as the
RBI, the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Home Affairs, Security and Intelligence Agencies of the
Centre and States, Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) etc., are working in tandem to thwart the
illegal activities related to FICNs.
3.1.4 Further, a special FICN Coordination Group (FCORD) has been formed in MHA to share
the intelligence/information amongst the different security agencies of State/Centre to counter the
menace of circulation of Fake Currency within the country.
3.1.5 NIA has been empowered by the National Investigation Agency Act to investigate and
prosecute such offences. The Government has also constituted a Terror Funding and Fake
Currency Cell in National Investigation Agency (NIA) to focus on investigation of Terror Funding
and Fake Currency Cases. The security features in the High V alue currency notes are being
constantly upgraded. RBI has also strengthened the mechanism for detection of counterfeit notes
by the Banks.
3.1.6 Regarding training of Nepalese and Bangladeshi customs officials in identifying and keeping
watch over FICNs and installation of hi-tech luggage scanner at their major airports land check

44
posts so that the baggages of passengers are thoroughly checked for counterfeit currency, the said
concerns are also being captured and being dealt with in the HS level bilateral talks.
3.1.7 Border Security Force (BSF) is deployed on Indo-Bangladesh and Indo-Pakistan Borders. All
possible efforts are being made to check/contain the illegal activities, including smuggling of FICN,
across these borders which includes construction of fencing and floodlighting. The BSF also keeps
vigil along the borders by way of patrols, deployment of high tech equipments etc. In addition,
there are also bilateral institutional mechanism/forums, in which these issues are discussed and
addressed suitably with mutual cooperation.
3.1.8 Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) has been deployed at Indo-Nepal Border as a Border Guarding
Force. Regular presence, round-the-clock patrolling, random checking and surveillance are carried
out by SSB to stop cross border criminal activities. Besides, State Police concerned is also keeping
a vigil. There are other institutional mechanism like Home Secretary level talks between two
countries, periodic Border District Coordination Committee (BDCC) meeting, real-time exchange of
information/intelligence etc. between the two countries to effectively deal with such issues.
Further Observation
3.1.9 The Committee is constrained to observe that despite various efforts made by the
Government, the problems of FICN still persists in the country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that immediate steps are required for constitution of Terror Funding Fake
Currency Cell in National Investigation Agency (NIA). Efforts of Reserve Bank of India by
constantly upgrading security features in the High Value Currency Notes and strengthening
of mechanism for detection of counterfeit notes should be made more effective in
eradicating the menace of FICN.
3.2 INFILTRATION FROM ACROSS THE BORDER
Recommendation
3.2.1 The Committee feels that though cases of infiltration from across the border and number
of persons apprehended have decreased in recent period, the Government should not feel
complacent. India is already burdened with a large number of infiltrators. The Committee
recommends that security at patches vulnerable to cattle smuggling identified by BSF should be
tightened so that smuggling of the cattle heads from India could be checked. The Committee also
strongly recommends that remaining works of fencing and flood lighting in border areas may be
completed as per targets. The Committee also recommends that issues such as acquisition of land
etc should be resolved as soon as possible to avoid delaying fencing and floodlighting works. The
Committee also recommends that shifting of the border fencing within 150 yards along Indo-Bangla
Border may be completed soon. (Para 3.11.23 ibid)
Action Taken
3.2.2 Cattle smuggling across IBB (from Indian to Bangladesh)over the time period has developed
as an organized trans-border crime. Reason being, there is high demand of beef in Bangladesh and
at the same time availability of cattle heads in India. Cattle smuggling is the reason behind most
of the trans-border crimes and has spilled over to the hinterland. This also has links with other
trans-border crimes like smuggling of FICN, narcotics etc.
3.2.3 In its efforts to check the cattle smuggling, BSF has identified in South Bengal, Malda,
North Bengal and Guahati frontiers and gave special attention to these patches. Efforts are also
being made to complete the feasible fencing and floodlighting works along these patches on priority

45
so as to further strengthen the vigil by BSF. Issues of land acquisition are continuously taken up
with the concerned State Governments for resolution.
Further Recommendation
3.2.4 The Committee reiterates that Government should take immediate effective steps
towards shifting of the border fencing within 150 yards along Indo-Bangla Border and
completing projects of Fencing and Floodlighting Works within set time frame and the
Committee may be apprised of the progress made in this direction.
3.3 NON REGISTRATION OF FIRS BY DELHI POLICE
Recommendation
3.3.1 The Committee is concerned over the fact that there are large number of complaints for not
registering FIRs by the Police Personnel at the Police Stations in Delhi. The Committee apprehends
that actual figures may be bigger than the number of complaints came to light since most of the
people especially poor and illiterate ones might have returned without lodging their complaints
which have not been reflected in the figures during the year 2010, 2011 and 2012. The Committee
recommends that there should be a separate cell of Delhi Police for registering such complaints
where representatives of NGOs, local bodies etc may be involved so that people trying to lodge
such complaints would do it. The Committee is of the opinion that non-registering of FIR
complaint by Police personnel should be viewed as dereliction of duty as well as unbecoming of
the police officers. The Government may consider setting up an authority to look into complaints
against Delhi Police. The Committee is exasperated over the fact that although 877 and 941 such
complaints were registered against non-registering of complaints in 2010 and 2011 respectively,
however, only 33 and 46 cases were found to be genuine. The Committee is of the considered view
that stringent action is required to be taken against the concerned officers for non registering of
FIRs. (Para 4.2.19 ibid)
Action Taken
3.3.2 Strict directions have been given to the staff posted in the police stations and dealing with
registration of FIRs to ensure prompt service and be polite and courteous to the complainants. A
Reception Desk has been established in each Police Station for the help of complainants. Staff has
been directed to register FIRs immediately on receipt of information regarding cognizable offences
irrespective of caste/creed/religion/status of the complainants. Vigilance Branch of Police
Headquarters conduct surprise checking by sending decoy complainants. Stern action is taken
against the police personnel who are found not complying with the directions. Telephone numbers
of senior police officers and their time table to meet/hear the complainants in person, has been
displayed on the Notice Board of each police station. In case the complainant is not satisfied with
the police action, he can approach the area magistrate under Section 155 Cr.P.C. for appropriate
orders. Besides, senior police officers and Hon’ble Courts, there are thirteen (13) authorities/
Commissions like National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), National Commission for Women
(NCW), National Commission for Schedule Castes (NCSC), National Commission for Schedule
Tribes (NCST) National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC), National Commission for
Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), National Commission for Minorities (NCM), Delhi
Commission for Protection of Child Rights (DCPCR), Delhi Minorities Commission, Delhi
Commission for Women (DCW), Central Information Commission (CIC), Public Grievances
Commission and Police Complaint Authority of the Government of NCT of Delhi who hear the
complainants and issue suitable directions to the police.

46
3.3.3 In addition to the 13 Commissions mentioned above the Hon’ble L.G., Delhi has a pro-active
public grievances redressal system and seeks quick reports/action on such complaints. The MHA
and CM Office also seek reports on such complaints from police.
3.3.4 In pursuance of the judgment dated 22.09.2006 of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in
W.P.(C) No.310/1996, titled Prakash Singh and Ors. Vs. Union of India and Ors., Ministry of Home
Affairs, Government of India has already decided to set up a Police Complaints Authority
Accordingly, GNCT of Delhi vide its Resolution No.F.12/04/2011/AR/1630-17/C, dated 27.02.2012
has extended the role of Public Grievances Commission and given it the added responsibility of
functioning as the “Police Complaints Authority” for the purpose of looking into serious complaints
against the Delhi Police, as an interim arrangement, till the Delhi Police Act, 1978 is replaced with
the new Police Act.
3.3.5 The steps taken by Delhi Police for proper and prompt registrations of FIRs are as under:–
(i) The staff is briefed/instructed regularly by senior officers.
(ii) Surprise checks by the senior officers are conducted on the staff.
(iii) V igilance Branch, PHQ conducts surprise checking by sending decoy complainants.
(iv) The public has the facility to ring up number 23213355 of the Flying Squad of the
Vigilance Branch for any emergent help in case of any harassment by police officials.
In order to encourage the general public to be more vigilant about criminal and corrupt
activities of police men. There is facility of P. O. Box No. 171 introduced since July
1999 through which public can send the complaints against such police men, so that
the complaints are attended properly and deterrent action is taken against concerned
police officials.
(v) Delhi Police has been advertising telephone numbers of District DCsP alongwith their
Fax Numbers. All Distt DCsP have been directed to maintain a register containing gist
of all such message received on the Fax and wherever necessary they must be acted
upon immediately. Public have also the facility to send their complaints through E-mail
against the corrupt police personnel.
(vi) The department revises the training syllabus, both for Basic Training and Refresher
Courses to inculcate a sense of community service and respect for values of society,
among the police personnel.
(vii) All complaints against police personnel are dealt with directly by senior officers.
Severe punishment is awarded to any officer found involved in such activities.
(viii) A time table is displayed at every police station when SHOs and other senior officers
are available to public to attend their grievances, problems/complaints.
(ix) E–mail services has been started where any citizen can lodge his complaint without
delay, apart from the Police Stations.
(x) The complaints Monitoring and Tracking System (CMTS), a computerized system has
been devised to effectively monitor and redressal of Complaints received from public
by Delhi Police
Further Recommendation
3.3.6 The Committee, however, is not convinced. Common people are still forced to rush
from pillar to post to get FIR registered in spite of all elaborate arrangement is in place.

47
The Committee has also been given to understand that there is tendency of converting
cognizable offences like snatching, theft, pick-pocketing etc. into ordinary complaints of loss
of property. The Government should look into this trend seriously keeping in view the
hardship being forced by a common man. The Committee feels that registration of FIR on
the direction of senior officers, courts and Commission is in itself a tedious task which
reflects dereliction of duty and it should be viewed very seriously. The Committee also

3.4 LACK OF REGULAR BUILDINGS FOR POLICE STATIONS
Recommendation
3.4.1 The Committee takes serious view of the fact that 72 police stations out of 180 police
stations are functioning without regular buildings. It is very unfortunate that in the Capital city
of the country, the Police stations are functioning without regular buildings. The Committee
recommends that the Government should take immediate steps to provide regular buildings to these
72 police stations at the earliest. (Para 4.2.20 ibid)
Action Taken
3.4.2 Presently, 108 Police Stations are running in regular buildings. 08 Police Stations are under
construction. The land in respect of 30 Police Stations is available. Remaining 34 Police Stations

3.4.3 The Committee is not convinced with the reply and is of the considered view that the

The Committee may be apprised of the development in this direction.

Recommendation
3.5.1 As regards crime figures, the Committee takes serious note of the increasing cases of
molestation, rape and kidnapping during the last three years. The Committee is of the view that

of police personnel in Delhi. In view of this, the Committee recommends that more and more

3.5.4 Delhi Police is committed to make the city a safe place for women. For this, we are taking
the following measures to prevent crime against women:–
(i) Orders for BPOs etc. for safety of women :- The Delhi Police has issued orders

travel alone in the cab and are dropped right at their door steps and accompanied by
the security guard.
(ii) Police presence at Bus stops :-  Over 300 Bus-stops saw police presence. Composite
teams from Police Stations, Traffic Units and the PCR teamed up to man police
pickets in identified areas.
(iii) Creation of Women Help-Desk :- Prominent help-desks are created to attend
women complainants in each Police Station.
(iv) Directions to PCR Van to help stranded women :- All PCR Vans are directed to
help stranded women during night. Any women can call PCR van by dialing 100 who
will be dropped to the nearest safe place.
(v) Women staff are deployed in beats and in PCR vans in the areas prone to crime
against women.
(vi) Surprise checks in buses, markets, cinema, road junctions, universities/colleges/
schools etc.
(vii) Gender Sensitization of Police personnel :- The Gender sensitization and legal
awareness programmes were organized for police personnel, in association with

3.6 UNDER REPORTING OF RAPE AND MOLESTATION CASES
Recommendation
3.6.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that the figures given by Delhi Police do not match
the cases reported in media about rape and molestation. Stringent action should be taken against
the culprits involved in harassing girls. The Committee understands that merely counting the
number of incidents does not justify the general perception. The Committee believes that a mass
campaign should be organised by Delhi Police against such incidents. (Para 4.2.22 ibid)
Action Taken
3.6.2 Maximum attention is paid to solving the incidents of rape and other crimes against women
in Delhi. All out efforts are made to bring the perpetrators of such crimes to book. During the year
2011, the work-out percentage of rape cases in Delhi was as high as 97.5% and of molestation
cases 95.4%. Investigation in these cases is carried out in most professional manner so that the
accused persons are properly linked to the Crime. Delhi Police also follow-up on the bail matters

3.6.5 Delhi Police is required to be more alert all the time and should give impetus on the
preventive measures for non-occurance of such incidents. The incidents of kidnapping also
