I. OPENING REMARKS OF CHAIRMAN
2.0 At the outset, the chairman welcomed the Members to the sitting and apprised them of the
agenda i.e. (i) to hear the Home Secretary on the relief and rehabilitation and rescue measures being
undertaken in Uttarkhand after cloud burst and flash floods and to (ii) hear the Cabinet Secretary,
Finance and Planning Commission Secretaries on ‘Strengthening the working of the Ministry of
DoNER for effective implementation of policies, programmes, schemes and projects meant for
North-Eastern Region’.
2.1 The Chairman, thereafter, read out a letter received from the Home Minister with regard
to rehabilitation and rescue measures in Uttarakhand after flash floods and cloud burst there
stating that there was no provision laid down in the Disaster Management Act or the guidelines
issued thereunder for declaring a disaster as a National Calamity. He added that as per the
information received from the State Government of Uttarakhand, 580 human lives had lost, 4,200
villages had been affected, and over 2,300 houses had been reported damaged and about 3,100
persons have been injured. The State Government was in the process of making damage
assessment and the number of lives lost may go up after debris is cleared. Essential commodities
including food packets were being air dropped. Food packets, water and medicines are being sent
to all the affected areas. Relief camps are being organised in different parts of the State. Medical
teams with sufficient medicines and equipments were being sent. Free transport was being
arranged for all the people till their respective destinations. Special train bogies were being
arranged in different trains to help the pilgrims to reach their destination. Stranded tourists had
been allowed free access to all State guest houses as well as tourist guest houses of the State
Governments. As on 1
st July, 2013, over one lakh people had been evacuated by all agencies to
safer places.
2.2 The Chairman also mentioned that he had also written a letter to the Hon’ble Chairman of
the Rajya Sabha as well as to the Hon’ble Speaker of the Lok Sabha requesting them to allow
Members of Parliament to donate money from their MPLAD fund for relief measures in
Uttarakhand. The Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha had written back that the Members of Parliament
were allowed to donate up to rupees fifty lakh from their MPLAD funds towards relief and
rehabilitation in the State of Uttarakhand.

75
2.3 The Chairman mentioned that the Committee would hear the Home Secretary in brief
and at a later stage, it would study the situation in depth because it would be diverting the
attention of Government officials engaged in relief and rescue operations by way of attending
the meetings.
[At this stage, witnesses were called in]
II. REHABILITATION AND RESCUE MEASURES IN UTTARAKHAND
3.0 The Chairman welcomed the Home Secretary and other officials of the Ministry of Home
Affairs and State Government of Uttarkhand and placed on record the appreciation of the
commendable job by personnel of NDRF, ITBP and Armed Forces under a joint command, in
rescuing the stranded pilgrims and locals. He then asked the Home Secretary to make his
presentation on the matter.
4.0 The Home Secretary submitted that the first responder in the disaster was the State
Government of Uttarakhand and immediately after that, the Government of India moved into action.
All the Ministries of the Government of India were mobilized. The National Crisis Management
Committee, under the chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary, thereafter met every day to review
the situation and coordinate all the assistance that was required to be rendered to the State
Government to ensure that everything was done as quickly as was humanly possible. He added that
the Government of India directed the Armed Forces, ITBP, the National Disaster Response Force
to start salvage, rescue, relief and succor operations and consequentially a very large number of
people were rescued. A member of the National Disaster Management Authority was stationed at
Dehradoon to coordinate the efforts. The National Executive Committee, under the Home Secretary
was meeting every day to review and take stock of the situation. Connectivity of telephone had
been established with many towns and the basic telephony was in operation but it may not
necessarily be possible for every mobile telephone to be working there. The State Government
authorities needed to continue the relief operations. Systematic efforts would be required to ensure
immediate restoration of basic road connectivity. The State Government needed to prepare a
Memorandum for Assistance from the National Disaster Response Fund. The State Government
also had to plan for long-term reconstruction and rehabilitation, which could be looked into by the
Planning Commission separately.
4.1 The Secretary, Disaster Management, State Government of Uttarakhand, thereafter gave a
brief of the sequence of the event of disaster that took place and the steps taken by the State
Government and Central Government. He stated that the focus was on Kedar Valley though the
State Government had information from other valleys like Badrinath, Ghangaria, Hemkund Sahib,
Gangotri and Yamunotri as the people there were safe with no problem of food and other civil
supplies. More than 300 persons were evacuated from Rambara, which was almost non-existent
and totally inaccessible for the rest of the world. The entire road connectivity was totally cut off
at different places and the emphasis was on restoration of road connectivity. Mule tracks and
kutcha roads were made to evacuate the people. Many local people in Badrinath, Gangotri and
Yamunotri will remain safe and there will be all kind of relief materials till the closure of ‘holy
kapaats’ of the ‘Char Dhams’ in third week of November, 2013. He expressed thanks and gratitude
for the assistance given by the Government of India, Indian Army, Indian Air Force, NDRF and
all other Government agencies.
4.2 With regard to Chairman’s query about delay to reach Garud Chatti, the Secretary
submitted that it was totally isolated and cut off from the rest of the world. There was no
helipad at all. It was amidst the jungle. Hence there was delay in reaching Garud Chatti but the
operation in Garud Chatti was completed within 48 hours and about three hundred persons were
evacuated.

76
4.3 Regarding reports in certain sections of media of looting the tourists and pilgrims at certain
places, the Secretary submitted that one case of this kind had come to the notice of the State
Government and police personnel were enquiring into it. Regarding exact number of dead persons,
the Secretary submitted that there was debris in Kedarnath and Ram Bada which was very high
upto 30 feet and the 560 count had come from visually counting the dead. The death toll may rise
in future after extraction. With regard to missing persons, the State Government had requested the
Chief Secretaries of all the State Governments and Union Territories to identify people from their
States who had been there in the chardham yatra, during this particular period of disaster, and then
revert back to us along with their detailed list. The State Government would then consider them
as missing. The State Government was also taking regular help from all service providers to locate
the position of different people in the Kedar Hills during this period of time. The number has been
estimated at 3,078. All care and caution has been taken to reach at this figure.
4.4 The Chairman and Members of the Committee, thereafter, raised the following querries:–
(i) Conflicting news about the forewarning given by the Meteorological Department and
by the ISRO;
(ii) No meeting of National Executive Committee. since September, 2008 till December,
2012;
(iii) Possibility of earthquake in Uttarakhand and adequate warning to the State
Governments;
(iv) Pooling of help form other State Governments;
(v) Status of prevention of diseases and epidemic in that area;
(vi) Position of drinking water; and
(vii) Neglect of environmental concerns by construction of dams and roads by blowing up
Himalayan ranges.
4.5 Concluding the discussion, the Chairman asked the Home Secretary to send written replies
on the queries raised and stated that the Committee would discuss NDMA, the relief and
rehabilitation programme in detail later on.
III. STRENGTHENING THE WORKING OF THE MINISTRY OF DONER ETC.
5.0 The Committee thereafter heard the Cabinet Secretary, Finance Secretary and Secretary,
Planning Commission.
(i) The subject of development and growth of the North-East is an extremely important
issue that engaged the Government and it is trying its best to ensure that the
development of the North-Eastern Region goes ahead apace. Though the funds, in per
capita terms, are definitely higher than the national average, but it requires a lot of
investment, particularly in agriculture and horticulture. The Government is conscious
of the need to strengthen the infrastructure in the States and under ‘Look East
Policy’;
(ii) There are a lot of problems and the major problem is of connectivity and
infrastructure. More intra-regional connectivity and airports’ infrastructure is required.
There are other issues in health or social sector schemes;
(iii) Problem in roads construction under the SARDP-NE or the Arunachal Package is not
with regard to the money but the implementation;

77
(iv) The DoNER is a co-ordinating Ministry and the co-ordination is best done from Delhi
where the other Ministries are located. Shifting of the Ministry to the North east on
the analogy of the Space Department and Atomic Energy would not be an overall
great advantage. Therefore the Ministry of DoNER should continue to remain in the
national capital;
(v) Effectiveness of the advocacy role of DoNER is not unique. Those are structural
issues, which can arise in other Ministries also where they are similarly placed and
the actual work is supposed to be done or executed or monitored by other different
line Ministries;
(vi) Ministries are more conscious of the need to spend and there has been a dip in
accumulated balances and accruals in the Non-Lapsable Pool for Central Resources.
Ministries are being sensitized to spend the funds more quickly and more effectively;
(vii) There are generic problems. The capacities of local PWDs are poor in terms of
funds. There are also issues relating to DPR preparation. It would be better if States
rely more on the EPC model to freeze the cost and that would have a positive effect
on time over-runs. The Government is pushing all the projects in that direction;
(viii) Lack of manpower and machinery is improving because big contractors have started
to come to the North-East and many of them after completing the projects, are
leaving the machinery behind because it is not economical for them to transport the
machinery back. Over the time, gradually there will be greater corpus of big
machinery there. The Government is trying to synchronise the construction in line
with the dry season at a quicker pace;
(ix) The State Governments, particularly Arunachal Pradesh, have to do something for
land acquisition since the major projects are essentially executed through the State
PWDs;
(x) Huge hydro power potential has to be tapped and developed. There are environmental
and forest clearances issues. 8-9 projects are in the pipeline. Problems relating to
evacuation of power and construction of roads and transmission lines have to be
simultaneously looked at;
(xi) The Government is trying its best to see that on the one hand the security concerns
and administrative issues are addressed, and at the same time, the funds and
governance issues relating to the actual execution of the development projects go ahead;
(xii) Ministry of DoNER has engaged W APCOS, a consultancy organization under the
Ministry of Water Resources for vetting of DPRs of projects up to Rs.50 crores
under the NLCPR scheme. On the issue of appointing Chief Engineer in the Ministry
of DoNER to strengthen capability to vet projects, opinion is divided because in
practical terms, it is unlikely that he would be able to prevail upon the engineering
wing in the line ministries;
(xiii) Retired engineers are being appointed as the National Quality Managers for third-party
monitoring;
(xiv) About appointing a senior officer in each Ministry as a Nodal Officer to look after
the projects, in many line Ministries, different projects might be handled by different
Divisions, headed by a Joint Secretary or some other officer. So, instead of
appointing one officer to deal just with all these projects, it would be better that the
Secretary himself reviews these projects more frequently from time to time;

78
(xv) The Prime Minister has directed to set up an E-GoM and the same would be set up
after report of the Committee of Secretaries. The DoNER will service the GoM;
5.2 Thereafer, the Secretary, Planning Commission made the following submissions:
(i) The issue of 100% funding instead of 90:10 has been an ongoing issue raised by
Chief Ministers of all the eight States for a long time. The overall view has been that
if some ownership has to be brought into the system, then, at least, some
contribution will come from within the States. If the entire amount came from the
Central Government, then there would be very little difference between the State’s
own development plans and that of the Central Government;
(ii) The issue of delay in DPR approvals has probably been raised by the States in the
context of the Special Plan Assistance. Budget cycles are such that States finalise
their budget between April to June and then, by the time they send the DPR, their
working season starts. The Central Government is trying to streamline the process
and it would review in a committee-mode in August itself and try to see that they
get the full working season. Annual DPRs are only for the Special Plan Assistance,
which are given to the States and are actually done by the States. However, for State
DPRs which are considered by the Secretary, DoNER and the line Ministries are
asked to give their technical inputs, it is a matter of pressing administratively a little
harder on them;
(iii) States will have to take the responsibility for the Maintenance of the completed
projects. Hand-holding and capacity-building for doing so need to be improved. The
Government would look at this issue in the course of the Twelfth Plan;
(iv) Since last year, a new window of NLCPR-Central has been created, where unspent
balances of Central Ministries would accrue into this fund and, as required, demands
would be placed before the Ministry of Finance for releases on case-to-case basis.
This is yet to be completely put on the ground;
(v) Regarding State-specific guidelines, most of the Centrally-sponsored schemes do not
meet the requirements of the North-Eastern States and there are many other States
also. Recently, the Cabinet has taken a decision that State-specific guidelines within
the overall core guidelines of every Centrally-sponsored scheme would be received
from the States, in the first instance, and would be looked into by a Committee
comprising of Secretary, Planning Commission, the Expenditure Secretary, the Chief
Secretary or any other representative of the State to tailor the schemes better to the
requirements of the States;
(vi) In addition, there has also been a decision that there would be a Flexi fund of ten
per cent in each Centrally-sponsored scheme which would be available to the State
to try innovations and tailor these schemes to their own requirements;
(vii) The only way to stop cost escalation is to complete the project. There are no two
ways of doing it. So, the effort has to be stepped up. We do need to press upon
the Ministries.
5.3 The Chairman, then invited the Finance Secretary to present his views on the select
subject. The Finance Secretary made the following submissions:–
(i) Till two years back, for the national projects of Railways, the Railways used to spend
the amount and the actual expenditure during the year was used to be provided by
the Finance Ministry towards the end of the year. Now upfront money on an ad-hoc

79
basis, based on the level of expenditure in the previous year is provided. The
expenditure on national projects shall be provided by the Finance Ministry. It is not
an issue of funds. It is an issue of their execution capability. There is no constraint.
They were not told that they had to spend less or spend within this amount;
(ii) Regarding holding of the funds by State Governments, normally the money must be
released within 15 days’ time for that particular project. If it was not done, then, the
State Government should pay interest on that amount, which would be utilized for
that project. But specific aspect regarding the Bodo Tribal Autonomous Council not
receiving the funds needed to be checked in detail;
(iii) Earlier the maintenance of completed projects was not being provided for in the
contract. Now a provision is being made in this regard. Initially, it was made that a
minimum three years’ mandatory maintenance would be provided by the contractor
after completion of the project. Now, for the EPC projects they are trying to raise
it to a level of five years and that five years’ maintenance will be built into the cost
of the project. Thereafter, in any case, it is the responsibility of the State
Government;
(iv) There has been a general principle that for all Central sector and Centrally-sponsored
schemes, land should be provided by the State Government. There is again a the

In case of centrally Sponsored fodder development Scheme, the proposals are not submitted

Schemes relating to Small Ruminants and Meat Products in NER
Implementation of schemes is very low. Hence active participation of States is required in

National Project for Cattle and Buffalo Breeding
Dairy animal population is limited in North Eastern States as at present milk consumption
is very low. Demand for the milk and milk products will further increase with the rapid
economic development of this region.
Productivity of dairy animals is lowest in the region than the other regions in the country.
Management of dairy animals is not remunerative to the farmers of the State.  Incentives
are not made available to the farmers for rearing dairy animals.
There is poor breeding infrastructure and very low Artificial Insemination (AI) coverage.
Quality breeding inputs are not available in these States. For breeding inputs these States
are dependent on other States.
Poor quality of bulls used in natural service and some of the NER States have no provisions
for natural service due to which inbreeding is going on in these States.
Deficiency of cattle feed and fodder in some of the States is major constraints to
development of dairy activities in these States. Most of the NER States are dependent on
the feed supply from other States. There is need to formulate cattle feed locally available
feed ingredients.

95
No programmes have been initiated by these States for development and conservation of
indigenous strains and breeds.
There is urgent need to put complete ban on slaughter of female dairy animals as a large
number of female calves are slaughtered to fulfil demand of meat in the State. Establishment
of feed lot farms for scientific rearing of male calves for use in meat industry are required
by most of the States.
Heifer rearing programme may be taken up on a massive scale in order to promote dairying
in NER region.
Crossing of swamp buffalo with recognized buffalo breeds may be taken up in NER region
to increase milk production as suggested by FAO in Philippines.
Disease outbreak and non availability of quality vaccines in these States is also a major
constraint in development of dairy sector in these States.
Dairy Development Schemes
Dairy cooperatives in States of NER are at nascent State. Dairy professional/technical
experts available in the region are at shortage. Implementation of dairy development projects
and utilization of fund under approved projects is therefore slow. Physical achievement does
not commensurate with financial release made under the projects.
Due to inordinate delay in implementation of projects together with problems relating to
remoteness and difficult terrain conditions of the region, often projected cost become
inadequate. Unspent balance under approved projects remains unutilized.
Under these circumstances, mid-course re-correction in terms of component cost and
activity consumes more time and results in further delay in project completion.
The North Eastern States may be advised on the following aspects
(i) To closely monitor and review the progress in implementation of approved/ongoing
projects.
(ii) To arrange submission of pending Utilization Certificate.
(iii) To sensitize fishermen organizations/associations and other implementing agencies to
avail benefit of the scheme.
(iv) To verify carefully the bonafides of Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), before
their proposals are forwarded to the Department.

1. NER States have a sizeable fish eating population and with the growing demand for
consumption, there is always shortage of fish supply to meet this growing demand.
Shortage of quality seed is a big constraint for enhancing fish production in these
States. At present these States depend upon States like Andhra Pradesh and West
Bengal for supply of fish and fish seeds. These States therefore need to develop
hatcheries and brood banks in big way by taking advantage of existing schemes of the
Centre.
2. As against the average national productivity level of 2900 kg/ha/year for freshwater
ponds, the productivity levels in NER are very low. Except for Sikkim (3500 kg/ha/
year) all other States have a productivity level of less than national average.

fishermen organizations, associations and other implementing agencies to avail benefit

management of post harvest infrastructure facilities through private entrepreneurs.

· The North Eastern States are densely forested, which causes immense problems
in carrying out the field work and other geological investigations.

98
· Law and Order problem
· Infrastructure, rail, road, air connectivity.
Suggestions
· Relaxation on the rules for NER for procurement of vehicle as at present the fleet
inner is very old and frequently goes under break down due to prevailing rugged
terrain condition of NER. Moreover outsourced vehicles are not readily available.
· Induction of sufficient fresh manpower suitable for carrying out field activities in
difficult terrain condition like NER.
· Augmenting infrastructure, including rail, road, inland water and air transportation
to facilitate a two-way movement of people and goods within the region and
outside, communication networks including broadband and wireless connectivity,
and harnessing of the vast power generation potential, all of which will open up
markets for produce from the region, attract private investment, create greater
employment opportunities and expand choices for people of the region. In
addition, opening up the land route through Bangladesh could enormously benefit
both the countries and diplomatic efforts should focus on improving relations with
the neighbours.
· Empowered Committee on Mineral development in North Eastern Region (NER)
with a view to facilitate fast decision making process and to ensure time-bound
action for sustainable development in NER.
(ii) Indian Bureau of Mines
Supply of machinery and Equipments:
· Response to Tenders is not satisfactory. Parties are not willing to supply the
material to the NE States.
· As per Audit observations, NER States are placing demands without feasibility
study.
· Certificate of installation and status of utilization in respect of Equipments are not
received from some of the parties and audit para is pending in the Kolkata
Regional Office.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY
(Department of Industrial Policy and  Promotion)
(i) A considerable period of time lapses before the subsidy is disbursed.
(ii) Time taken for processing of claims at various level  in the concerned States is too
long and the State Governments do not have effective ways and means of monitoring
claims processing at various level.
(iii) Claims are being received mainly from the States of  Assam, Meghalaya and Tripura.
Other States are hardly claiming any subsidy.
(iv) Instances of fake/inflated claims and inability of States to undertake effective scrutiny.
(v) Meeting of State Level Committee are not held timely.

99
MINISTRY OF MINORITY AFFAIRS
National Minorities Development and Finance Corporation (NMDFC)
(a) Weak infrastructure of the State Channelising Agencies (SCAs) and consequently a
very weak delivery system.
(b) Limitation of resources.
(c) Unwillingness of good NGOs to work at the existing interest margin.
Multi-sectoral Development Programme (MsDP) for Minority Concentration Districts (MCD)
(a) Project proposals are not received in time.
(b) Project proposals are recommended to the Ministry without ascertaining the availability
of land.
(c) Many States/UTs have not standardized the design and cost for the works taken up.
This leads to delay in approval.
(d) Delay in transfer of Central share of funds by the States/UTs to the districts/
implementing agencies.
(e) State share not released to the districts/implementing agencies in many projects.
(f) Slow utilization of funds and late submission of Utilization Certificate.
(g) Quarterly Progress Report (QPRs) is not sent in time.
(h) Review meetings and meetings of Empowered Committee not attended at appropriate
level.
Scheme for Leadership Development of Minority Women
During 2012-13, the scheme could be implemented in Manipur only amongst the North
Eastern States due to non-receipt of proposals from other states. However, during 2013-14, in
order to generate awareness about the schemes and programmes of the Ministry, awareness
generation camps have been organized in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Meghalaya. Further,
awareness is also generated through publicity campaigns in various States including North-East
through Print Media and Electronic Media.
Computerization of records of State Waqf Boards
The complete data of waqf properties are not available with the State/UT Waqf Boards.
(i) Paucity/shortage of staff in the State/UT Waqf Boards.
Strengthening of State Waqf Boards
The scheme could not be implemented as the in principle approval of Planning Commission
is still awaited.
MINISTRY OF DRINKING WATER AND SANITATION
There is paradox of prevalence of water scarcity, even drought in many parts of NER,
some rivers dry up during non rainy season due to run off rainwater from hillsides, This problem
can be tackled by rejuvenation and conservation of forest.

100
Habitations in NER are located in hilltops away from the rivers and rely on the meager
water sources and direct rainfall. Roof top rainwater harvesting needs to be promoted in a big way.
More community rainwater collection tanks and reservoirs also need to be built.
Fragmentation and proliferation of villages on acoount of dispute with chieftains cause the
number of households in those villages too small to be viable for water supply schemes due to high
per capita cost. Setting up of new villages needs to be put to a halt so that planning and
implementation of not only water  supply schemes but also other government programmes are not
affected by mushrooming of new villages.
The capacity of water supply and distribution system needs to be augmented.
Water meters needed to be installed in all water connections in order to induce water
conservation.
To avoid pollution in surface water sources like rivers and lakes, States Flood Zone Area
Act should be invoked to remove encroachments.
Phumdi (floating islands) dwellers are being rehabilitated but further encroachments need to
be stopped.
Landfills into the rivers and lakes should be stopped.
Regulation and restrictions need to be put in place for managing industrial effluents and
discharge of waste products in the rivers and lakes.
All water supply schemes proposed to the Ministry of DoNER for funding should be
examined by the Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation for techno-economic aspects and all the
schemes funded by the Ministry of DoNER should be approved in SLSSC. Similarly combined
convergence within the States is also required between the Public Health Engineering Department
which is implementing water supply schemes, Irrigation and Flood Control Department, State
Disaster Management Authority in terms of finance, dovetailing of schemes and manpower to
address various issues.
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE
(Department of AYUSH)
CONSTRAINTS/PROBLEMS
There are very few AYUSH Hospitals and Dispensaries in the entire NE Region. The existing
facilities have poor availability of AYUSH medical and para-medical manpower.
SUGGESTIONS
(i) A separate Directorate of AYUSH could be established for NE Region. This matter has
already been taken up with the NE States during various meetings of Health Secretaries
held in the Department.
(ii) To overcome the shortage of Doctors, maximum number of AYUSH Doctors may be
engaged at PHCs/CHCs/DHs.
2. National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)
CONSTRAINTS/PROBLEMS
(i) Although, the NE Region abounds in medicinal plants resources, yet these resources
have not been properly tapped. Medicinal plants are collected and exported to other
parts of the country or abroad. However due to lack of facilities, more than 30%
medicinal plants material is wasted in the region.

101
(ii) There is no co-ordination between State Medicinal Plants Boards and State Missions
on Medicinal Plants.
(iii) Pendency of UCs for minor amounts often results in non-release of major grants to
the NE Region.
SUGGESTIONS
(i) Developing of medicinal plants zones/clusters will give a major boost to the Sector and
create sustainable livelihood systems for the people in the region.
(ii) There are many medicinal plants, which can be cultivated in the region aimed at
diversification of agriculture, particularly in areas under shifting cultivation. Medicinal
plants could be cultivated in the region as intercrop, main crop and during the
intervening cycle of shifting cultivation with proper buy-back arrangements. This
would lead to their conservation in wild habitats.
(iii) There are many medicinal plants, which are unsustainably and destructively harvested.
Therefore, there is an urgent need to conserve medicinal plants by establishing chain
of Medicinal Plants Conservation Areas (MPCAs), taking into account the biological
(taxonomic identity, distribution and population), social (awareness, ownership and
alternatives) and legal (tenure and benefit sharing) aspects in all Forest Types/Sub
Types/Agro Climatic Zones, so that there is sufficient and viable gene base.
(iv) For co-ordination purposes, NE Council and Ministry of DoNER should co-ordinate
medicinal plants related activities, particularly for establishing medicinal plants
processing zones/clusters and the issues common to different States in the Sector.
(v) For liquidating the pendency of UCs, a Corpus Fund for the purpose could be created
under the North Eastern Council (NEC) for refund to the NMPB of small amounts.
Thus, pendency of UCs would reduce and fresh funds could be released.
(vi) NEC should help the NMPB in establishing Medicinal Plants Facilitation Centres in
different parts and districts and designate a Nodal Officer to handle and co-ordinate
operational/management issues. NEC should also take up with all the Forest
Departments for following a uniform transit policy for transportation of the medicinal
plants produced in the region and from the region to other parts of the country.
3. Development of AYUSH Institutions
CONSTRAINTS/PROBLEMS
Due to incomplete proposals from the State Governments in NE region and pendency of
UCs against the grants released to State Governments in respect of the Institutions, it has not been
possible to provide the funds to the State Governments in NE region to the budgeted amount.
SUGGESTIONS
State Governments in NE region should be sensitized to send complete proposals and
liquidate pendency of UCs.
MINISTRY OF PANCHAYATI RAJ
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR) is implementing the e-Panchayat Mission Mode
Project (MMP), under the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) for e-enablement of all Panchayats
which will make their functioning more efficient and transparent.

102
1. PRIASoft- Except Assam, Sikkim and Tripura none of the PRIs in other NE States and
UT of Andaman and Nicobar Islands are maintain their accounts through PRIASoft.
The States of Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya and Nagaland have not yet issued
Government Orders for adopting Model Accounting System (MAS).
2. PlanPlus- Except Assam, Sikkim and Tripura, none of the PRIs in other NE States
have uploaded their Annual Action Plans in PlanPlus.
3. The National Panchayat Portal (NPP)- Dynamic websites have been created for most
of the State departments (except Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland). But except
Tripura no other NE State has registered or uploaded content in these websites.
4. Local Governance Directory (LGD)- Except Assam, Manipur, Sikkim and Tripura, none
of the NE States and have started mapping their villages with their Gram Panchayats/
equivalent units.
5. Training of the Trainers (ToT)- So far none of the functionaries in the States of
Meghalaya and Nagaland have utilized trainings imparted by the Ministry on PES
applications.
6. None of the functionaries and elected members in the States like Nagaland, Mizoram,
Meghalaya have been imparted training on basic IT literary through DOEACC/NIELIT.
MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES
There is immense potential for Horticulture crops and also for Non-Horticulture products as
well as resultant processing requirements for various fruits and vegetables grown in North-East
Region including exotic fruit. There is an urgent necessity to develop food processing related
infrastructure like cold chains, enhancing processing capacities; to ensure better marketing not only
in India but also in South East Asia markets due to its proximity geograbhically and also culturally,
which will earn foreign exchange also. Hence more allocation of funds may be required for North-
East Region areas to develop Agrucultural/Horticultural/food processing sectors in the region.

Commission based upon the expenditure trend and committed liabilities of CAPFs.
Recommendation
1.3.3 The Committee feels that it would not be easy for the Ministry of Home Affairs to manage
the expenditure over stated projects during 2013-14 as reduction of Rs. 2,525 crores is not a meager
amount and, moreover, the Ministry is planning for raising 16 battalions during the year. The
Committee observes that with reduced allocation, the Ministry would not be able to raise those
battalions. Keeping in view the fact that the demand for sophisticated weapons and gadgets is
growing more and more because of increasing rate of crime and also because of increasing
population, the Committee feels that there is every need to enhance allocation rather than reducing
allocation.
(Para 2.17.7 ibid)
Action Taken
1.3.4 The allocation made by Ministry of Finance against the projection of MHA based upon the
requirement of CAPFs is not sufficient and will badly hamper the process of procurement of Arms
and Ammunition, requirement of new infrastructure for establishments, requirement of augmentation
of existing establishment and requirement of surveillance equipments. In this regard, based upon the
allocation made to CAPFs, the expenditure trend, committed liabilities in CAPFs, the additional
requirement for 2013-14 will be projected at Supplementary Stage/Revised Estimate stage to
Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission so as to ensure that the requirement of CAPFs do not
suffer due to lack of funds.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.3.5 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry of Home Affairs which is in sync with
the observation of the Committee. At this juncture, reduction of budgetary allocation to the
Ministry of Home Affairs for projects pertaining to CAPFs would not be better in the
interest of national security. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
Ministry of Home Affairs should take up the matter with the Planning Commission and the
Ministry of Finance for grant of enhanced budgetary allocation.

6

Recommendation
1.3.20 The Committee also takes note of the submission made by the Ministry that China spends
around about 119 billion dollars on defence and 123 billion dollars on internal security. The
Committee understands that China has a bigger economy than India, as India’ s GDP is about one-
fourth of China’ s GDP but as far as our allocation for internal security is concerned, it is one-
tenth of China’ s Budget for internal security. The Government should consider higher allocation to
the internal security in view of its strategic importance and keeping in view the fact that India
is facing internal disturbances on several counts. A separate long term planning should be made
for this.
(Para 2.17.15 ibid)
Action Taken
1.3.21 As compared to China, the internal security challenges in India are much more complex due
to various factors including regional conflicts, religious fundamentalism, insurgency in different

8
parts of the country, Jehadi terrorism posing threat to most parts of the country, continued
militancy in JandK and activities of anti-India forces across the Indian borders. Economic disparity
and huge unemployed/partially employed population and various other social factors have also been
causing strain in the maintenance of public order in different parts of the country.
1.3.22 There is definitely a need for long term strategic planning for internal security of the
country for which enhancement in the Budget is needed. However, the requirement of funds for
the internal security has to be examined keeping in mind the various other social and developmental
commitments of the Government.
1.4 LEFT-WING EXTREMISM
Recommendation
1.4.1 Left Wing Extremism is the single biggest threat to India’s internal security. The maoists are
directly challenging the democratic fabric of our country. Left Wing Extremism is violent in nature
and has pre-defined political objectives of seizing political power through barrel of gun. They do not
believe in parliamentary democracy. Maoists’ violence, which persisted for a long time has assumed
serious and threatening proportions. The Committee feels that while pursing security related and
development related activities, the maoists should also be challenged ideologically at various fora
such as seminars, media etc. Though the Home Secretary contends that there is improvement in the
situation, the Committee feels that there is no marked visibility of the improvement.
(Para 3.6.13 ibid)
Action Taken
1.4.2 A Central Sector Scheme namely Media Plan is being implemented for the Left Wing
Extremism (LWE) affected areas. The main objective of the Scheme is to familiarise people in the
LWE affected States about the various ongoing schemes of the Government for the infrastructure
development, job creation, education and skill development programmes including skill upgradation,
in order to enable them to avail the benefits under these schemes so that they are not lured by
the Maoists.
1.4.3 During the last Financial Year i.e. 2012-13, 
R 6.00 crore was allocated under the head of
Advertisement and Publicity (Media Plan). The fund was utilized for conveying relevant messages
to LWE affected areas through broadcast of audio spots over All India Radio (AIR), presenting
4560 programmes through the Song and Drama Division and organizing the 5
th Tribal Youth
Exchange Programme at 4 places viz. Gangtok, Mysore, Alwar and Pune through the Nehru Yuva
Kendra Sangathan (NYKS) which envisaged participation of 2000 Tribal Youths from the worst
LWE affected areas. Apart from this, the Institute of Social Science, New Delhi is in the process
of conducting 08 Seminars on LWE related issues which is funded by the MHA. In the past, MHA
has also published newspaper advertisements and posters through the DA VP.
1.4.4 As a result of multi-pronged approach of the Central Government in dealing with the
problem of Left Wing Extremism, the LWE violence level has come down during the last two
years, as may be seen from the following table:
Year Incidents Deaths
2010 2213 1005
2011 1760 611
2012 1415 415

9
Recommendation
1.4.5 The Committee is well aware of the fact that maoists have expanded their areas of influence
considerably by exploiting social, economic and political grievances of local poor population. The
maoist problem is the result of the lack of adequate resources to the poor people and tribals, and
hence the maoist affected regions remained underdeveloped with less infrastructure facilities. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Central and State Governments should ensure that the
fruits of development should reach the LWE infested areas as well to bring back the misguided
people to the mainstream of the society. More and more employment of the youth from those areas
will go a long way in improving the situation.
(Para 3.6.14 ibid)
Action Taken
1.4.6 The Government of India has adopted an integrated approach in dealing with LWE activities
in the arenas of security, development, ensuring entitlements of marginalized sections, good
governance and public perception management. The Integrated Action Plan (IAP) being implemented
by the Planning Commission in 82 selected Tribal and Backward Districts, inter-alia, including
71 LWE affected districts; the Road Requirement Plan (RRP) being implemented by the Ministry
of Road Transport and Highways in 34 most adversely LWE affected districts; and the Skill
Development Scheme being implemented by the Directorate General of Employment and Training,
Ministry of Labour and Employment in 34 most adversely LWE affected districts, are three
important development schemes that focus on the LWE affected areas. Apart from these, there are
other development Schemes like Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) and Indira Awas
Yojana (IAY) (M/o Rural Development); Sarva Siksha Abhiyan (SSA), Rashtriya Madhyamik Siksha
Abhiyan (RMSA), Sakshar Bharat (D/o School Education and Literacy, M/o Human Resources
Development); Implementations of provisions of Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas
Act), 1996 (M/o Panchayati Raj); National Rural Health Mission (M/o Health and Family Welfare);
Bal Bandhu Scheme (National Commission for Protection of Child Rights) etc. that cover LWE
affected areas also. Further, the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) deployed in LWE affected
areas have also undertaken small skill development/employment oriented programmes in LWE
affected areas under the Civic Action Programmes.
Recommendation
1.4.7 The Committee is of considered view that schemes such as development of socio-economic
infrastructure and services such as school buildings, Anganwadi Centres, Primary Health Centres,
Drinking water Supply, Village Roads, Electric lights in public places such as PHCs and schools
etc. under Integrated Action Plan (IAP) for Selected Districts should be implemented in a big way.
The Committee is of the firm view that providing basic infrastructure facilities in LWE infested
areas can change the mindset of inhabitants and check their support to Left Wing Extremism.
(Para 3.6.15 ibid)
Action Taken
1.4.8 The Planning Commission is implementing the Integrated Action Plan (IAP) in 82 Selected
Tribal and Backward Districts, inter-alia , including 71 LWE affected districts, for accelerated
development of the affected areas. The nature of works taken up under the IAP includes public
infrastructure and services which create a perceptible impact on the ground and among the local
communities. Macro-level monitoring of the IAP is being carried out by the Committee headed by
the Secretary, Planning Commission and regular video conference meetings are being held with the
District Collectors/District Magistrates and the Development Commissioners of the States

10
concerned. As on 06th June, 2013, an amount of R 6090 crore has been released so far under the
Scheme and against which an expenditure of R 4435.60 crore (72.83 %) has been reported. The
number of Projects completed so far under IAP is 82568.
Recommendation
1.4.9 The Committee expresses its concern over the expansion of maoists influence in new areas
particularly in North-Eastern region of the country. The presence of LWE in the north-eastern parts
of the country can derail the socio-economic developmental projects of the Central and State
Governments as a result of which, efforts of the Government could go in vain. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Government must show its determination to flush out maoists from
these areas.
(Para 3.6.16 ibid)
Action Taken
1.4.10 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State subjects, action with respect to maintenance of law
and order lies primarily in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with the
various issues related to Left Wing Extremist (LWE) activities in the States. The Central
Government monitors the situation closely and supplements and coordinates their efforts in several
ways.
1.4.11 As per available inputs, the CPI (Maoist) have been trying to forge links with insurgent
groups in the North Eastern States, particularly in Assam. The State Governments have been
sensitized in this regard and they have been requested to take urgent steps to tackle the situation
so as to obviate any possibility of these States emerging as another LWE theatre. A number of
significant arrests have been made of top leadership of the Maoists in Assam, which has
considerably impaired their capacity in the North-East.
1.5 TERRORISM IN J&K
Recommendation
1.5.1 The Committee is of the view that the impact of good governance should be visible at the
ground level in the remotest areas of the valley. The Committee recommends that the Government
in tandem with State Government should make an all-out effort for socio-economic development
of the State which could heal the deep wounds of people of Jammu and Kashmir victimised by
terrorism. Besides, the Government should also utilize “advocacy and publicity” to make people
aware about terrorism and its negative fallout. More employment opportunities should be provided
to the youth of the State. Private sector should also be encouraged in selecting youth from the area
for employment.
(Para 3.8.8 ibid)
Action Taken

Schemes Udaan, Himayat have been launched to involve private sector in employment generation
in the State.
Special Industry Initiative for J&K (SII J&K) ‘UDAAN’: (Implementation by Ministry of Home Affairs)
1.5.3 Based on the recommendations of the Expert Group constituted by the Prime Minister, the
Government of India launched the Scheme Special Industry Initiative for Jammu & Kashmir in the

11
nature of partnership between the corporates of India and Ministry of Home Affairs. The scheme
is being implemented by National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC). The Programme aims at
providing the skill and enhance employability of 40,000 unemployed youths of J&K who are
graduate/post graduate. Total budget for the Scheme is Rs.1000crore. out of which MHA share is

college drop-outs. As on 10 th May, 2013, 7929 candidates have been trained and 5434 candidates
have been placed in jobs.
Special Scholarship Scheme for J&K:
(Implementation by Ministry of Human Resources Development)
1.5.6 Based on the recommendation of the Expert Group constituted by the Prime Minister, the
Scheme has been launched with the aim to encourage the J&K youths to take advantage of the

scholarships for general courses, 250 for engineering courses and 250 for medical studies) over

1.5.7 The Special Scholarship Scheme for Jammu & Kashmir started in the year 2011. In the first
year, only 420 applications were received and 38 students were found to be eligible and awarded

scheme.
1.5.8 In the academic year 2012-13, 5186 nos of application received. Out of this, the number

& Kashmir. J&K State has been given a quota of 768 scholarships.

“A provision under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005
(MGNREGA) has been made to provide at least one hundred days of guaranteed wage
employment in every financial year to every household whose adult members volunteer to
do unskilled work. Besides MGNREGA, other Scheme like Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar
Yojana (SJSRY); Prime Minister’ s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) and
National Rural Livelihood Mission and entrepreneurial development programmes and

12
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) are being implemented throughout the

FURTHER RECOMMENDATION

1.6 COASTAL SECURITY
Recommendation
1.6.1 The Committee is anguished to note that the proposed procurement of boats under Coastal
Security Scheme Phase-II due to procedural wrangles is still halfway and a substantial amount
allocated for the purpose could not be utilized during 2012-13 which led to the reduction of
allocation from 
R 170 crore to R 80 crore in RE 2012-13 which is causing delay in completion
of projects. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the process of procurement of boats
should be completed during 2013-14 as assured by the Ministry with enhanced allocation without
time and cost overrun. The Committee also recommends that other components of the Coastal
Security Scheme such as construction/procurement of coastal Police stations, jetties, Marine Police
Operation Centres, large vessels, Rigid Inflatable Boats, four wheelers and motor cycles should be
completed at the earliest as any delay could further delay the putting in place of Coastal Security
Scheme. The Committee is of the view that Phase-II of the Coastal Security Scheme must be
implemented within set time frame to avoid any further delay in ensuring the safety of the long
stretch of India’ s coast.
(Para 3.12.10 ibid)
Action Taken
1.6.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs is expediting the procurement of boats under Phase-II of
Coastal Security Scheme, and boats would be delivered soon to the coastal States/UTs for
enhancing the surveillance and patrolling.
1.6.3 The construction work for Coastal Police Stations, Jetties and Marine Police Operations
Centres and procurement of four-wheelers and two-wheelers is being done by Coastal States/UTs.
They have been requested to expedite the construction work and procurement of vehicle and
complete the same within stipulated time. Necessary funds for the same has already been released
to Coastal States/UTs.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.6.4 The Committee recommends that there should not be any delay in construction of
Coastal Police Stations etc. and procurement of vehicles. The Ministry may take it up with
the states.
Recommendation
1.6.5 The Committee appreciates that some coastal states are considering to raise specific cadre
for Coastal Security. The Union Home Ministry should take this idea further. The Committee feels
that coastal States should be motivated and provided possible help to set up separate cadre for
coastal police and till such arrangements are made, it is advisable that the local State Police
personnel should be deployed for Coastal Policing with proper training.
(Para 3.12.11 ibid)

13
Action Taken
1.6.6 The proposal for raising of Special Marine Police Battalion on the pattern of Indian Reserve
Battalion is under examination in MHA. The deployment of manpower in the Coastal Police Stations
and for manning the boats is being done by Coastal States/UTs. At present, the training
requirements of the State Marine Police is being met by the Indian Coast Guard. Coastal States/
UTs have also recruited some ex-Navy and Coast Guard personnel for manning the boats.
Recommendation
1.6.7 The Committee feels that all the sensitive coastal areas of the country should be fortified
to check smuggling, crime, infiltration, terrorism, which are serious threats to the nation. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Navy which is responsible for overall maritime
security including coastal security and offshore security should work in close coordination with
State Police and Coastal Police to ensure safety and security to the coast of the country.
(Para 3.12.12 ibid)
Action Taken
1.6.8 A three tier Coastal security ring all along our coast is provided by Marine Police, Indian
Coast Guard and Indian Navy. Government has initiated several measures to strengthen Coastal
Security, which includes improving surveillance mechanism and enhanced patrolling by following an
integrated approach. Joint Operational Exercises are conducted on regular basis among Navy, Coast
Guard, Coastal Police, Customs and others to check the effectiveness of this approach adopted for
security of coastal areas including island territories. Further, continuous review and monitoring of
various mechanisms have been established by the Government at different levels, involving various
agencies, including the State/Union Territory authorities. The intelligence mechanism has also been
streamlined through the creation of Joint Operation Centres and multi-agency coordination
mechanism. Installation of radars covering the country’s entire coastline and islands is also an
essential part of this process. Issue of biometric identity card to coastal population including
fishermen and registration of all type boats/vessels plying in Indian water are the other steps taken
by the Govt. to strengthen Coastal Security.
1.7 BORDER MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
1.7.1 The Committee observes that the main objective of effective border management is to secure
the country from ulterior motives of enemy countries such as illegal migration, infiltration,
smuggling etc. while facilitating legitimate trade and commerce across the border. The Committee
believes that Border Roads in good condition would help in better Border Management. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that construction of roads on Indo-Nepal Border, Indo-
Bangladesh Border and Indo-Bhutan Border should be completed in a time bound manner as per
desired specifications. The Committee also notes that Ministry is contemplating to set up a separate
construction organization under its ambit. Such proposal would reduce delay in achievement of
physical and financial targets. The Committee recommends that this proposal may be pursued in the
right earnest with sufficient technical expertise and staff strength.
(Para 3.14.19 ibid)
Action Taken
1.7.2 Construction of 313 Kilometers road along Indo-Bhutan Border with an outlay of 
R 1259
crores has been approved by CCS. TC&HLEC has approved the DPR for 61.8 Kilometer road with

14
an estimated cost of R 293.76 crores. Efforts are being made to persuade the State Govt. of Assam
to bear the cost of land acquisition and statutory clearances.
1.7.3 Construction of 1377 Kilometers road along Indo-Nepal Boder with an outlay of R 3853
crores has been approved by CCS. The project is scheduled to be completed by five years w.e.f.
2011-12. The State Govrnment of U.P., Bihar and Uttarakhand have been persuaded for timely
completion of the border roads in scheduled period as per specification. The construction of the
border roads has already been started.
1.7.4 Out of sanctioned length of 1540.72 km. of border roads, work to the extent of 947.60 km
of roads has been completed along Indo-Bangladesh Border. The balance works are under progress
and are likely to be completed in the given time-frame. Maintenance of roads along IBB is looked
after by CPWD and funds are released to the agency for maintenance and repair works of the said
border roads .This would facilitate better border domination by the Border Security Force (BSF).
1.7.5 The proposal of setting up a separate construction organization by MHA is already under
process in MHA. Moreover action has already been initiated to incorporate the proposal of setting
up the separate construction organization by MHA in the Draft Border Infrastructure (Development)
Bill, 2013 which is also under process in MHA.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.7.6 The Committee notes the reply and would like to be apprised of the progress of
construction of roads along the borders which India is sharing with its neighbours.
Recommendation
1.7.7 The Committee expresses serious concern over infiltration attempts made from across the
border particularly across the Line of Control. The Committee recommends that security mechanism

1.8 CYBER CRIMES AND SECURITY
Recommendation
1.8.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that though the Ministry of Home Affairs, has the prime
responsibility for internal security concerns but it has little role in combating cyber threat. The
Committee observes that cyber attacks have emerged as a new but serious threat to the country and
the Government should pay serious attention to it. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should evolve an institutionalised mechanism to deal with this kind of new age threat
and make our cyber security mechanism effective to prevent sabotage, espionage and other forms of
cyber threats. The Government should explore possibility to evolve a National Cyber Security
Architecture involving all the intelligence agencies of Central as well as State Governments. Cyber
attacks can be launched from distant corner of the world with the click of the mouse, hence can’t
be tackled by individual level. The Committee, therefore, recommends that India should go into
bilateral or multi-lateral negotiations with other countries to counter the threat of cyber terrorism.
In preventing cyber threats, Ministry of Home Affairs should play an important role.
(Para 3.15.2 ibid)
Action Taken
1.8.2 In order to have a National Cyber Security Architecture to deal with cyber threat, a
proposal is under consideration of the Government. The proposed cyber-security architecture
envisages a multi-layered approach for ensuring defense in-depth and will allocate the responsibility
for overall cyber security amongst different organizations.
● Bilateral multi-lateral negotiations with other countries
(I) In order to deal with cyber security issue, in the Homeland Security Dialogue
(HSD) between India and USA, one Sub group led by MHA has been constituted
on cyber security and critical infrastructure protection.
(II) EU-India Consultation on Cyber security and Cybercrime is initiated and led by
MEA.
(III) Discussion with some other countries like Israel, Russia and Spain on combating
crime is also initiated by MEA.
1.9 FAKE INDIAN CURRENCY NOTES (FICN)
Recommendation
1.9.1 The Committee understands that the Central Government in close coordination with concerned
State Governments must try to check the challenge of this new economic security threat and affected
States should be motivated and persuaded to step up their drive against FICNs. The Home Ministry
should impress upon the Finance Ministry to make it mandatory for banks operating in a particular
area to evolve a mechanism of a nodal officer to deal with this threat who would report the seizures
of the FICNs to concerned authorities. The Committee also feels that circulation of FICNs is a form
of economic terrorism and the Government must make all efforts to neutralize it.
(Para 3.16.2 ibid)
Action Taken
1.9.2 To address the multi-dimensional aspects of the FICN menace, several agencies such as the

17
RBI, the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Home Affairs, Security and intelligence of the Centre and
State, CBI are working in tandem to check the inflow of fake Indian currency notes.
1.9.3 The legal regime has been further strengthened by way of recent amendments in the
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 wherein the damage to the monetary stability of India
by way of production or smuggling or circulation of High Quality Fake Indian Paper Currency,
Coin or any other material has been declared as ‘terrorist act’.
1.9.4 Further, one special FICN co-ordination Group has been formed in MHA to share the
intelligence/ information amongst the different security agencies of State/ Center to counter the
menace of circulation of Fake currency notes in the country. IB, CBI, NIA, R&AW and DRI
continuously share operational intelligence to neutralize FICN smugglers.
1.9.5 NIA has been empowered by NIA Act to investigate and prosecute offences relating to
FICN. The Government has also constituted a Terror Funding and Fake Currency Cell in NIA to
focus investigation on Terror Funding and Fake currency cases.
1.9.6 The security features in the High Value currency notes are being constantly upgraded by the
Ministry of Finance/ RBI which has also strengthened the mechanism for detection of counterfeit
notes by the Banks.
1.9.7 In order to counter the menace of FICN, efforts have been made to raise the issue at
multilateral and bilateral fora. The JWGs with Nepal and Bangladesh have made special provision
for the operation cooperation of security agencies on the interdiction of FICN smugglers and
contraband. A Joint Task Force with the Government of Bangladesh has also been constituted to
monitor cases of smuggling and circulation of FICN. The Task Force shall monitor the
investigation of FICN cases filed with State Police and shall ensure filing of charge sheet in such
matters expeditiously. It will also monitor the source of original abroad and its delivery and modus
operandi for further circulation in India.
1.9.8 The Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all States/UTs have been requested that a police
station in each district Police Headquarters may be designated as the nodal Police Station wherein
the offences relating to FICN recovered by Banks can be reported. The Banks will also
correspondingly designate a nodal officer in each of the Districts in their respective Banks who will
be vested with the responsibility of reporting the seizures of the FICN in the said District. RBI
has also been requested to designate a nodal officer in each district for lodging FIR in such nodal
Police Station.

1.19 OCCUPATIONAL STRESS IN PARAMILITARY FORCES
Recommendation
1.19.1 The Committee understands that long years of postings of para-military forces personnel in
difficult areas distant from their permanent residence, long working hours, sleep deprivation, denial
of leave, lack of healthcare facilities, delay in promotions, poor quality uniforms, lack of clarity
in order etc. are the many reasons responsible for stress amongst them and are also forcing them
to quit the paramilitary forces. The Government should address the stress issue very seriously. The
immediate superiors should be regularly in touch and gauge the behavior and attitude and any
abnormality should be immediately attended to. The Committee recommends that the findings/
recommendations of the Report submitted by IIM, Ahmedabad should be implemented by the
Government in letter and spirit.
(Para 4.13.2 ibid)
Action Taken
1.19.2 IIM, Ahmadabad’s Report is under examination. A presentation is scheduled to be made by
Professor Dheeraj Sharma, IIM, Ahmadabad, on the subject. However, CAPFs are already taking
care to address the majority of issues due to which stress level could be minimized. All possible
measures are being taken to reduce occupational stress and the some of the major steps are :-
(i) Implementing a transparent, rational and fair leave policy;
(ii) Grant of leave to the Force personnel to attend to their urgent domestic problems/
issues/needs;
(iii) Regular interaction, both formal and informal, among Commanders, officers and
troops to find out and address their problems;
(iv) Revamping of grievances redressal machinery;
(v) Regulating duty hours to ensure adequate rest and relief;
(vi) Improving living conditions through provision of basic amenities/ facilities for troops
and their families;
(vii) Motivating the forces through increased risk, hardship and other allowances;
(viii) Provision of STD telephone facilities to the troops to facilitate being in touch with
their family members and to reduce tension in the remote locations;
(ix) Better medical facilities for troops and their families including introduction of
Composite Hospitals with specialized facilities;
(x) Organising talks by doctors and other specialists to address their personal and
psychological concerns;
(xi) Yoga and meditation classes for better stress management;
(xii) Recreational and sports facilities and provision of team games and sports etc;

26
(xiii) Providing welfare measures like Central Police canteen facility to the troops and their
families, scholarships to their wards, etc.;
(xiv) Giving status of ex-CAPF personnel to the retired personnel of CAPF, which is
expected to boost the morale of the existing CAPFs personnel and also expected to
provide better identity, community recognition and thus higher esteem and pride in the
society to the Ex-CAPF personnel.
1.20 COORDINATION BETWEEN STATE AND PARA-MILITARY FORCES
Recommendation
1.20.1 Para-military Forces happen to be unaware of the terrain where they are deployed,
therefore, they deserve much cooperation and support from local police. They are after all there
to assist State police force only. The Committee recommends the Government to impress upon the
State/UT Governments for ensuring better co-ordination between the para-military forces and the
State-Police Forces. The Committee also recommends that mechanism of Unified Command should
be reviewed from time to time to ensure better coordination.
(Para 4.14.4 ibid)
Action Taken
1.20.2 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State subjects, action with respect to maintenance of law
and order lies primarily in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with the
various issues related to Left Wing Extremist (LWE) activities in the States. The Central
Government monitors the situation closely and supplements and coordinates their efforts in several
ways, inter-alia, including providing Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) to assist the State
Police Forces to deal with the LWE problem. The deployment and operational strategy of security
forces for Anti-naxal operations is devised jointly by the State Police and the CAPF concerned. The
issue of improving the co-ordination between the State Police Forces and the CAPFs is emphasized
by the MHA regularly.
1.20.3 The most adversely LWE affected States of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha and West
Bengal have constituted a Unified Command to carry out carefully planned Anti-naxal operations.
The MHA has requested the State Governments concerned to hold the meetings of the Unified
Command at least once in every month to facilitate fine-tuning of the Anti-naxal operations. The
Union Home Minister has also written to the Chief Ministers of these States to consider chairing
the meetings of the Unified Command at his/her level and to ensure holding of these meetings at
least once in a quarter.
1.21 HOME GUARDS
Recommendation
1.21.1 The Committee is aware of the fact that Home Guards are governed by the Home Guard
Acts and Rules of their respective States/Union Territories. However, the Ministry of Home Affairs
should impress upon the State/UT Governments to improve the working conditions of the Home
Guards. They do not get fixed remuneration as they are paid pocket expenses when they are called
for duty which makes their life miserable. The Committee recommends that Government should
consider to make service-conditions of Home Guards more lucrative and sustaining as the job
description of Home Guards, even if voluntary, demands better remuneration and facilities. In all
the States, there are a large number of vacancies in the State Police Forces. Until the vacancies
are filled, Home Guards services may be used to the maximum extent.
(Para 5.7 ibid)

27
Action Taken
1.21.2 A Director General of Police is the Commandant General of Home Guards in the State. He
is assisted by Addl. Director General of Police/Addl. Commandant General and Inspector General
of Police/Deputy Commandant General. These officers in the State Home Guards Head Quarters are
drawn from Indian Police Service cadre. There are also Deputy Inspector General/Deputy
Commandant General and Assistant Commandant General/Divisional Commandant level officers
from Home Guards Officers cadre posted in the State Head Quarters to assist the Commandant
General. Divisional Commandant/Asstt. Commandant General head the organization at the district
level. District Commandants reporting to the District Magistrate supervise the organization at the
district level.
1.21.3 The primary role of Home Guards is to serve as an auxiliary to the Police in maintenance
of law and order and internal security, help the community in any kind of emergency such as air-
raid, fire, cyclone, earthquake, epidemic etc., help in maintenance of essential services, promote
communal harmony and assist the administration in protecting weaker sections, participate in socio-
economic and welfare activities and perform civil defence duties. They render valuable assistance
to police in regulation of traffic, crowd control maintenance of internal security, communal
harmony etc.
1.21.4 W ith a view to make Home Guards an effective force, they are trained in various police
crafts like regular drill, map reading, security, intelligence collection, law and order maintenance,
rifle/pistol/automatic gun handling, traffic duty, disaster management, fire fighting, first-aid
leadership etc. at State level Home Guards Training Institutes.
1.21.5 An advisory is being issued through DG(NDRF and CD) to all the States/UTs for better
service conditions of Home Guards.

Recommendation
1.22.1 The Committee notes the Ministry’ s submission that Mainstreaming Civil Defence in disaster
risk reduction with a total outlay of 
R600 crore has been proposed to be implemented during 12th
Plan period for which Planning Commission has given in-principle approval and draft EFC note
is being finalized in consultation with Integrated Finance Division of MHA. The Committee

should be taken in this regard. Civil Defence set up should also be closely linked with Disaster

Action Taken

R 65.22 crore at R.E. stage in 2012-13 has been kept for two plan schemes viz. revamping

st March, 2013. Two new schemes viz.
mainstreaming Civil Defence in disaster risk reduction with a total outlay of R 300 crore and

28
time to get final approval of the competent authority for these two new schemes, a token provision

1.24 DISASTER MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
1.24.1 The Committee is aware of the fact that India is vulnerable to many natural and man-made
disasters due to geo climatic conditions and terrorism and extremism. The Committee is of the view
that the main objective of any disaster management project should be disaster mitigation alongwith
minimizing the loss of lives and property. The Committee understands the need for further disaster
preparedness at the grass root level.
(Para 5.12.9 ibid)
Action Taken
1.24.2 MHA has initiated various mitigation projects with the objective to minimize risks caused by
various disasters. Some of the mitigation projects initiated are:
(1) National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) (Phase-I): The main aim and
objective of this project is to strengthen the structural and non-structural cyclone
mitigation efforts, to reduce the cyclone risk and vulnerability in the coastal districts
prone to cyclones and in building capacities for cyclone risk mitigation therein. The
government has approved the implementation of Phase-I of the Centrally Sponsored
Scheme of National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) for Andhra Pradesh and
Odisha at a cost of 
R 1496.71 crore. The project is being implemented by National
Disaster Management Authority.
(2) National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project (NERMP): The objective of NERMP is to
enhance the preparedness to face earthquakes and to reduce the losses to lives and
property caused by earthquakes. This project was approved at a total cost of  R24.87
crore to be implemented by National Disaster Management Authority on 5th April,
2013.
(3) National School Safety Project: The project was sanctioned on 21st June, 2011 with
a view to promote awareness and education activities, demonstrating disaster risk
management, training and capacity building and assessing vulnerability and taking
mitigation measures. The total estimated cost of this project is 
R 48.47 crore.
Recommendation
1.24.3 The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should impress upon the State/UT
Governments to raise separately, specialized Disaster Response Force, instead of using existing
force during the disasters as only specialized Disaster Response Force can exert the suitable
response to tackle disaster.
(Para 5.12.12 ibid)
Action Taken
1.24.4 MHA impress upon the State/UT Governments at various occasions to raise their State
Disaster Response Force for providing response to the States/UTs. At present 15 States i.e.
Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram, Tripura, Assam, J&K, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Tamilnadu,
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala, Rajasthan, Odisha and Uttarakhand have been raised their SDRF.

31
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.24.5 The Committee notes the reply and desires that remaining States may be persuaded
to raise SDRF.
Recommendation
1.24.6  The Committee notes that the Government is implementing National Emergency
Communication Plan (NECP) Phase-II since 2011-12. The Committee also notes that the provision
of 96.03 crores is sufficient for the year 2013-14, subject to the condition that after approval of
NDRF infrastructure, more funds would be required. The Committee recommends that fund

Action Taken

R 76.789 crore. A
provision of R 25.00 crore has been kept for the financial year 2013-14 and it is expected that the

Recommendation

building complex. Since, Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has allotted land, the Committee

(Para 5.12.14 ibid)
Action Taken
